description: The Tauri IPC surface for StackVo Desktop — contract v1. Derived 1:1 from the Express routes in core/ui/server/routes/ and the Socket.io events in core/ui/server/, plus the commands the desktop app needs that no HTTP endpoint ever provided. This file is the agreement between the Vue front end and the Rust core; both sides are generated/checked against it.

conventions.naming: snake_case, <domain>_<verb>. The same string is the Rust #[tauri::command] fn name and the JS invoke() key.

envelope.before: Express returned { success, data?, message?, meta? } and the axios interceptor unwrapped .data — a 200 with success:false was treated as an error.
envelope.after: Tauri commands return Result<T, StackvoError>. Ok(T) is the payload directly (no envelope). Err(e) rejects the invoke() promise. The success:false-with-HTTP-200 ambiguity disappears.
envelope.migration: client/src/lib/api.js is the ONLY file that changes: its interceptor logic becomes a thin invoke() wrapper that re-throws StackvoError as an Error with .code and .hint attached. Pinia stores are untouched.

conventions.argCasing: Rust params are snake_case; Tauri auto-converts camelCase from JS. Send snake_case explicitly to avoid ambiguity.
conventions.longRunning: Any operation that can exceed ~2s (build, compose up, image pull) MUST NOT block on its return value. It returns an OperationId immediately and reports progress via events. This replaces the 600s nginx proxy timeout hack.
conventions.idempotency: start/stop/restart on an already-in-that-state container succeed silently (matches current DockerService behaviour).

shape.hintKey: string? — set when the hint came from the catalogue in src-tauri/src/hints.rs. The frontend renders errorHints.<hintKey> from its locale and falls back to `hint` when the key is absent or untranslated; `hint` always carries the English, which is what the log and the MCP surface get. src-tauri/tests/hint_translations.rs fails the build if a catalogued hint has no translation in en.js or tr.js.

codes.BUILD_FAILED: Docker build returned non-zero. `details.log_path` points at logs/build/<service>.log.
codes.CONFLICT: Port or domain already claimed by another project.
codes.ENGINE_UNREACHABLE: Docker daemon not running or socket/pipe not accessible. Replaces the ECONNREFUSED stack spam that isDockerUnreachable() papered over. The UI MUST offer engine_start().
codes.FORBIDDEN: An administrator's policy file forbids this — today, writing a `.env` key listed in its `locked` array. Deliberately distinct from PERMISSION_DENIED, which means the OS refused and can be answered by elevating: this one can never be, so the UI MUST NOT offer a retry. `details.keys` names the settings and `details.source` the policy file, which is the only thing the user can act on. See src-tauri/src/policy.rs.
codes.GENERATE_FAILED: The generator ran and failed. `details.log` carries stderr.
codes.INVALID_INPUT: Failed schema validation. `details` carries the field path.
codes.INVALID_MANIFEST: stackvo.json exists but violates project.schema.json. `details.path` names the offending key.
codes.NETWORK_ERROR: A host this app had to reach did not answer, or answered badly — the package registry over HTTPS is the only source of this today. Deliberately NOT ENGINE_UNREACHABLE, whose whole point is that the UI offers engine_start(): nothing can be started to fix this one, so a UI offering the same button would be offering the wrong thing. The message always names the URL, because the address is the only thing the person at the keyboard can act on.
codes.NOT_FOUND: Container, project or service does not exist.
codes.NO_WORKSPACE: No StackVo directory is selected, or the selected one no longer looks like a StackVo checkout. Desktop-only: the web UI could never hit this because it was mounted inside the repo it managed. The UI MUST offer workspace_pick().
codes.UNSUPPORTED: Requested runtime/extension/server/platform feature has no implementation in v1 (e.g. runtime=python, extension=pdo_oci, external terminal off macOS).

errors.policy: No error message may contain a raw shell command line or a value matching the secret redaction regex from env.schema.json.

agents_install.why: Writes the `stackvo` MCP entry into one client's configuration file, so registering the server is a click rather than hand-edited JSON. Returns the path written.
agents_install.notes: Reads the file, inserts one key and writes it back — never renders from a template, so every other server and every unknown key survives. Takes a `.stackvo-backup` beside the file first, and writes atomically. The three arguments after `client` are one grant and are rendered by `grant::Grant::to_args`, so the flags in the file and the authority the server enforces are the same sentence. `allowWrites` alone is still all twelve writing tools, `stack_down` among them; `projects` bounds the registration to those projects, which removes every writing tool a project cannot bound (twelve become four) and hides the other projects from the reads as well; `minutes` ends the writing half that long after each start of the server. All three are passed from the UI and default to off, every project and no limit — the server's own defaults. Writes `STACKVO_ROOT` into the entry's env when a workspace is selected. Errors: NOT_FOUND when stackvo-mcp is not on this machine, INVALID_INPUT for an unknown client or a file that is not plain JSON, CONFLICT when the servers key holds something that is not an object. Audited as `agent_install`, with the grant in the detail. Codex is TOML and is edited with toml_edit so comments, key order and quoting survive; the JSON clients keep their own indentation and key order for the same reason. Zed's path is not documented by Zed and differs between ~/.config/zed and ~/Library/Application Support/Zed, so both are looked for and whichever exists is written.

agents_remove.why: The way back out. A registration that can only be added is one people avoid adding.
agents_remove.notes: Removes only the `stackvo` entry; an empty `mcpServers` left behind is not tidied away, because that would be this app deciding something about a file it does not own. Removing what is not there succeeds, so a second click is not an error. Audited as `agent_remove`.

agents_status.returns: { binary: string | null, source: 'sibling' | 'build' | 'path' | null, root: string | null, clients: Array<{ id: string, label: string, path: string, present: boolean, exists: boolean, parseable: boolean, command: string | null, current: boolean }> }
agents_status.why: The README asked the reader to find their assistant's configuration file, work out its shape and paste a JSON block into it with a path they had to supply themselves. Every rival with an MCP server installs itself. This is the read half: which clients are on this machine, which already point at the server, and whether the binary exists to point at.
agents_status.notes: Reads only, and works with no workspace selected — the answer is about the machine, not the stack, and hiding the pane until a folder is chosen would hide it exactly during setup. `binary` is null when stackvo-mcp cannot be found, and then agents_install refuses rather than registering a path that does not exist; `source` says which copy was found. `parseable` false means the file cannot be edited by its own parser — JSON with comments (VS Code's format), or TOML that is halfway through being edited — which is reported rather than rewritten, because stripping comments would delete the user's own notes. Eight clients: six JSON, plus Codex whose file is TOML and Zed whose map is called `context_servers`. IMPLEMENTORS: a client's file MUST come back in its own shape — key order and indentation included. Measured against real files with examples/agent_config_probe.rs, which round-trips an install and an uninstall and compares byte for byte. See src-tauri/src/agents.rs.

app_log_open.why: Follows one of those files. Shares the event pair with container_logs_open because the viewer renders one kind of line; a second pair would have meant a second frontend listener free to drift from the first. Closed with container_logs_close — one registry of abort handles, one way to stop a stream.
app_log_open.notes: `id` is an opaque `app:` or `server:` handle from app_logs, never a path. Paths do not cross the boundary in either direction: a log viewer that accepts an absolute path from its own frontend is a file reader for the whole disk. The id's components are checked for traversal before the filesystem is touched, and the resolved path is checked against its root again afterwards, because a symlink inside the project can escape with no `..` in sight. Polled twice a second rather than watched — a notification still only says that something changed, so the read-the-delta path exists either way. A file shorter than the reader's offset was truncated or rotated (`> laravel.log`, or a daily channel rolling over) and restarts from the top instead of going silent for ever.

app_logs.why: The container stream carries stdout and stderr, which is what the entrypoint and the web server say — not what the application records. A Laravel exception goes to storage/logs/laravel.log, an nginx 502 to the mounted error.log, and a queue worker that died to its own file under supervisord. None of those reach stdout, so none of them were visible anywhere in the app.
app_logs.notes: Reads the host filesystem, not the container: the generated compose mounts projects/<name> at /var/www/html and logs/projects/<name> at /var/log, so both roots are already there. No engine required — which is the point, because a container that crashed on boot is exactly when its log is worth reading and exactly when there is nothing left to exec into. Discovery recurses, because Laravel channels nest (storage/logs/parser/parser-2026-07-28.log is a real path from the checkout this was built against), and is capped at depth 3 and 60 files so a stray node_modules cannot turn it into a full-disk walk.

app_logs_all.why: The per-project viewer answers "what did this project write". It cannot answer "which of my eight projects just errored", which is the question you have when you do not yet know where to look. Herd sells the cross-project view as a Pro feature.
app_logs_all.notes: A project is a directory under projects/ holding a stackvo.json — an unadopted checkout is somebody's folder, not something this app follows. No engine is consulted anywhere on this path, so with Docker stopped this is the one list in the app that is still complete.

app_logs_all_open.why: One live tail across every project, so an error surfaces without first guessing which project to open.
app_logs_all_open.returnsNote: Returns the first scan's coverage rather than emitting it. An event would race the caller — the spawned task can emit before the frontend holds the stream id it filters events by, and the coverage line would then stay blank until the next rediscovery thirty seconds later. logs:sources carries updates only, because only an update has somewhere to arrive.
app_logs_all_open.notes: **Live only, with no history — a decision, not an omission.** Nothing in this module parses a timestamp (Laravel, nginx and supervisord do not agree on a format), so the only chronology available across sixty files is the order bytes arrive in: real for new output, invented for old. Each file is therefore adopted at its current end and only what follows is shown; history stays in app_log_open, which reads one file and can honestly show all of it. Rediscovery every 30s is the other half — a daily channel rolls over into a filename that did not exist when the tail started, so a fixed file set would go quiet exactly at midnight. Files found by a later scan are adopted at offset zero, because everything in a file that new was written while the tail was already watching. Capped at 60 files, newest first, with what was dropped reported through logs:sources rather than trimmed silently. Closed with container_logs_close — one registry of abort handles, one way to stop a stream.

apps_available.returns: { terminals: App[], editors: App[], browsers: App[] }
apps_available.notes: Terminals, editors and browsers present on this machine, each with { id, name, icon, available, default }. Entries that are not installed are returned with available:false rather than omitted, so the picker can grey them out — a list that silently drops them reads as lack of support. At most one entry per list carries default:true — the one that would be used when the preference is unset, which is the first installed entry for terminals and editors and the system-default entry for browsers. Without it the picker was blank on a fresh install while the app happily opened *some* terminal.

bootstrap_complete.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
bootstrap_complete.notes: Writes the marker that makes workspace_get report bootstrapped:true. Called by the first-run screen after its last step, so a run that failed or was skipped is offered again next launch.

catalog_get.v1Change: Served from the bundled contracts (php-extensions.json + env.schema.json), no longer re-parsed out of .env on every request. Runtimes without generators are marked available:false rather than silently offered.

cert_apply.why: Reissues the wildcard certificate for the domains the projects actually have, and — when the CA is not trusted yet — installs it. Without this the certificate goes stale the moment a project is created, and on Linux and Windows the CA is never trusted at all: the Bash helper's trust step returns early on anything but macOS, so those users get a browser warning and no explanation.
cert_apply.notes: Trust installation delegates to `mkcert -install` rather than reimplementing four trust stores (macOS keychain, Linux ca-certificates, NSS for Firefox and Chrome, Windows Root). mkcert may need a password for the system store; on Linux it shells out to sudo, which a GUI process has no terminal for. That failure MUST be reported with the exact command to run, not swallowed — a CA that silently failed to install looks identical to one that worked until the browser disagrees. Issuing the certificate itself writes only inside the workspace and never elevates.

cert_plan.why: Same order as hosts_plan: say what would change before doing it. Reissuing replaces the file Traefik is serving, and `installCa` can touch the system trust store, so neither should be the first thing the user learns about it.
cert_plan.notes: `domains` is the exact argument list mkcert would be invoked with — the same value cert_apply uses, not a second computation that could differ.

cert_status.why: HTTPS was already working and entirely invisible. `core/cli/utils/generate-ssl-certs.sh` issues an mkcert wildcard covering stackvo.loc and every project domain, and traefik.sh installs it as the default certificate — but nothing in the app could say whether mkcert was installed, whether the CA was trusted, whether the certificate had expired, or which domains it actually covered. A user whose new project shows a browser warning had no way to learn why.
cert_status.notes: Reads only: it never runs mkcert and never writes. The SAN list and expiry are parsed out of the certificate itself rather than inferred from the project list, because the file on disk is what the browser validates against — a list of what SHOULD be covered would agree with the certificate right up until it mattered. `trust` reports where the CA is trusted store by store — see the type. It is the measured answer to what the category's leader has published as "exploring real certificates instead of the mkcert CA": the problem a public certificate solves here is not that a local root is inferior, it is that the root is not trusted everywhere and nothing said where. Firefox is asked with `certutil` against the first profile that has an NSS database; one profile is enough, because mkcert installs into every profile it finds in one pass.

cert_trust_in_terminal.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
cert_trust_in_terminal.notes: Opens the user's terminal running `sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain <ca>` — the write mkcert itself performs, without mkcert's pre-check, which reports the CA already installed whenever it is merely present in a keychain. macOS grants the authorization only interactively, so sudo needs a terminal to ask in.

compose_down.why: `stackvo down` existed only in the CLI — the web UI could never stop the stack, because doing so would have killed the UI itself.

container_logs_open.why: Log following existed only as `stackvo logs` in the CLI. The UI had no way to tail a container.

container_stats_history.notes: Sampler runs at 60s (startStatsSampler). v1 MUST persist history across app restarts — today it lives in memory and dies with the container.

projects_build_all.returns: { operationId: string, built: string[], failed: string[] }
projects_build_all.why: The app bar carries start-all, stop-all and restart-all, and rebuilding had no stack-wide half at all — project_build is per project. Changing a PHP version, a base image or a generator template is a change to EVERY project's Dockerfile, and doing that twenty times by hand is the loop this closes.
projects_build_all.notes: NOT one `docker compose build`. A bare one is a single process and one broken Dockerfile ends it, leaving the projects behind it unbuilt with nothing on screen saying which those were — the failure generator::render already answered for a broken manifest: report the one that fell and carry on. So the builds are SEQUENTIAL, each its own `docker compose build <name>`, and `failed` NAMES every project that did rather than counting them ("two failed" sends somebody to look at twenty projects; naming them sends them to two). Compose caches layers between them, so an unchanged project is seconds. ONE operation in the console rather than one per project — it is one press and one thing to watch — and ONE generate at the start, because `generate` writes every project's Dockerfile in a single pass. `noCache` defaults to FALSE and that is the decision: "rebuild" and "pull every layer again from scratch" are different jobs and the second takes minutes per project, so the flag is for somebody who means it. Takes the `stack` inflight lock, the same subject containers_start_all / stop_all / restart_all hold — rebuilding while the stack is being restarted is two commands writing the same containers. The project list is read off disk rather than through projects_list, which asks the engine: a stopped daemon is a reason this button exists rather than a reason it cannot answer. Not audited: building an image is routine traffic, the bar audit.rs states.

db_dump.why: Lerd sells snapshots, Laragon sells automatic backups, ServBay sells both; StackVo had no way to take a copy of a database at all. The tools are already inside the container — `mysqldump`, `pg_dump` and `mongodump` ship with the images the stack runs.
db_dump.notes: Streams the dump straight from `docker exec` into the chosen file rather than buffering it: a production-sized database does not fit in a UI process's memory, and the failure would arrive as an out-of-memory kill with no explanation. The password is passed through the child's environment and named — not valued — on the docker command line, so it does not appear in `ps` output on a shared machine.

db_instances.why: A move names two instances, and `mysql-8-0` and `mysql-8-4` both answer to `mysql`.

db_move_apply.why: MUST re-check the plan rather than trusting the caller's — the plan crossed the IPC boundary and came back. MUST hold BOTH instances busy: a move reads one database and replaces another, and either being started or dumped underneath it is a torn result nobody could explain. Goes through a file rather than a pipe, and the file is KEPT on failure with its path in the error — at that moment it is the only copy of the source outside a container and the target is already replaced.

db_move_plan.why: Plan-then-apply, the same shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply, because the target is EMPTIED and that sentence has to be on screen before anybody presses anything. MUST touch no container.

db_restore.why: A backup nobody has restored is a file, not a backup.
db_restore.notes: DESTRUCTIVE: this replaces the contents of the target database. The UI MUST name the database and require confirmation before calling it. Reads the file into the container's stdin, the mirror of how the dump was written. `snapshotFirst` takes a copy of what is about to be replaced, into `before-restore-<stamp>` — its own reserved prefix rather than the scheduler's `auto-`, because `last_automatic` matches that one and a restore would otherwise push the next scheduled backup out by a full interval, and because `expired` prunes automatic copies against one window that a run of restores would empty. The safety copies get their own window instead — the last 3 per service, pruned when one is taken rather than by the scheduler, because the schedule defaults to off and a net that only tidies up when a feature nobody switched on runs is a disk that fills. A FAILURE TO TAKE IT STOPS THE RESTORE: the caller asked for a net, so doing the irreversible thing without one would answer a different question. It is a flag rather than always-on for the one case that would otherwise be trapped — a database too broken to dump is exactly the one somebody is restoring over.

db_snapshot_delete.why: Removes one copy. The way out of a directory that would otherwise only grow.
db_snapshot_delete.notes: Missing is success, so a second click is not an error. Deliberately not audited: this deletes a copy, and the act that has to be accounted for is the restore, which is.

db_snapshot_restore.why: Puts a named snapshot back, replacing what is in the database.
db_snapshot_restore.notes: The same restore db_restore performs, so it is audited as `db_restore` with the snapshot's path. NOT_FOUND when the file is gone — the listing is the filesystem, so a snapshot deleted outside the app is simply absent rather than a broken index entry. `snapshotFirst` is the same net `db_restore` offers and for the same reason: this is the path people actually use, so leaving it off here would have put the safety on the rarer of the two. It is taken AFTER the named snapshot is known to exist — a copy taken and then a failure because the thing being restored was never there is a net for nothing.

db_snapshot_take.why: Takes a named copy, into a path the app owns. Returns the operation id; progress and completion arrive on the same db:* events db_dump uses.
db_snapshot_take.notes: The name is refused rather than sanitised when it is not usable as a filename — silently turning `../escape` into something else gives back a snapshot under a name the user did not choose and will not find. `auto-` is reserved so nobody can create a snapshot the scheduler would later prune. An existing name is ALREADY_EXISTS, never an overwrite: a snapshot silently replaced is the copy somebody thought they still had. Serialised per service against db_dump and db_restore.

db_snapshots.returns: Array<{ service: string, name: string, path: string, bytes: number, takenAt: string, automatic: boolean }>
db_snapshots.why: `ddev snapshot` and `lerd db:snapshot` name a point in time and restore it by that name. db_dump could already write a file to a path chosen in a save dialog, which is raw material — a dump in Downloads is not something anybody comes back to.
db_snapshots.notes: The registry IS the directory: <root>/backups/<service>/, the name is the file stem, and takenAt is the file's modification time. No index file, because a second answer to 'what snapshots exist' drifts the first time somebody deletes one in Finder, and the recovery is a restore naming a file that is not there. Only files with the engine's own extension are listed. `automatic` marks the ones the schedule took — the only ones retention may remove. See src-tauri/src/snapshot.rs.

db_targets.why: Which database services can be dumped, what they are called, and whether they are running. The credentials were already read out of .env and rendered in the services list; what was missing was anything to do with them.
db_targets.notes: Reads .env and the engine. A service that is enabled but not running is still listed, with `running: false` — the reason a dump cannot start right now is worth showing next to the button that is disabled because of it.

debug_bridge_clear.notes: Removes the file rather than truncating it: the container may write as a different user, and a host process can always delete an entry from a directory it owns even when it cannot write the file.

debug_bridge_events.notes: A cursor, not a stream: the producer is a container appending newline-delimited JSON to a file, and there is nothing to subscribe to. Events are only appended, so everything past `since` is new and a missed poll costs nothing. A `since` past the end means the file was cleared or rotated underneath the caller, and the answer starts again rather than being empty for ever. Each Event carries { at, kind, label?, file?, line?, request?, sapi?, duration?, outcome?, value? } and `kind` is one of `dump`, `request` or `job`. A `dump` is a moment; a `request` is one execution with its status and how long it took, written from PHP's own shutdown hook so it appears for any framework and after a fatal; a `job` is one thing the queue finished with, folded into the same file by the host from the worker's own output — Laravel's queue events cannot be subscribed to from an auto_prepend_file, because Composer registers its autoloader in front of anything that file registers. IMPLEMENTORS: reading this also ingests the queue's half, but only while capture is on; a kind a build does not recognise must be SHOWN, not dropped.

debug_bridge_overview.returns: { project: string, enabled: boolean, mounted: boolean, running: boolean, events: number }[]
debug_bridge_overview.why: The per-project pane cannot answer "which of my eight projects just dumped something" — the question you have before you know which project to open. It is the same argument that made the log viewer a page, and it is what lets that page poll only the projects worth polling.
debug_bridge_overview.notes: One row per PHP project the bridge can serve; a Node project is not a place a dump can come from and is not listed. Reads files plus one container inspection each — no compose, no engine required for `enabled`, which is a file on the host and true whether or not Docker is running.

debug_bridge_set.why: Catching dumps used to cost a container recreate, because the mechanism was two environment variables and a container's environment is fixed at creation. Every debugging session started with a wait.
debug_bridge_set.notes: Creates or removes one file in a directory the container already has mounted. No compose command, no recreate, no worker cycle. The bridge re-reads the flag on every request AND inside every emit, so a long-running queue worker stops writing the moment it is switched off rather than at its next restart. The switch also drops the queue's cursor in both directions, so turning capture on never replays the hour before it.

args.name: string
args.command: string? (defaults to the detected npm script)

devserver_set.notes: State is `projects/<name>/.stackvo/devserver.json` — a file rather than a manifest key, because the manifest schema is additionalProperties:false and because a file under .stackvo/ is commit-friendly: a teammate's clone gets dev mode with everything else. Its existence is the switch; its contents are the command. Node only; a PHP project is refused, and the overlay renderer refuses again for a config file dropped in by hand, since /app does not exist there and mounting over it would replace the site with an empty directory. The overlay is layered LAST of the six compose files, because it is the only one that overrides rather than adds — anything after it would merge onto a service already in a different mode.

devserver_status.why: P2-15 was written as "proxy the Node dev server through Traefik with HMR", which sounds like a routing change. Reading node.sh against the other five server generators turns up something larger: **a node project has no bind mount at all**. nginx/caddy/apache/swoole/frankenphp all call generate_common_volumes; node.sh calls nothing, and its Dockerfile does `COPY . .` and `RUN npm install` at build time. The container holds a SNAPSHOT of the source. Hot reload was not misconfigured — it was structurally impossible, and no amount of WebSocket plumbing helps when there is nothing to reload.
devserver_status.notes: Three things have to be true at once, reported separately because they come apart and each has a different fix. (1) The source is live — a bind over /app plus an ANONYMOUS VOLUME on /app/node_modules, without which the bind shadows the install the image did for its own platform, or worse, exposes the host's macOS build of the same native packages. (2) The dev server is what is running — `npm run dev`, not the manifest's production start command. Both are the overlay's job. (3) The dev server accepts the request, and that one is in the USER'S repository. Read out of Vite's own source (hostValidationMiddleware, verified against the copy in this repo's node_modules): a Host header that is not localhost, not *.localhost, not an IP and not matched by server.allowedHosts gets a flat 403 — so a .loc domain presents as a site that is plainly up and returns 403, with nothing pointing at the dev server's config. The HMR client is the second half: StackVo's node router is websecure-only with tls=true, so the page loads over 443 while the dev server listens on 3000, and Vite's client would dial wss://domain:3000, which nothing routes, and degrade silently to full reloads. `snippet` is the exact config with the project's domain already in it. It is GENERATED, NEVER WRITTEN: silently rewriting somebody's build config is not a thing a local environment manager should do, and a snippet they paste is one they have read.

diagnostics_bundle.returns: { path: string, bytes: number, entries: Array<{ name: string, bytes: number, truncated: boolean }> }
diagnostics_bundle.why: Settings could open the log folder and nothing more, which leaves the reporter to find the right file among seven daily ones, know that the doctor output is separate, and remember the version and platform. One archive gets the maintainer the same set every time.
diagnostics_bundle.notes: path comes from the system save dialog, as mail_attachment_save's does — the front end names no destination this process did not receive from the user. Contents: about.txt, preflight.json, doctor.json, engine.json, the rotating log and any crash reports. Every log line is passed through logging::redact a second time on the way in, because a bundle built today may hold lines written by a build whose redaction rule was narrower. Logs are capped at 1 MiB each and `truncated` says which were cut. Nothing is read from .env and no project source is included. The archive also carries environment.json, the one file in it written to be read by a program rather than a person — flat, path-free and credential-free, so `diagnostics_compare` can hold two of them against each other.

args.path: string (a bundle, or the environment.json out of one)

diagnostics_compare.returns: { differences: Array<{ key: string, here?: string, there?: string }>, same: number, theirVersion?: string }
diagnostics_compare.why: "It works on my machine" is the oldest complaint in this category and every product in it answers that the container solves the problem — which it does not: the same compose file on two Docker versions is two different things. This app already packages the state of a machine; what it could not do was put two of them side by side.
diagnostics_compare.notes: Compares THEIR file with what this machine is right now, not with a stored copy of ourselves — the question is always what is different now. Their side is read first: a file that cannot be read is the answer, and there is no reason to walk this machine to find that out. The comparison is over `environment.json`, a flat fingerprint the bundle now carries — deliberately NOT over about.txt/doctor.json/preflight.json, which are shaped for a person to read and whose diff is mostly noise (a socket path, a pid, a byte count that moved). It holds no paths, because a home directory differs on every machine and would report two identical setups as different in five places, and no credentials or .env values, because the file is meant to be handed to a colleague. Only differences are returned and agreement is counted: a report that prints two hundred identical lines buries the four that matter. A key only one side states is a difference with a missing half — "you have redis-7-2 and they do not" is a different sentence from "you are on 7.2 and they are on 7.0". Accepts a whole zip or the extracted JSON, tried in that order rather than guessed by extension, because renaming a correct file must not make it unreadable. Errors: NOT_FOUND when the bundle predates environment.json — named rather than shrugged at — INVALID_INPUT for a file that is neither. Not audited: nothing is changed and nothing leaves the machine. See src-tauri/src/diagnostics.rs.

dns_check.why: dns_status reads files and sockets this app owns, which cannot answer the only question a user has: does THIS MACHINE resolve a name under the suffix. Reading back a resolver file proves a write happened. So this asks the responder over UDP and TCP, asks the machine through getaddrinfo, and asks whether public names still resolve — four answers because the repair for each is different.

dns_resolver_install.why: Writes /etc/resolver/<tld> with a password. Deliberately separate from dns_start, the same separation hosts_plan/hosts_apply has: one is a socket this app owns, the other changes how the whole machine resolves names, and folding them into one button would make a password prompt appear from something that reads like turning on a feature.

dns_resolver_remove.why: Turning it off has to be as easy as turning it on. MUST undo the reload as well as the file — a drop-in removed from a dnsmasq nobody told is a machine still asking a port that may be gone.

dns_start.why: Binds 127.0.0.1 on a high port — 53 needs root at every start and does not need to, because macOS resolver files take a `port` directive. MUST be idempotent for the same suffix and MUST restart for a different one: a responder left serving the old TLD answers for names nothing renders and refuses the ones it does.

dns_status.why: /etc/hosts needs a password per project and cannot express a wildcard at all, which is why the wildcard half was left undone.

dns_stop.why: Stops and waits for the thread, so the socket is actually free afterwards.

docker_disk_usage.why: docker_system_resources reports totals; the question a full disk raises is *which project*. Every StackVo container with its image size and writable layer, plus stack-built images whose container is gone — the bytes nobody remembers spending. No native-binary competitor can ship this at all.
docker_disk_usage.notes: imageDedicated separates images this stack built (stackvo-<name>, freed by removing the member) from shared upstream images (mysql:8.0, freed by nothing short of docker rmi). Sorted largest first.

docker_prune.why: SystemResources has reported reclaimable bytes since Phase 1 with no way to act on the number. Dangling images accumulate on every rebuild, and this app rebuilds a lot — every Xdebug toggle, every extension change.
docker_prune.notes: Images means dangling images only (the engine's default prune set — rebuildable by definition). Volumes are a separate flag because the engine's "unused" means "not currently mounted", and the database of a stopped project qualifies; the UI warns before passing volumes:true. buildCache is a level rather than a flag because its two useful values are different bargains: 'dangling' reclaims only records nothing references any more — what project_delete already does for itself after removing the project's image, since Docker offers no per-project handle on the cache (the filters are until/id/parent/type) — while 'all' also takes the layers every project image shares, because they all build from the same PHP base and the same extension installs. 'all' costs no data and costs every remaining project a full rebuild; the UI states that before passing it. Guarded by the 'prune' inflight subject.

doctor.why: The boot gate answers "can the app run"; this answers the failures that arrive later, one failed compose up at a time. The single most common one — a host port already taken — compose reports as "address already in use" with no word on by what. The doctor names the culprit: the stack's own container (fine), someone else's container (named), or a host process (named, with pid).
doctor.notes: Diagnosis only. Every repair stays behind its own command — preflight_fix, hosts_apply (behind its reviewed diff), generate_run, compose_up, docker_prune — so no confirmation flow is bypassed. Degrades honestly: no workspace ⇒ port and generated checks read unknown; engine down ⇒ space is null, port owners cannot be named, and core containers read unknown rather than failed. `core` lists the containers in the compose `core` profile (Traefik today), read from generated/stackvo.yml rather than from a name hardcoded in Rust, each with { service, container, state, exists, running, image }. `exists` is separate from `running` because compose down removes containers: "stopped" and "never created" arrive from different actions and want different repairs, and reporting both as not-running sent people looking for a stopped container that was not there.

doctor_drop_extension.why: The doctor's design rule is a repair next to every finding — hosts get the reviewed diff, stale output gets regenerate, disk gets prune. The extension check shipped without one, which left the panel naming a problem and offering nothing.
doctor_drop_extension.notes: **Removing the extension changes nothing about what runs, and that is the point.** The generator already drops one it cannot install — silently, which is the bug CONFLICTS.md C-06 records — so it is already absent from every built container. This does not remove a capability; it stops the manifest claiming one the container never had. No alternative is offered because the catalog leaves none: `imap` is `install: core` with `removedIn: 8.2` and no PECL package, so on 8.2+ there is nothing StackVo could install instead. If the project genuinely needs it the answer is an older PHP version, which is the project owner's decision and not a button. Writes through the paths the rest of the app uses — manifest::write for a project, env_writer for .env, which backs the file up and serialises against the other writers. Removing an extension that is already gone is a no-op rather than an error: the state the caller wanted is the state on disk.

editor_attach.why: The other half of ide_debug_*, which wires an IDE on the HOST to a debugger in the container; this opens the editor INSIDE it — language server, extensions, terminal, composer and artisan all in the image, with no PHP on the machine. VS Code has no attach-by-name command line, so the whole feature is an address: vscode-remote://attached-container+<hex>/<workdir>, where <hex> is the hex of {"containerName":"/stackvo-<project>"}. All three facts it is built from — the container name, the workdir and the bind mount — were already in this tree.
editor_attach.notes: Re-reads editor_status rather than trusting the screen: a container that stopped or lost its mount between the render and the click is refused with the reason, because a disabled button is not a check. NOT_FOUND when the container is not running or VS Code is not on this machine; UNSUPPORTED when the workdir is not a bind mount — an editor opened onto a snapshot saves happily and loses every line on the next rebuild, which is a refusal and not a warning. Two launch paths: `code --folder-uri` when the launcher is on PATH, and on macOS `open -a <bundle> vscode://vscode-remote/…` when only the application is installed — the URL handler is registered by the app itself, so it is the one that works on a machine where nobody ran Install 'code' command. Not audited: nothing is written, and the act is a window opening. See src-tauri/src/editor.rs.

editor_jetbrains_write.returns: string (the path written, which is what the user points PhpStorm at)
editor_jetbrains_write.why: The PhpStorm half (decision 0036). JetBrains has no attach-to-a-running-container connection type — Gateway offers SSH, WSL, Dev Containers and the cloud plugins, and that is not one of them. What PhpStorm does have, measured in the IDE rather than read off a page (PhpStorm 2026.2 bundles clouds-docker-gateway, whose own devcontainer schema carries the keys), is Dev Containers in the COMPOSE flavour. A dev container built from an image or a Dockerfile is a second container beside this project's; one that names StackVo's own compose files and this project's service IS the container already running.
editor_jetbrains_write.notes: Writes under `<root>/generated/devcontainer/<project>/devcontainer.json` and never into the project: the file names absolute paths under this user's home, so a committed copy would resolve to nothing on a teammate's machine — the opposite of project_devcontainer_write, whose whole point is to be committed. The compose file list is read out of runner::compose_base_args, so it is the same list every compose command this app runs uses, overlays included. Three fields each refuse a default that would be wrong here: `shutdownAction: none` (the compose default stopCompose would take the workspace down when the IDE closes), `overrideCommand: false` (the default replaces the service's command, which in a PHP project is the thing serving the site) and `runServices: [service]` (unspecified means every service in every file). What it cannot avoid is stated instead: the plugin's own advanced setting says the main service is always recreated, so attaching restarts this project's container. See src-tauri/src/editor.rs.

editor_status.returns: { project: string, editorInstalled: boolean, readiness: { container: string, workdir: string, serverDir: string, libc: 'glibc' | 'musl', running: boolean, sourceLive: boolean, serverKept: boolean, blockers: Array<'notRunning' | 'sourceIsASnapshot'>, caveats: Array<'musl' | 'serverIsNotKept'>, attachable: boolean, folderUri: string, handlerUrl: string }, jetbrains: { installed: boolean, path: string, exists: boolean, current: boolean, service: string, recreates: boolean, musl: boolean } }
editor_status.why: The question that had to be answered before the attach address was worth having: can this container carry an editor at all. Read from the container's own mount table rather than from the manifest, because the two can disagree — turning the dev server on writes an overlay and the overlay does nothing until the container is recreated, and when they disagree the container is the one that is right.
editor_status.notes: Reads only. `sourceLive` is the refusal: a bind mount AT the workdir, so neither the /var/log bind every PHP container carries nor a named volume at the workdir counts. A stopped container reports `notRunning` alone — deriving 'the source is a snapshot' from an empty mount list would be a refusal invented out of having asked nothing. `caveats` never refuse: `musl` is a note that this is an alpine image (VS Code publishes a musl server, JetBrains does not), and `serverIsNotKept` means the container predates the editor overlay's named volume and will re-download the server after every rebuild. `folderUri` and `handlerUrl` are derived on every read and never stored, so a renamed project cannot leave a stale address behind. `editorInstalled` is about the machine, not the project. `jetbrains` is the other editor's half and is a file rather than an address: `current: false` on an existing file means it names a compose list from before an overlay changed, which is worse than no file — see editor_jetbrains_write. `musl: true` is where the alpine caveat stops being a caveat: VS Code publishes a server built against musl and JetBrains publishes none, so the backend cannot start in that image at all. See src-tauri/src/editor.rs.

engine_start.why: Launch Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) or `systemctl --user start docker` (Linux). Resolves the chicken-and-egg problem end to end.
engine_start.notes: Best-effort. Returns Ok as soon as the launch is issued; the caller waits on engine:status_changed.

engine_status.why: There was NO endpoint for this. The web UI could not report a stopped Docker daemon because the UI itself was a container that could not start. This is the single most important new command — it is what makes the desktop app usable when Docker is down.
engine_status.polling: Called on startup and on a 5s timer while disconnected; emits engine:status_changed on transition.

env_defaults.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
env_defaults.notes: The values compiled into the binary. Carries no secret and needs no workspace: it describes the app, not a checkout. The settings form uses it to mark a value as a default and to offer going back to one.

env_get.notes: MUST redact secret-matching keys unless `reveal: true` is passed and the user has confirmed in-session.

env_set.why: Settings.vue is a 24-line stub because .env was read-only over HTTP. Writing MUST preserve comments, key order and blank lines — a naive rewrite destroys a 159-key hand-annotated file.

generate_run.why: `stackvo generate` was only ever invoked as a side effect of project_create / service_enable, via execAsync on a shell string. Making it a first-class command is what lets the fs-watcher regenerate automatically.
generate_run.notes: Since the takeover, this writes with the Rust generator directly — no shell is spawned, and bash is no longer a generation prerequisite.

generate_with.why: Was the staged handover: Bash ran in every mode and `rust` refused to write on any byte difference. The takeover completed at 28/28 files identical on real data, the Bash engine was retired, and the Rust generator is the only writer.
generate_with.notes: Kept for headless callers; the UI's engine selector is gone because there is no longer an engine to select. `verify` survives as a drift check — does the disk still hold what the generator would write — which catches hand-edited generated files. generate_run is the plain write path.

generator_verify.why: The migration gate. A fixture suite only covers the cases someone thought to write down; this renders every generated file with the Rust port against the user's real projects and real .env, so a divergence surfaces on their machine before anything depends on it.
generator_verify.notes: Reads only — it never writes a generated file. `readyToTakeOver` is true when every file matches byte-for-byte.

git_available.why: The clone option is hidden without it. A webview cannot answer "is a program installed", and the answer has to survive an app launched from the Dock, which inherits launchd's PATH rather than a login shell's — the same class of fact that made $LANG useless for locale detection.
git_available.notes: Checks PATH and then the usual absolute locations. Apple's git at /usr/bin/git is on both; a Homebrew git at /opt/homebrew/bin is on neither in a packaged app, and a PATH-only check would tell a user with git that they have none.

handover_apply.why: Write the instance table from `.env`, once.
handover_apply.notes: Recomputes the plan rather than accepting one: a plan decides ports against the machine as it was, and a stale preview could claim a port something else has since taken. `.env` is copied to `.env.pre-market.bak` BEFORE anything is written and its service keys are marked rather than removed, so the revert is deleting services/instances.json. Refuses when a table already exists — a second run would adopt the same volumes twice.

handover_preview.why: The one migration that touches a workspace somebody is already using. handover.rs is built plan-then-apply so the reasons survive; a UI with only the apply half would have thrown them away.
handover_preview.notes: Pure: computes the plan and writes nothing. `blockers` non-empty means the handover is refused as a whole — a version enabled in `.env` and absent from the catalogue is never migrated to its nearest neighbour, because that is an unrequested upgrade performed on a datadir. `missing` names what to install to unblock it: a preview that only refused was a dead end with the answer one page away and unnamed.

help_doc.why: Every card in the interface carries a help button; this is what the button reads. What a button does is prose somebody will want to correct the day after a release, so the current copy is pulled from the repository (raw.githubusercontent.com, docs/help/<locale>/<topic>.md on main) rather than being as old as the build. Documented in PRIVACY.md: the request names the topic and the locale, which is a fact about what the person was stuck on.
help_doc.notes: Three sources in order: the repository over HTTPS (once per topic per run, 5s timeout), the cache written under the app directory from the last successful pull, and the copy carried by bundle.resources — so the network decides how current the text is and never decides whether there is text at all, and a failed fetch is silent rather than an error. A 200 whose body does not open with `# ` is refused rather than cached: a captive portal answering with its login page would otherwise replace a good document on exactly the network where the real one cannot be reached. `topic` is matched against `[a-z0-9-]{1,64}` before it touches a path or a URL: it arrives over IPC, and `..` in a topic would read any file on the machine, or fetch any file in the repository, into a web view. An unknown locale reads the English document rather than erroring — a reader who set a language nobody has written for is better served by a page than by an error about their own settings — and a topic with no document anywhere is NOT_FOUND naming the topic. Looks in the bundle resource directory first, then the repository's own docs/help, so `tauri dev` and an installed application both find it. The registry of valid topics is src/lib/help.js; tests/help-topics.spec.js fails on a card whose topic it does not know and on a document written in one language and not the other. See src-tauri/src/help.rs.

host_stats.v1Change: Backed by the `sysinfo` crate on the host instead of reading /proc from inside a container. The 293-line HostStatsService with its macOS fallbacks collapses to a direct, correct read — this is the clearest early win of the port.

hosts_apply.why: Removes the manual `sudo tee -a /etc/hosts` step from the README. MUST show a diff and require explicit confirmation before elevating; MUST back up the file; MUST only touch lines inside a StackVo-managed marker block.
hosts_apply.notes: Writes the previewed text via the OS elevation prompt (osascript / pkexec / UAC). Only lines inside the `# >>> stackvo >>>` marker block are rewritten; everything else in the file is byte-identical. A cancelled prompt is PERMISSION_DENIED, not a crash.

hosts_missing.why: Every project domain with no hosts entry. Drives the one-click fix; the web UI could detect this but had no way to act on it.

hosts_missing_core.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
hosts_missing_core.notes: Only <suffix> and traefik.<suffix> — the two names the stack is addressed through, and the set the preflight gate blocks on. hosts_missing is the everything list, for the dashboard's fix-all banner.

hosts_overview.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
hosts_overview.notes: Every domain the stack serves with its hosts state, plus entries inside StackVo's own block that nothing wants any more. MUST offer only StackVo-managed lines as stale: a hand-written entry belongs to whoever wrote it.

hosts_plan.why: Computes the exact replacement text WITHOUT elevating, so the UI can show a diff and ask first. Elevating and explaining afterwards would be the wrong order for the one operation that touches a system file.

hosts_status.why: readHostsFile() could only READ a read-only mount and report isDomainConfigured. Same capability, but now it feeds a fix action.
hosts_status.notes: Rust-internal: projects_list uses it to fill `domainConfigured`. Deliberately not wrapped for JS — the list payload already carries the answer, and a second round trip is a way for the two to disagree.

ide_debug_apply.why: Writes the debug configuration into the project so the mapping is right the first time rather than after somebody has typed it twice.
ide_debug_apply.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: only the one configuration named `Listen for StackVo: <project>` may be written; every other configuration, and any key this code does not know, MUST come back unchanged, and a copy is kept beside the file as `.stackvo-backup` first. The entry is replaced WHERE IT STANDS — the list is the IDE's dropdown and its order is somebody's preference. `pathMappings` is written remote-to-local with `${workspaceFolder}` on the local side, never this machine's absolute path: launch.json is committed. A launch.json with comments in it (which is what VS Code itself creates) is REFUSED rather than rewritten. A target whose `method` is `shown` — PhpStorm, which keeps its configuration in memory and rewrites it on exit — is refused with UNSUPPORTED; there is no way to edit it safely underneath a running IDE. Audited.

ide_debug_remove.why: The undo. A tool that writes into somebody's repository and cannot take it back out is one they do not press the first time.
ide_debug_remove.notes: Removes only the configuration this app added, by name. An empty `configurations` left behind is left behind — removing the key would be deciding something about a file this app does not own. Removing from a file that has none is not an error.

ide_debug_status.returns: { project: string, port: number, ideKey: string, serverName: string, hostPath: string | null, containerPath: string, listener: { port: number, process: string | null, pid: number | null, unknown: boolean }, targets: Array<{ id: string, label: string, method: 'written' | 'shown', path: string, detected: boolean, exists: boolean, parseable: boolean, installed: boolean, current: boolean, snippet: string }> }
ide_debug_status.why: Every competitor's step-debugging page is the same page — here is the port, here is the host, here is the path mapping, now type them into your IDE — and all five name the path mapping as the usual reason a breakpoint never hits. xdebug_status already computes both halves of that mapping and left them on screen as two strings to copy. This is the read half of filling them in.
ide_debug_status.notes: Reads only. `listener` is the fact that is in no file: who holds the debug port right now, read from the OS's listening-socket table (the same one doctor uses), never by connecting — a connection to a DBGp port is a debug session the IDE would log as one that dropped. `unknown: true` means the table could not be read at all, which is distinct from nothing listening. `method: 'shown'` means this app will not write that IDE's file and offers `snippet` to paste instead; see ide_debug_apply. See src-tauri/src/ide.rs.

imports_scan.returns: Array<{ source: 'xampp' | 'laragon' | 'mamp' | 'valet' | 'sail', path: string, sites: Array<{ name: string, path: string, domain: string | null, bytes: number, partial: boolean, detected: Detected, taken: boolean, services?: string[] }> }>
imports_scan.why: Competitive review §L. XAMPP has been frozen on PHP 8.2 since 2023 and lost its add-on ecosystem in September 2025; Laragon went commercial in 2025 and was forked. Those are the two largest installed bases in the category and every rival is courting them — EnvKit imports Laragon in bulk, ForgeKit lists six sources. StackVo could read neither.
imports_scan.notes: Reads only, and works with no workspace selected. `taken` says a directory of that name is already under projects/, so the list can say so before anything is clicked. `bytes` is measured because importing copies, and a size caps out at 20,000 entries with `partial: true` rather than walking a node_modules to the last byte on a page that lists eleven sites. XAMPP's own dashboard directories are excluded. Laragon's per-site vhost supplies `domain`; XAMPP serves by path and has no name to read, so it is null and adoption asks. See src-tauri/src/imports.rs. Seven tools, in four shapes. XAMPP, Laragon and MAMP keep one directory of sites. Valet keeps none — it PARKS directories (every child is a site) and LINKS individual ones as symlinks — so it is read from its own config.json, tld included. Sail is not an installation at all: it is a composer package inside a project, identified by a docker-compose.yml that names laravel/sail, which is why it never appears in this scan and is reachable only through imports_scan_at. Herd is VALET'S SHAPE with another root (~/Library/Application Support/Herd/config/valet) and goes through Valet's reader rather than a second one; two things are Herd's own and both are read — ~/Herd is parked whether or not the config says so, and the site's PHP version is pinned in the socket its nginx config points fastcgi_pass at, which makes Herd the only source whose sites arrive with a version somebody CHOSE. DDEV is the fourth shape: a registry (~/.ddev, read by the leaf key `approot` so it survives the file being reorganised) plus a declarative .ddev/config.yaml per project. That file is why DDEV is worth the most of the seven — every other source makes this app infer the PHP version, the document root and the web server from the code, and DDEV's file DECLARES them along with the database engine. The declaration wins over detection and only where it speaks, gated on the detected runtime so a php_version cannot be laid over a project detection called Node (W-02); the config's own commented template (`# php_version: "8.4"`, no space after the hash) is skipped, because taking the first line that mentions a key would read the example instead of the answer on every DDEV project there is. `services` is populated for Sail alone, from the compose file's own service list mapped onto this app's catalogue (pgsql→postgres, mongodb→mongo); a service with no counterpart is left out rather than substituted, and every other source leaves the field empty because their sites do not state what they need.

imports_scan_at.why: The same, for an installation somewhere this app did not think to look — the well-known paths are installer defaults and people move things.
imports_scan_at.notes: null when the directory holds no htdocs (XAMPP) or www (Laragon), which is the honest answer for 'that is not one of those'. INVALID_INPUT for a source name that is not one of the seven. MUST accept every source imports.rs can read — `Source::from_id` and the scan both walk one list (`imports::ALL`) rather than each keeping a copy, and `foreign_import.rs` holds the front end's own list against it in both directions. It accepted two of the five, so somebody whose MAMP was not in /Applications — or who wanted a Valet or Sail project, neither of which a scan can find — was told the tool was not one this app can read. For Sail the path may be the project OR a directory holding several: both are what somebody means by pointing at it.

imports_take.why: Brings one site into the workspace. The generator bind-mounts ${PROJECTS}/<name>, so a project lives under the projects directory or it does not exist — an import is a file operation, and this is that half only.
imports_take.notes: The manifest is NOT written here: the caller follows with project_adopt, so an imported project goes through the same validation, the same domain question and the same name rules as any other adoption. Copies by default. `move` copies first and removes the original only once the copy is complete — the reverse order turns a full disk into a site that exists in neither place — and a failure to remove is logged rather than rolled back, because deleting a correct copy to honour the word 'move' destroys the half that worked. Nothing is ever written into the other installation. A half-finished copy is removed: adoption would otherwise find it and produce a project missing files nobody can name. Errors: ALREADY_EXISTS when the name is taken, NOT_FOUND for a path that is not a directory, INVALID_INPUT when the projects directory is inside the site being imported. Audited as `project_import`.

args.ports: Record<handle, number>? — optional, null when nothing moved

instance_apply_settings.why: Write an instance's settings and rebuild its container with them. Replaces service_apply_settings, which wrote them to .env.
instance_apply_settings.notes: MUST reject keys the manifest does not declare, MUST reject a masked value being written back, and MUST reject emptying a setting the manifest marks required. `enabled`, `primary` and `version` are not settings and are not reachable here — each has its own command, and two controls for one field is how they come to disagree. Ports are the deliberate exception: they arrive as their own argument rather than in `patch`, because they are not settings, and they arrive *here* rather than through a command of their own because both need the container stopped and recreated — two commands would do that twice for one press of one button. A port is refused when the manifest does not declare the handle, when another instance holds the number, when the machine is already listening there, or when the patch would publish one number under two handles. The rebuild is the point: `instance_restart` keeps the environment the container was created with, so a setting saved and then restarted appears to have been applied and has not.

args.settings: Record<string, string>? — what the create form collected; null creates with the package's defaults
args.ports: Record<handle, number>? — null allocates every port

instance_create.why: Create an instance of an installed package. Returns its id — the slug of service@version, which every derived name comes from.
instance_create.notes: A supplied secret is written to the keystore before the container has ever run, which is the only moment an image reads one. A requested port is used or refused, never moved: the allocator's job is to find *a* free port, and handing back 3407 to somebody who typed 3307 is a different thing. Unrequested ports allocate as before.

instance_disable.why: Switch an instance off. NOTHING IS DELETED — not the volume, not the image.
instance_disable.notes: service_disable deletes all three, and in a single-version world that was right: 'off' should be a state rather than a label. It stops being right per version. Somebody switching MySQL 8.0 off to try 9.4 wants 8.0's rows when they switch back. Deleting lives behind instance_remove and market_uninstall, where the word on the button matches what happens.

instance_enable.why: Write the instance down as on, regenerate, then bring its compose profile up. The order is the one service_enable uses: the compose file has to describe the container before compose is asked to start it.
instance_enable.notes: The hosts entry is keyed on the SERVICE, not the instance — a service with a domain declares instancing.multiple:false, so there is exactly one instance of it. Per-instance subdomains are a separate, smaller job.

instance_list.why: What is installed, how many times, and which one answers to the pre-package name.
instance_list.notes: `packagePresent` is false when the instance names a package that is not installed. That is a state a user has to see, not an error that hides the row.

instance_plan.why: What creating this instance would produce, before it does — so a first-boot password can be chosen at the one moment an image will read it.
instance_plan.notes: Writes nothing and reserves nothing. The ports are what the allocator would choose right now; `instance_create` allocates again for real, because between the two something else may have taken one. A port the allocator cannot place comes back null rather than failing the call, so the form can name it and let the user choose. `refused` is reported rather than thrown, so a single-instance service opens a dialog that says why instead of no dialog at all. A secret's value here is the manifest's published first-boot default and is NOT masked: there is no instance and no keystore entry, and masking a string that is in a file on disk would be theatre.

instance_promote.why: Move the pre-package name — `stackvo-mysql` — to another version of the same service.
instance_promote.notes: One write, not two. The state between 'clear that one' and 'set this one' is a table with no primary, and if the process dies there every project pointing at the old name resolves nothing. Two instances holding one alias is refused: Docker answers at random, and the symptom is 'it connects to the wrong database sometimes'.

instance_remove.why: Forget an instance. Volumes are left alone.
instance_remove.notes: If the removed instance was primary, the oldest survivor takes the alias. A service with instances and no primary is one whose pre-package name resolves to nothing, and every project pointing at it breaks at once.

instance_restart.why: The container, without touching what the instance table says. Distinct from enable/disable, which change whether the instance is part of the stack at all.
instance_restart.notes: Goes through the same lifecycle helper as project_* and service_*; the id is validated against the instance table first, because it is not in the service catalog and never will be.

instance_reveal.why: The real value behind a masked secret, for the one instance and the one key.
instance_reveal.notes: Returns the manifest's default when the keystore holds nothing, because that is what the container is running with — a reveal showing an empty box for a service reachable with `root` would be a lie of omission. Errors: NOT_FOUND for a key the manifest does not declare, INVALID_INPUT for a key that is not a secret.

instance_settings.why: What one instance is configured with, as its manifest declares it. Replaces service_settings, which read SERVICE_<ID>_* keys out of .env — a name that identifies a service, of which two versions can be running.
instance_settings.notes: Order is the manifest's, not sorted: a package author who put the database name above the password meant that. Values resolve the way render::context resolves them — what is stored, then the manifest default — because a form that showed one value while the compose file rendered another would be a form about nothing. Secrets are masked without consulting the keystore, so the mask is the same length for a set password and an unset one. `options` is an offer, not a constraint.

instance_start.why: The container, without touching what the instance table says. Distinct from enable/disable, which change whether the instance is part of the stack at all.
instance_start.notes: Goes through the same lifecycle helper as project_* and service_*; the id is validated against the instance table first, because it is not in the service catalog and never will be.

focus_plan.returns: { keep: FocusVerdict[], stop: FocusVerdict[], declaresNothing: boolean }
focus_plan.why: "Run only what this project needs and stop the rest" is the most-wanted verb on a laptop, and this app is the only one in its category that can pose the question: stackvo.json DECLARES what a project needs around it, and the instance table says what is installed. Competitors switch services on and off one at a time because they have no manifest to declare a need in.
focus_plan.notes: A query — nothing is stopped by asking. Only service instances are considered and only running ones can appear in `stop`; projects are never touched, and Traefik is not an instance so it cannot be reached from here, which is right rather than a special case — stopping the router would take the focused project down with everything else. Required dependencies are followed transitively and kept with reason `dependency`, because stopping what a declared service needs breaks the thing that was asked for; OPTIONAL dependencies are not followed, since an optional service that happens to be running is exactly what focus is for. Every instance of a declared service is kept: a workspace running MySQL 8.0 and 8.4 has two instances for one id and the manifest cannot say which, so keeping both is the answer that cannot cost somebody their afternoon. `declaresNothing` reports an empty `services` list, which the manifest documents as "nothing declared, not nothing needed" — the plan is still computed so a screen can show what WOULD happen, and focus_apply refuses it. A dead engine degrades to "nothing is running" rather than failing. See src-tauri/src/focus.rs.

focus_apply.returns: { keep: FocusVerdict[], stop: FocusVerdict[], declaresNothing: boolean }
focus_apply.why: The verb behind focus_plan. Split from it for the reason preset, worktree and release all split: stopping five containers is reversible and still not something to do to somebody without showing them the list first.
focus_apply.notes: The plan is MADE AGAIN here rather than taken from the caller — the same rule provider states, for the same reason: the screen that offered the button may be minutes old, and a service started in between must not be stopped by an approval given before it existed. INVALID_INPUT when the project declares no services, because acting on an unfilled field would stop the whole workspace and the person who pressed the button would have no way to know that is what they asked for. Takes the `stack` in-flight guard, so it cannot run beside an up/down. One instance failing to stop does not abandon the rest: stopping four of five and reporting the fifth beats stopping none, and the returned plan says what was attempted. Nothing is deleted — instance_stop only, so data directories and settings survive. NOT audited: every act here is undone by starting the instance again, which is the line audit.rs draws. See src-tauri/src/focus.rs.

instance_stop.why: The container, without touching what the instance table says. Distinct from enable/disable, which change whether the instance is part of the stack at all.
instance_stop.notes: Goes through the same lifecycle helper as project_* and service_*; the id is validated against the instance table first, because it is not in the service catalog and never will be.

lan_status.why: The screen has to be able to say three different things: here is the address a phone can use, this machine has no address to offer, and the name baked into the compose file is from a network this laptop is no longer on.
lan_status.notes: `address` is null both when there is no network and when the address is public — the second is a refusal, because handing out `shop.<public-ip>.sslip.io` would publish a development site under a name anybody can resolve. `stale` reads the rendered compose file rather than recomputing: the question is whether what was written still matches what would be written. The certificate is the local CA's and the visiting device does not trust it, so its browser warns; that is a missing trust anchor on a device this app cannot reach, not a fault it can fix. See src-tauri/src/lan.rs.

landing_refresh.why: The sidecar serves a FILE, so starting a project after the page was written leaves it stale with nothing having stopped. Rewriting is therefore a different action from serving, and one button doing both would restart a container to update a list.
landing_refresh.notes: Writes atomically into generated/landing/index.html and returns the fresh status. Safe to call while the container is running: nginx serves whatever is on disk at request time and the mount is read-only from its side.

landing_start.why: An operation rather than a mutation: the first start pulls nginx, which belongs in the operation console rather than behind a frozen button.
landing_start.notes: Renders the page BEFORE starting the container — nginx answers 403 for an empty directory, which reads as a broken proxy rather than as a page that has not been written yet. A sidecar in the shape tunnel_start already established: one `docker run` on the stack network with Traefik labels, --rm so stopping is removal. The generated compose file is deliberately untouched — it is compared byte for byte against the Bash generator's output, and a service only this app knows about would break that comparison for a page. nginx:alpine rather than the alpine:3 this app already pulls, because Alpine's busybox is built WITHOUT the httpd applet (measured: `httpd: applet not found`). The page is one static file with no scripts, no fonts and no requests of its own — a landing page that needs the network to render is blank exactly when something is wrong — and every name on it is HTML-escaped, because a project is a directory and a directory can be called `R&D`. Measured end to end with examples/landing_probe.rs: the container is started against the live stack, https://stackvo.loc is requested with the system trust store and no --insecure, and the bytes that come back are compared with the bytes that were written; the container and the scratch directory are removed either way.

landing_status.returns: { running: boolean, container: string, url: string, rendered: string | null, projects: number, services: number }
landing_status.why: Every rival in the category ships one and it is the address people bookmark. StackVo has had the NAME for it since the beginning with nothing answering on it: core_domains already writes the bare suffix into the hosts file and certs::required_domains already issues for it, so opening https://<suffix> got Traefik's own 404 — a name the app went out of its way to make resolve, serving nothing.
landing_status.notes: `rendered` is read off the file's own timestamp rather than remembered, so an app restart, a hand-edited page and a workspace copied from another machine all stay truthful. A project with no domain is left OFF the page rather than listed as an unclickable row. landing_stop.why: Turning it off has to be as easy as turning it on.
landing_stop.notes: `--rm` means stopping is removal, so nothing is left answering on the name after the page is switched off.

licences_notice.why: MIT, BSD, ISC and Apache-2.0 all require the copyright notice and the licence text to travel with the software. A NOTICE.md in a source repository does not reach the person who received a .dmg, and pointing them at the repository is the same answer as not shipping it.
licences_notice.notes: Returns the generated NOTICE.md verbatim — markdown covering every Rust crate and npm package that ships, resolved for all platforms at once so one notice describes every bundle. include_str! rather than a bundle resource: a resource is a run-time path that can resolve to nothing, and an app that silently ships no attribution is the failure this closes. Generated by tools/generate-notice.mjs from Cargo.lock and package-lock.json; `npm run notice:check` fails the build when a shipped dependency is missing from it.

locale_get.why: The window and the tray have to open in the same language, and neither could read the machine's on its own. The tray fell back to $LANG, which a Finder-launched app does not have; the window fell back to navigator.language, which in a WKWebView answers from the bundle's localised resources — this app ships none. Both defaulted to English on a Turkish machine.
locale_get.notes: Resolution order lives in `locale.rs` and is one order for both surfaces: the choice in preferences.json, then the OS (AppleLanguages/AppleLocale on macOS, HKCU Control Panel\International on Windows, LC_ALL/LC_MESSAGES/LANG elsewhere), then English. Only ever returns a language the app has strings for — a near miss like pt-BR resolving to a half-translated UI is worse than an honest English one. The front end must NOT write the answer back to preferences.json: that would turn a detection into a stored choice and freeze the first machine's language for ever.

locale_pack_delete.why: A language somebody installed has to be removable.
locale_pack_delete.notes: Removing one that is not there is success — the caller is asking for it to be gone, and it is.

locale_pack_read.why: The messages, for the front end to merge over English.
locale_pack_read.notes: INVALID_INPUT for a tag that is not a language tag, and for a file that is not JSON. Measured with examples/locale_pack_probe.rs, which writes a pack into the real config directory, lists it, reads it back, breaks it on purpose to check the error is reported, and removes it.

locale_pack_write.why: How 'start a translation' works: the front end sends the English catalogue as the starting point.
locale_pack_write.notes: The messages come from the front end because the front end is where the catalogue lives — asking Rust to produce a template would mean a second copy of every string in this app, which is the duplication trayLabels already exists to undo. Written atomically. Adding a language stops being a code change: a pack is one JSON file in the app's config directory with the same shape as the shipped catalogue. The front end merges it over English and registers it, so an untranslated screen is in English rather than showing raw keys, and vue-i18n's per-key fallback makes a partial pack a working pack — which is what makes starting one possible at all. NO machine translation and no seeding a new pack with English silently relabelled: a missing string that falls back to English is honest, a fabricated one is a sentence somebody has to find and disbelieve.

locale_packs.returns: Array<{ tag: string, label: string, path: string, strings: number, broken: string | null, direction?: 'rtl' | 'ltr' }>
locale_packs.why: The language set used to be a constant in three places — locale.rs, i18n/index.js and the tray's fallback table — so a third language meant a source change and a rebuild. Nobody who can actually translate this app can do any of that, which is why this sat on the list as '~2,000 strings': the strings were never the blocker, the rebuild was. The progress figure counted the strings a pack HELD, and the seed is the whole English catalogue — so an untouched pack read `2000 of 2000 (100%)` the moment it was created. It counts what differs from English now.
locale_packs.notes: A pack that does not parse is LISTED WITH ITS ERROR rather than skipped — a hand-edited file with a trailing comma that simply vanishes from the picker is the worst failure this could have. A pack names itself through `language.label`, because this app cannot hold a name for a language it has never heard of. The tag is validated as a BCP 47 language rather than accepted, because it becomes a file name in a directory this app writes into. Adding a language stops being a code change: a pack is one JSON file in the app's config directory with the same shape as the shipped catalogue. The front end merges it over English and registers it, so an untranslated screen is in English rather than showing raw keys, and vue-i18n's per-key fallback makes a partial pack a working pack — which is what makes starting one possible at all.
