NO machine translation and no seeding a new pack with English silently relabelled: a missing string that falls back to English is honest, a fabricated one is a sentence somebody has to find and disbelieve. `direction` is how a pack states which way its language reads, and it is the one key whose absence was invisible: layout direction was a single appearance switch applied to every locale at once — right for the two languages shipped here, both left to right, and wrong the moment a pack is Arabic or Farsi. Two of the five languages the nearest competitor ships are right-to-left; before this, such a pack rendered left to right until its reader found a switch in Settings that then mirrored English as well. A pack that states it wins for its own locale, because direction is a FACT about a language and the switch is a PREFERENCE — the preference still decides for every locale that has not stated one. Anything other than the two words reads as absent rather than as an error: a pack is a hand-edited file, and one typo in one optional key should cost the direction, not the language. `locale_pack_write`'s seed carries `"direction": "ltr"` for the same reason a translator cannot ask for a key they have never seen.

usage_report.returns: { date: string, rows: Array<{ name: string, kind: 'project' | 'service' | 'stack', cpuSeconds: number, gbHours: number, samples: number, budgetCpuMinutes?: number, budgetGbHours?: number, overBudget: boolean }>, cpuSeconds: number, gbHours: number }
usage_report.why: Docker is expensive and this app's own README says so rather than arguing with it. Every rival built on containers has the same cost and none of them measures it, which leaves "why is my laptop hot" to Activity Monitor and its nine processes called com.docker.backend. Being the one product that can answer "shop has held 4.2 GB-hours and used 38 minutes of CPU today" is a better position than denying the cost.
usage_report.notes: No new measurement: sample_container_stats has read CPU and memory once a minute since the port and threw them away after two hours, because a sparkline was all they were for. This accumulates the same readings. The interval is MEASURED per container rather than assumed to be the sixty-second timer, and a gap longer than five minutes contributes nothing — a laptop closed on Friday and opened on Monday must not be billed for the weekend at its Friday rate; the sample still counts and the clock still moves, only the time is refused. cpuSeconds is seconds of ONE core, directly comparable to what `time` reports; gbHours is memory HELD rather than consumed, because memory is occupied and not spent. Rows are heaviest first, and every container is named including the stack's own router and mail catcher — a total that quietly left them out would understate what Docker costs here. Shared services get their own row and are NEVER divided between the projects that use them: any split would be invented, and a number somebody could act on has to be one they can check. For the same reason only a project carries a budget. Budgets live in preferences under `usageBudgets` (`{ cpuMinutes, gbHours }` per project name) because a threshold is a machine's decision — the same repository on a colleague's laptop has different room to spare — and a zero is treated as no budget rather than as always-over, since a cleared field arrives as zero. A day outside the thirty-day retention is simply absent rather than an error. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/usage.rs.

logs_info.returns: { directory: string|null, newestFile: string|null, totalBytes: number }
logs_info.notes: Where the diagnostic log lives. New to the desktop app — the container UI wrote to stdout, which docker logs captured and nobody kept. The path differs per platform (~/Library/Logs on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows, XDG_STATE_HOME on Linux — which is where the specification puts logs, and where this moved once ~/.local/share was noticed to be the wrong half of XDG) and none is somewhere a user would look unprompted. The folder is named for the app, not for its bundle identifier; `appdir` owns that choice for both this and the config directory.

mail_attachment_save.why: Reading a captured invoice PDF meant leaving for the browser UI.
mail_attachment_save.notes: partId is a handle the catcher issued and path comes from the system save dialog — the front end names neither the source nor the destination.

mail_clear.notes: DESTRUCTIVE in the small: it empties the inbox. The UI MUST confirm, but this needs no backup — a mail catcher is a bin by design.

mail_delete.notes: One message, not the inbox. The servers disagree on the verb's address: MailHog takes the id in the path, Mailpit takes a JSON body of ids on the collection route. No confirmation — a catcher is a bin; only the whole-inbox clear keeps its dialog.

mail_html_check.why: The report a developer actually opens a catcher for: how this markup fares across 186 real mail-client features. Mailpit only — null on MailHog, which is how the UI knows to hide the tab instead of showing zeroes.
mail_html_check.notes: Warnings are sorted worst-first; a report whose first row is a construct every client supports buries the one that breaks Outlook.

mail_link_check.why: Dead links in a transactional mail are found by the recipient today.
mail_link_check.notes: **This leaves the machine** — it fetches every link in the message, so it is never run as part of opening one; the UI asks for it explicitly. 30s timeout, because it waits on third-party servers.

mail_message.notes: Mailpit returns decoded text and HTML parts. MailHog returns the raw MIME document and leaves decoding to the caller, so `html` is always null there — showing a half-decoded multipart as if it were the message would be worse than showing the source.

mail_messages.notes: Both wire formats are normalised in Rust. They agree on almost nothing: MailHog spells an address as `{Mailbox, Domain}` and buries the subject in a header array, Mailpit uses `{Name, Address}` and a field. Reading either as the other yields an inbox of blank rows that still look like messages.

mail_relay_get.returns: { enabled: boolean, host: string, port: number, username: string, security: 'starttls' | 'tls' | 'none', from: string, allowedRecipients: string[], hasPassword: boolean, keystore: boolean }
mail_relay_get.why: The catcher catches everything, which is right, and it is not the whole job: the message somebody actually needs to check is the one that renders differently in Outlook, or the invoice a colleague has to look at — both of which mean THIS ONE MESSAGE, TO A REAL ADDRESS. Every rival calls that release and StackVo could not do it. Deliberately not the other shape: pointing the application at a real SMTP server would send the forty password resets a test suite generates in an hour to whatever addresses the fixtures happen to contain.
mail_relay_get.notes: Never returns the password: `hasPassword` is a boolean, and there is no command in this app that reads a stored credential back. `keystore` says whether the OS store is reachable at all, so a machine where it is not says so rather than silently storing nothing. Mailpit does the relaying and reads its settings from its own environment; this app reaches that environment through a COMPOSE OVERLAY, the same mechanism site.rs and perf.rs use — so the service package is untouched, nothing is re-sealed, and a workspace that has never configured a relay renders exactly the bytes it did before. The catcher's compose service is found BY IMAGE (`axllent/mailpit`), not by name: the key is `mailpit` on a .env workspace and `mailpit-1-30` on one that moved to the instance table. The password is in the OS keystore and the settings file carries no value; it IS written into generated/, which is the same partial answer that holds for service passwords and is said out loud rather than implied. `allowedRecipients` is a regular expression to Mailpit, so each entry's dots are escaped — unescaped, `me@test.com` would also permit `me@testxcom`, which is an address somebody could own. A value containing a line break is REFUSED, because a newline ends a YAML scalar and everything after it is read as configuration somebody else wrote.

mail_relay_set.why: Somewhere to put the relay, once somebody has been told a release was refused.
mail_relay_set.notes: `password` has three states and they are all different intentions: `null` leaves the stored one alone, `''` removes it, anything else replaces it. A relay that is switched ON must have a host, a port and a sender address — a provider rejects a From it does not own, and the error comes back as a number. The overlay is rendered immediately as well as before every compose call, so a failure to write it is reported while somebody is looking at the pane. Mailpit does the relaying and reads its settings from its own environment; this app reaches that environment through a COMPOSE OVERLAY, the same mechanism site.rs and perf.rs use — so the service package is untouched, nothing is re-sealed, and a workspace that has never configured a relay renders exactly the bytes it did before. The catcher's compose service is found BY IMAGE (`axllent/mailpit`), not by name: the key is `mailpit` on a .env workspace and `mailpit-1-30` on one that moved to the instance table. The password is in the OS keystore and the settings file carries no value; it IS written into generated/, which is the same partial answer that holds for service passwords and is said out loud rather than implied. `allowedRecipients` is a regular expression to Mailpit, so each entry's dots are escaped — unescaped, `me@test.com` would also permit `me@testxcom`, which is an address somebody could own. A value containing a line break is REFUSED, because a newline ends a YAML scalar and everything after it is read as configuration somebody else wrote.

mail_release.why: The whole point of a relay: one caught message, sent on to a real person.
mail_release.notes: Mailpit only. MailHog has no equivalent and that is REPORTED rather than worked around — releasing by opening our own SMTP connection would make this app a mail sender, with a TLS stack and a credential in this process, to add a feature to a catcher somebody has already replaced. Mailpit's own refusal sentence is carried through unchanged when no relay is configured: a generic "release failed" sends somebody looking at their SMTP provider for a setting that is missing here. The recipient is typed by the user rather than taken from the message's own To — the reason to release is that somebody ELSE has to see it, and re-sending to the fixture address is the one thing that is never useful.

mail_search.why: A catcher with fifty captured mails needs a search box more than it needs another button. The query reaches the catcher verbatim, so Mailpit's own syntax (from:, to:, subject:, quoted phrases) works as documented rather than being reimplemented worse here.

mail_status.why: StackVo has shipped a mail catcher all along and never showed it — reading a captured message meant leaving for a browser tab, which is exactly the round trip four competitors charge for removing.
mail_status.notes: Reads both MailHog and Mailpit. The upstream template installs the unmaintained `mailhog/mailhog`; Mailpit is what the ecosystem moved to, and swapping renames a service, its .env keys, its container and its volume — a migration for every running stack. Supporting both is the same stance the app takes everywhere else: it manages a checkout, it does not dictate one. `error` is set when the container is up but its API did not answer, because that otherwise renders as an empty inbox, which is a lie.

args.destination: string — a directory that does not exist yet, or an empty one

market_bundle.why: Write everything an air-gapped machine needs into one directory, on a machine that still has a network. market.offlineBundle is the only way a catalogue reaches a machine with no network, and until now nothing could produce one — the consuming half shipped without the producing half.
market_bundle.notes: The output is a source: `LocalSource` reads it and the far end cannot tell it from a checkout, so `market_refresh` against it and then `market_install` complete the round trip. registry.json is copied byte for byte rather than re-serialised, because the signature is over the bytes and manifestSha256 chains from them. Every manifest is verified against the index while bundling — the same check `market_install` makes, moved to the machine with a person at it rather than the one with no network. A withdrawn version keeps its index row and loses its files: the row stays so the far end can learn what happened, and market_install refuses to install one before fetching anything. A destination that is not empty is refused; a failed bundle is removed rather than left looking whole. A tar of this directory is a packaging of it, not a second mechanism.

market_catalog.why: What is published, and for each version whether it is already installed and whether an instance is using it — so the UI can offer Install or refuse Uninstall without a second round trip.
market_catalog.notes: Empty when nothing has been fetched. An `eol` version is listed and installable; the picker hides it behind 'show older versions' rather than withdrawing it, because somebody's workspace may name it.

market_install.why: Fetch one package, verify it whole, and put it where the renderer looks.
market_install.notes: The manifest is refused as BYTES when it does not hash to what the index says — before any field of it is read. The package is unpacked into a scratch directory, verified, and only then moved into place: a half-written package is the one failure a client cannot recover from on its own. Refused before any byte is fetched when policy.market.allowedPackages excludes the service, and after the manifest is parsed when policy.market.allowedRegistries excludes its image's registry — the second needs the manifest, which is why it is not beside the first.

args.location: string — an https:// address or a directory path

market_probe.why: Answering 'is my address right' without doing the thing. The first address anybody pastes is the repository's web page, which a working server correctly 404s, and there was no way to find that out except by refreshing and reading the failure.
market_probe.notes: Caches nothing and remembers nothing: it fetches into a scratch directory and removes it. A GitHub repository URL is translated to its raw base and BOTH are reported, so the answer explains itself. An index older than the cached one is reported as `goesBackwards` rather than raised as an error — that refusal belongs to market_refresh, and knowing about it beforehand is the point of a probe.

args.location: string — an https:// address or a directory path; which one it is comes from the string

market_refresh.why: Read a catalogue from wherever this machine gets one — an https:// address, an offline bundle, or a directory the user picked. Which one comes from the string. The signature is checked before the index is parsed when a signature is asked for; a signature the publisher published is checked without anybody asking, a source that stops signing is refused, and policy.market.requireSignature only tightens further.
market_refresh.notes: `location` is input, not configuration: the source is remembered, not obeyed, and both sources refuse a path that walks out of them. Precedence is policy.market.offlineBundle, then policy.market.registryUrl, then what the user gave — a machine handed a bundle was not expected to reach anything. http:// is refused outright: nothing verifies a signature yet, so TLS is the whole of the protection. policy.market.requireSignature raises Trust to Signed, which refuses rather than downgrading — the one policy key that can only tighten. The index is fetched with If-None-Match; a 304 keeps the cached copy. Any single file over 8 MiB is abandoned mid-stream, counted on bytes received rather than on Content-Length, which the sender chooses (T-8). Runs on a blocking thread: the Source trait is synchronous so pkg and render need not know what a runtime is, and the HTTPS source blocks on the runtime handle.

market_status.why: A machine that has never fetched a catalogue has none at all — nothing is embedded — so 'not fetched yet' and 'the catalogue is empty' are different sentences and the market page shows a different thing for each.
market_status.notes: `signed` reports whether the CACHED INDEX was signature-verified when it arrived, read back from market/source.json — not whether this build can verify. Those are different sentences and only the first belongs on a screen: a machine that pins the official key still holds an unverified catalogue whenever the last refresh came from a directory somebody picked, which is every offline install. It was a hard-coded false for as long as no key was pinned, which made it true by accident. `verifiedBy` names the key, so "verified by the official key" and "verified by my organisation's mirror key" are distinguishable.

market_uninstall.why: Remove a package's files. Data is not touched — that is behind purgeData on a command that also stops containers.
market_uninstall.notes: Refuses while an instance still names the package. The filesystem would allow it and the renderer would then refuse that instance forever, with the reason two screens away.

migrate_apply.notes: Adopts first, enables services second, and the order is load-bearing: adoption is the half that can fail on a schema violation, and enabling services for a project that then did not get created leaves the stack carrying a database nothing uses. Skips adoption when the directory already has a manifest, so re-running it against a managed project only reconciles the services. Re-scans afterwards, so the reply describes the state that now exists rather than the one that did before the write.

migrate_scan.why: The other half of P2-12. The folder half shipped with adoption in Sprint 4 — detection infers runtime, server and document root from artisan/wp-config.php/composer.json. What it cannot see is everything the person who wrote the compose file already decided: the PHP version, the domain, the extensions, and — with no equivalent in any marker file — WHICH BACKING SERVICES the project needs. A compose file with mysql:8.0 and redis:7.2 is a statement about the stack; adoption alone leaves the developer to rediscover it from a stack trace about a refused connection.
migrate_scan.notes: **Docker parses the YAML, not this app.** `docker compose config --format json` is the reference implementation of the Compose spec: it resolves anchors, `extends`, .env interpolation and profiles, and normalises every shorthand (a label list becomes a map, "8080:80" becomes a structured port, a relative bind becomes an absolute path). The alternative was a YAML crate, and that was the wrong trade twice: serde_yaml is archived, and deny.toml here says a DIRECT dependency going unmaintained still fails the build; and a hand parser would be wrong on real files — xdebug::generated_services parses by indentation only because it reads a file this project generated, whose shape is fixed. Compose is already a hard preflight requirement, so this adds no dependency at all; when it is missing the answer is an error, not a half-parse. Three kinds of compose service are told apart because they become three different things: the one with a `build:` (or a php/node image) is the APPLICATION and becomes the manifest; nginx/apache/caddy become the manifest's `server` field and NOT a StackVo service, because StackVo runs the web server inside the project container and importing it as a sidecar would give the project two; everything in the catalog becomes a service to enable. Anything else is NAMED in `unmapped`, never dropped — a migration that silently ignores the one service the project actually needs is worse than one that refuses, because it looks finished. Reading only; the reply's `spec` is already validated against project.schema.json, because reviewing a spec that would then be refused is a review of nothing.

oauth_callbacks.returns: { path: string, local: string | null, public: string | null, providers: Array<{ id: string, label: string, accepts: 'any' | 'publiconly', note: string }> }
oauth_callbacks.why: This sat on the list as 'an OAuth callback for .loc' and was not defined enough to build. Reading what the providers require settles it: a redirect URI is a BROWSER REDIRECT, not a fetch — the provider sends a 302 and never resolves the hostname — so https://shop.loc/auth/callback works for the flow, because the browser is on this machine, the name is in this machine's hosts file and the certificate is issued by a CA it trusts. What varies is whether the provider will accept the string at REGISTRATION time, and that is a per-provider rule that is invisible at their console.
oauth_callbacks.notes: Implements no OAuth: no client, no token exchange, and no store for a secret — the application being developed does all of that, and an app that held somebody's client secret to be helpful would be one more place for it to leak from. Returns two strings and the rule for choosing between them. The tunnel URL is read live inside the command rather than passed in, because a quick tunnel's address changes on every start and a callback registered from a stale one fails at the last step of a flow with an error naming neither side. `path` is normalised — leading slash added, duplicate slashes collapsed — and a query string or fragment is REFUSED rather than stripped: most providers compare the registered URI to the redirect exactly. See src-tauri/src/oauth.rs.

open_folder.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
open_folder.notes: Shows a directory in the system file manager. Its own command rather than the opener plugin's open_path, whose permission is documented as enabling the command with no scope — and a scope wide enough for an arbitrary workspace is a scope over everything. MUST reject a path that is not an existing directory.

open_in_browser.why: A project's own domain deserves the browser the developer works in, not whatever the OS last associated with https. The opener plugin has no notion of which browser.
open_in_browser.notes: Also the fix for a real defect: `opener:allow-open-url` was granted without a scope, and open_url answers ForbiddenUrl when nothing matches — so every visit button in the app did nothing at all, silently. http/https only; a launcher that took file:// or a custom scheme from its own front end would be a way to start arbitrary things. Falls back to the system default when the chosen browser cannot start.

open_in_editor.notes: Editor command from preferences; default: detect VS Code, fall back to the OS handler.

open_path.notes: Implemented in the front end via the opener plugin rather than as a Rust command: the plugin already does exactly this, and wrapping it would add a hop with no behaviour of its own. The capability is allow-listed in capabilities/default.json.

open_url.notes: Same as open_path. The plugin restricts schemes; the allow-list in capabilities/default.json is the control point.

package_files.returns: Array<{ path: string, kind: 'compose'|'config'|'companion', companion: string|null, overridden: boolean, at: string }>
package_files.why: The files of one installed version a workspace may take over, and which of them it already has (decision 0031).
package_files.notes: The list comes from the MANIFEST, not from the directory: the compose fragment, the config templates and each companion's fragment. The manifest itself is never in it — it declares the image, the ports and the volumes, so a workspace that could override it could run one thing while the catalogue reported another. `at` is where an override would live whether or not one is there, so a caller can open the file in the user's editor without a second round trip.

package_lint.why: What sealing would change and what would still be wrong afterwards, with nothing written.

package_override.why: Copy one published file into the workspace so it can be edited, and return where it landed.
package_override.notes: Writes under <root>/overrides/<service>/<version>/, NOT into the package: nothing under market/packages/ changes, so the manifest's hashes still hold and a reinstall is exactly as safe. Re-sealing the fetched package would have been the other answer and is worse — the next market_install undoes it with no record it existed. Refuses a path the manifest does not ship, refuses one already overridden (that file is somebody's edit), and refuses outright when policy.market.allowOverrides is false. The bytes copied come through the catalogue, so they are bytes pkg::verify has just agreed match the manifest.

package_override_revert.why: Drop the workspace's copy; the published file takes over on the next render.
package_override_revert.notes: Deletes rather than restoring the published bytes into the override — a pristine copy on disk is what makes 'overridden' mean 'was installed', which is the state skeleton.rs documents at length as the one to stop producing. Reverting something never overridden succeeds: the caller asked for a state, not an operation. Not gated on policy, because it can only move a workspace towards what the publisher shipped. Destructive and not undoable — the front end confirms first.

package_scaffold.why: C-1. Writes a package that is valid on the first read — identity, manifest, fragment, hashes already correct. MUST build the path from the workspace root and checked components: the webview names a service and a version, never a directory. MUST refuse to overwrite an existing version, and MUST leave an existing package.json alone so adding 8.4 does not rewrite the identity somebody filled in for 8.0.

package_seal.why: Recomputes the hashes after an edit and THEN validates — parse, manifest check, compose policy — refusing the whole operation if any fail. Writing the hashes of a fragment the policy rejects would be a tool for producing packages that install and cannot run.

perf_export.why: The price of the feature, paid explicitly: the container reads its dependencies from a volume an editor cannot see, so autocomplete needs a copy on the host. It is a SNAPSHOT and the screen says so — the container keeps writing to the volume and this copy does not follow. Replaces the host directory rather than merging into it: a half-updated vendor/ is worse for an index than an old one, because nothing about it says which half is which.

perf_forget.why: Deletes the volume. Its own act and never part of turning the layer off — a checkbox that throws away thirty thousand files as a side effect is one nobody should trust.

perf_set.why: MUST seed the volume from the host copy BEFORE writing the setting, and MUST fail without writing it if that copy fails. A fresh named volume is empty — Docker seeds one from the image only where the image has content there, and no PHP image ships a vendor/ — so a setting saved first and a copy that failed afterwards is a site that 500s on the next request from a switch that reported success. Turning it OFF copies nothing and deletes nothing: the volume may hold the only copy of a vendor/ that took ten minutes to build. MUST refuse a path that is not relative to the project — the value becomes a container path AND part of a volume name, and it arrives from a JSON file that may have come with a git clone.

perf_status.why: A bind mount costs 2-3x a named volume on metadata and writes, which is the measured reason a Docker workflow feels slow on macOS and Windows. This lists the directories worth moving off the host filesystem for one project, whether each is currently in a volume, how big that volume is, and whether the host still has a copy for an editor to index. Suggestions describe the project in front of them — vendor for PHP, storage/framework and bootstrap/cache when it is a Laravel, node_modules when there is a package.json — and are never applied on their own.

php_ini_set.why: The half of P1-9 that was cut on evidence: `memory_limit` and `upload_max_filesize` are not manifest keys and cannot become them (the schema is additionalProperties: false), and the file the docs pointed at was mounted by nothing.
php_ini_set.notes: `null` removes a directive rather than setting it to PHP's default — this file is an override layer, and leaving `memory_limit = 128M` behind because it matches today's default would keep overriding a php.ini the user may later change underneath it. Removing the last directive removes the FILE, so the mount goes with it on the next compose invocation. Comments, order and directives this app does not manage survive a patch untouched; the file is the user's and safe to commit. Values are format-checked before they are written, because PHP does not fail loudly on a malformed directive — it warns to a log nobody is watching and keeps the old value, which presents as "the setting did nothing".

php_ini_status.why: Every competitor exposes memory_limit and upload_max_filesize; StackVo could not, because .stackvo/php.ini was documented but never real — docs/*/configuration/project.md lists it and the old web UI's DockerService.js:388 lists it, but `php.ini` appears NOWHERE in core/cli. No generator mounted it, so dropping the file in did nothing. The mount had to exist before a form was worth building.
php_ini_status.notes: Three states kept apart, like Xdebug's. `exists` is the file on disk. `mounted` is read from the RUNNING container, never inferred — `stackvo up` from the Bash CLI layers three compose files, not five, and will recreate the container without the mount; None means nothing is running. `needsRecreate` is the two disagreeing. PHP reads its ini at process start, so editing a value in the bind-mounted file changes nothing until the container restarts — which is a third thing again, and the reason none of this is one boolean.

pick_directory.why: Adopting an existing folder as a project is impossible today; paths are typed by hand.
pick_directory.notes: Used directly by the front end. `workspace_pick` is the Rust command that matters, because it pairs the picker with validation and persistence.

audit_trail.returns: { entries: AuditRecord[], total: number, unreadable: number }
audit_trail.why: The audit trail was written from eighteen places and read from none — of the commands in this contract, not one named it. audit.rs states its audience as "whoever has to account for the machine", and that person could only produce the record by knowing it is JSON Lines and knowing which directory the logs go in. Writing a record nobody can be shown is most of the cost of a record and none of the benefit.
audit_trail.notes: Newest first, which is the opposite of the order the file is written in and the order somebody scanning for "what just happened" reads in. Capped — default 200, ceiling 2000 — because this is the one file in the app that is never rotated, so an uncapped read is worst on exactly the machine where the trail matters most; `total` is every line in the file, so a screen showing fifty of nine thousand can say so rather than implying it is the history. A line that does not parse is SKIPPED and counted in `unreadable` rather than failing the call: the same judgement append_to makes, for the same reason — a half-written final line from a process killed mid-append must not make the rest unreadable, and damage in the file is itself something the reader needs to be told. Read-only and never audited itself: reading a record is not an act the record is for. No workspace is required — the trail lives beside the logs, not in the workspace, so it answers on a machine whose checkout has been moved. An absent file is an empty trail rather than an error, because nothing irreversible having been done yet is the normal state. `action` comes back as a string rather than the writer's &'static str, so a verb this build no longer emits still reads back — which is what an unrotated historical record means. Each record may carry `undo` — what would put the act back, or the sentence saying why nothing would — and `undone`, which is DERIVED on read rather than stored: the file is append-only, so an act cannot be edited to say it was reversed, and the later `undo` line naming its `at` is the only honest way to know. Lines written before those fields existed read normally; they simply carry neither. See src-tauri/src/audit.rs.

args.at: string (the `at` of the line to put back)

audit_undo.why: A record that says what an assistant did and cannot put it back is half of the answer. The compensation is worked out BEFORE the tool runs — what `stackvo_stack_down` stopped exists only before it stopped it — and stored on the line, so what is offered later is what was true at the time rather than a guess about a machine that has since changed.
audit_undo.notes: Executes the plan on the named line and nothing else: the steps are MCP tool names and they go through `mcp::call`, so the record and the act cannot drift apart. Three refusals, each its own answer: UNSUPPORTED when the line carries no compensation — a restart went through the state an undo would return to, a generate overwrote output that was not kept, a reissue replaced a certificate that was not kept, and the line's own sentence is repeated rather than a second one invented; UNSUPPORTED when the act did not happen, because a refused or failed call carries no plan and reversing something that never ran is a change nobody asked for; CONFLICT when it was already put back, which is a read of the append-only join rather than an edit — the original line still says what it said, and a later `undo` line names its `at`. NOT_FOUND for an `at` that is not in the last 2000 lines. A sequence, not a transaction: if the fourth of six steps fails the first three stay done, `Undone` carries how many of how many ran, and the failing step's error is what comes back. Audited as `undo` whichever way it went — a half-completed undo is the line somebody most needs to find later. The grant used is the full one deliberately: this is the app, with the person at the keyboard, running a plan the app wrote itself; applying an assistant's limit to the human undoing the assistant would be the wrong way round. See src-tauri/src/undo.rs.

policy_status.returns: { active: boolean, source: string|null, managed: string[], locked: string[], registryPrefix: string|null, images: PolicyImage[], market: PolicyMarket, error: string|null }
policy_status.why: A fleet of machines has settings somebody other than the person at the keyboard cares about — the domain suffix, the web server, and on a network without Docker Hub the registry every image is pulled from. Without this the Settings panes can only grey a field out, and a greyed-out field with no reason reads as a broken app rather than a managed one.
policy_status.notes: Reads one JSON file: /Library/Managed Preferences/com.stackvo.desktop.json on macOS, %ProgramData%\StackVo\policy.json on Windows, /etc/stackvo/policy.json on Linux; STACKVO_POLICY_FILE overrides all three. Read once per process, like every managed-preferences reader — a restart is how a change is picked up. This is NOT a security boundary and must not be presented as one: the override variable and, usually, the file itself are within the user's reach. `managed` and `locked` carry keys only, never values — env_get redacts secrets and this must not be a way around that. `error` is a parse or rule failure and is returned rather than swallowed, because a policy that quietly does nothing is one the administrator believes is in force; a broken file yields an empty policy and never a refusal to start. See src-tauri/src/policy.rs. The `market` block reports where packages may come from. It is reported in full rather than as one flag because its whole purpose is to let somebody who has just been refused an install read WHICH rule refused it. `additionalKeys` is a count, not the keys.

policy_compliance.returns: { active: boolean, source?: string, clauses: Array<{ id: string, subject: string, state: 'holding' | 'bypassed' | 'silent' | 'unmeasured', detail?: string }>, holding: number, bypassed: number, silent: number, unmeasured: number, attestable: boolean }
policy_compliance.why: policy_status answers what the administrator's file SAYS. Nothing answered whether any of it is in force on this machine, which is the question the person who deployed the file has. The two come apart for one reason and it is not misconduct: a policy arrives on a machine that was already set up. The registry mirror rewrites references as files are GENERATED, so a project nobody regenerated since Tuesday still pulls from Docker Hub. allowedPackages is checked as something is INSTALLED, so a service installed last month stays installed when the list that would have refused it lands today. requireSignature decides what the NEXT refresh accepts and says nothing about the index already cached.
policy_compliance.notes: Four states, and the third is the one that makes the report honest. `silent` means the policy has no opinion: every list in the market block means "no opinion" when empty, never "none", and a report that folded that into a pass would score a machine with no policy at all as fully compliant. `unmeasured` means no evidence either way and its reason is always in `detail` — it covers a fact this app cannot see (the generated tree would not read, a package manifest would not load) AND a clause with nothing here to apply to (a pin naming a repository this build never runs), because neither is evidence of compliance. `attestable` is false while anything is bypassed OR unmeasured, and it is named attestable rather than compliant deliberately: verify makes the OPPOSITE call with its `unknown` because it asks "can I work?", where an unasked question is not evidence of trouble; this asks "can somebody sign their name to this?", where it is exactly what must not be swallowed. And the layer being reported on is not a security boundary — policy.rs says so in its first paragraph — so this is not a certificate. Every measurement is of state already on disk: the .env as written (Env::parse, not load — load applies the policy last, so asking the loaded environment whether the policy took effect is a question whose answer is true by construction), the generated tree, the package directory, the remembered catalogue source, the override files, the project manifests. The engine is never asked, because a compliance report that needs Docker running is one nobody can run when they most need it. The mirror clause is answered by the mirror itself — if policy::rewrite over a file's own bytes would change them, it never reached that file — rather than by a second scanner here, which would be a second opinion about build stages and already-qualified registries and the wrong one would be this one's. Ids are stable and the UI holds the sentence, the preflight arrangement. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/compliance.rs.

preflight.why: Everything that has to be true before the app can do anything: a checkout, a reachable daemon, compose v2, the shared network, a projects directory, bash, and mkcert. Without it the app opened regardless and each button failed on its own terms — three different errors, one cause each, none stated up front.
preflight.notes: Runs before the first screen. `Unknown` is a distinct state from failure: with the engine down there is no answer to "does the network exist", and reporting one sends the user after the wrong problem. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

preflight_fix.why: A requirement that reports a problem the app could have fixed itself is a diagnosis pretending to be a product. `fixable` on each Requirement says which ids this accepts.
preflight_fix.notes: Rejects any id it cannot fix rather than silently succeeding — a no-op that returns Ok would report the requirement as repaired on the next poll and it would still be broken. Accepts 'network', 'projects' and 'engine'; the UI reaches engine start through engine_start (it polls for the daemon coming up), the 'engine' arm here is for headless callers. Declared retroactively.

prefs_get.notes: Replaces the localStorage-backed usePreferences composable with the Tauri store plugin.

preset_apply.notes: Re-plans from the file rather than trusting a plan the frontend hands back: between the review and the click, .env may have been changed by a service toggle in another pane, and writing a stale diff would silently undo it. Writes through env_writer, which backs the file up, preserves comments and ordering, and serialises against the other .env writers. `needsRegenerate` says what has to happen next — enabling a service changes what the generator emits, so the change is not live until regenerate-then-up.

preset_export.why: The roadmap said "turn the commit-friendly stackvo.json into a flow". Read against the code that framing is wrong: stackvo.json needs no flow — it is already in the project directory, already schema-validated, and a teammate who clones the repo already has it. What they do NOT get is the STACK: which of the twenty services are enabled and at which versions. That lives in .env, the one file nobody commits, because it is also where every password is. So the clone succeeds, the manifest is perfect, and the project still will not start until somebody says "you need MySQL 8.0, Redis and Elasticsearch on". That sentence is the preset.
preset_export.notes: A preset can never carry a secret, and that is enforced by construction rather than by filtering. `services` entries hold `enabled` and `version` — two named fields, not a passthrough map — so there is no code path by which SERVICE_MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD reaches one; it is not that a filter drops it, it is that there is nowhere to put it. `settings` is an ALLOW-LIST of five global keys, not a deny-list: Env::is_secret matches on suffix, so a key added upstream tomorrow called SERVICE_FOO_APIKEY would sail through a deny-list. An allow-list fails closed against a file this app does not own. Disabled services are included too — a preset listing only what is on cannot express "and turn Elasticsearch off", which is half of what makes two machines match. Ports and paths are excluded on purpose: they are properties of one developer's machine, and importing somebody else's is how two people end up fighting over 3306.

preset_plan.why: Importing a colleague's stack must never be a blind write over your own. Same shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and cert_plan/cert_apply — the pattern this app already uses everywhere a change leaves its own process.
preset_plan.notes: Rejections are NAMED, never silently dropped: an unknown service id, or a settings key outside the allow-list, appears in `rejected` with its reason. A preset that quietly ignores half of what it was given is how somebody concludes the feature works and then spends an afternoon on the service it skipped. Unknown ids are refused here rather than becoming a SERVICE_<JUNK>_ENABLE key in the user's .env and a compose profile that matches nothing — the failure mode CONFLICTS.md C-09 records. A file that is valid JSON but not a preset (`kind` mismatch) is an error, not a plan with zero changes: pointing the importer at a package.json has to say so rather than look successful. A preset from a NEWER version is refused rather than half-read.

preset_save.notes: Pretty-printed, because the point of the file is being read in a pull request. Written atomically.

profiler_clear.why: Profiling fills a disk fast — the 200,000-iteration loop that shaped the parser produced a 10 MB file from one run — so "clear these" has to be one button, not sixty.

profiler_delete.notes: `id` is a bare `cachegrind.out.*` file name, checked before it is joined to a path — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open runs on.

profiler_flame.why: And the reason the word flame graph can now be used. profiler_tree draws what cachegrind holds — the SUMMED cost of "A called B" over every place A called B — so a function reached from two callers is one box carrying both, and no arrangement of those edges recovers which caller was expensive. An Xdebug trace holds every entry and exit with its depth, which is a stack: folding those gives one box per distinct path, with its own measured width. MUST be a separate command from profiler_tree rather than a flag on it, because the two are different claims about the same picture and a reader cannot tell them apart by looking.

profiler_read.notes: Cachegrind, read off real Xdebug 3.4.0 output rather than from a specification. Four properties decide the parser. (1) Names are COMPRESSED and the ids are NOT in order — a real file defined fl=(2) before fl=(1), and cfn=(n) can reference a name defined further down, so names are resolved at the end; resolving as you read produces blanks. (2) Every call gets its own block: a 200,000-iteration loop produced **200,004 fn= blocks across 1.6 million lines**, so aggregating by name is not a nicety. (3) A cost line's meaning depends on what preceded it — after fn= it is SELF cost, after calls= it is the INCLUSIVE cost of that call, attributed to the callee. Getting that wrong doubles every caller's self time and is invisible in the output. (4) Units are declared in the file (`events: Time_(10ns) Memory_(bytes)`), not fixed — assuming microseconds would be wrong by two orders of magnitude on this build. `percent` is a share of `selfTotal`, not of the file's `summary`: that denominator is the one that makes "how much of the work happened in here" true and adds to 100. A gzipped file is REFUSED with an explanation rather than parsed into nonsense. Capped at 256 MB with `truncated` reported, because a truncated profile with no warning is a performance conclusion drawn from half the data.

args.name: string
args.develop: boolean? — omit to leave it as it was

profiler_set_mode.notes: `coverage` is the fourth mode and the only one that records nothing of its own: it switches on the API PHPUnit calls, and the report is written by PHPUnit. So `profiles` and `traces` stay empty for it and a screen MUST NOT offer a recording list. `develop` is NOT a fifth mode — `xdebug.mode` is a list, and `develop` is what makes var_dump readable and puts a stack trace on a warning, so it rides alongside whichever mode is set and XDEBUG_MODE becomes e.g. `debug,develop`. Omitting the argument leaves it as it was, because the mode picker and the develop switch are two controls over one file and a picker that cleared the other every time would be a setting nobody could keep. Stored in `projects/<name>/.stackvo/xdebug.json`, beside php.ini and devserver.json, for the same two reasons: the manifest schema is additionalProperties:false, and a file under .stackvo/ travels with a clone. On/off stays in `php.extensions`, because that is what compiles the extension in. Switching to `profile` writes `generated/xdebug/<name>.ini` and mounts it read-only at /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/zzz-stackvo-xdebug.ini. **Why an ini and not the environment**: measured against a running container, XDEBUG_CONFIG does carry `output_dir` and `start_with_request` — both took effect — but it silently ignores `use_compression`, and Xdebug 3.4 gzips by default. One compressed file is the difference between a profile view and a parse error. `zzz-` rather than `zz-` because zz-stackvo.ini is the USER's php.ini from php_ini_set; a name sorting before it would let a hand-written xdebug.output_dir send profiles somewhere this app cannot read, which presents as profiling that produced nothing. The mode itself stays in XDEBUG_MODE and is deliberately absent from the ini: the environment variable takes precedence over xdebug.mode, so setting both invites them to disagree.

profiler_status.why: P3-17 named Blackfire and SPX, and both are the wrong door. Blackfire ships a template already and needs an ACCOUNT — a signup wall in a local development tool. SPX, XHProf and Excimer are not in contracts/php-extensions.json (only xdebug is), so adding one is a change to a contract shared with upstream, the same class of decision as the Mailpit swap. **Xdebug is already a profiler**: xdebug.mode=profile writes cachegrind files, the extension is in the catalog, and the overlay that sets XDEBUG_MODE already belongs to this app. That is the one route with no contract change attached.
profiler_status.notes: Profiling is a MODE of the existing Xdebug toggle, not a second switch — the extension has to be compiled in either way, and two switches for one extension is two states to explain instead of one. The mode is `debug` or `profile`, never both: they want opposite start triggers (stepping wants to connect on the next request, profiling wants a trigger so an idle stack does not write a multi-megabyte file per page load), so a combined mode would have to break one of them. `trigger` is the name a request must carry — XDEBUG_TRIGGER as a cookie, GET, POST or environment value.

profiler_tree.why: `profiler_read` answers where the time went — a table of the costliest functions — and cannot answer what called that, which is the question a flame view exists for. The parser was already reading caller→callee edges to attribute inclusive cost and was discarding the caller.
profiler_tree.notes: A call TREE, not strictly a flame graph, and the difference is stated rather than glossed: a flame graph is built from sampled stacks, so a box's width is how often that exact path appeared. Cachegrind holds no stacks — it holds edges summed over every place A called B. A function called from two places is one box here with the total, two boxes there. What a branch means is 'reaching B through A cost this much in total', which is answerable and is the question people bring to a profile; 'this path was taken this often' is not, and no arrangement of the edges recovers it. Separate from profiler_read because the tree is thousands of nodes and the table is sixty rows. Recursion stops at the first repeat on the path and the frame is kept and marked. See src-tauri/src/profile.rs.

args.name: string
args.spec: ProjectSpec (optional — defaults to what was detected)
args.overrides: { domain?, phpVersion?, server?, extensions? } — each replaces one detected value

project_adopt.why: Writes stackvo.json for a directory that is already there, then regenerates. The counterpart of project_create, which requires the directory to be absent.
project_adopt.notes: Refuses when a manifest already exists — adopting a managed project would silently overwrite settings the user chose. The spec is validated against project.schema.json exactly as project_create's is; detection fills the form, it does not bypass the check. `overrides` sit on top of detection rather than replacing it, one value at a time: detection reads the code and can say "this is Laravel, its document root is public", but it has no way to know the user wanted `shop.loc`, and the three PHP fields are the scaffolding gap — a composer.json states the version the framework NEEDS (`"php": "^8.3"`), which read as an answer pins a new Laravel to the floor of its own range, nothing in a checkout names a web server, and detection has no opinion about extensions at all, so an adopted project took the generator's seven-entry fallback. The PHP three apply only when the detected spec has a `php` block, so a Node template cannot pick up a second runtime block (W-02). Passing a full spec still bypasses detection entirely; passing overrides does not. Also writes the project's hosts entry and extends the certificate — see project_create.

args.names: string[] — folder names under the project directory

project_adopt_many.why: The project directory IS what Herd and Valet call a park, and `project_adoptable` already reads every child of it and says what each one is — but the list offered one button per row, so a machine with eleven unmanaged checkouts needed eleven clicks. On the checkout project_adoptable was written against, 11 of 21 directories were in that state.
project_adopt_many.notes: Not a loop over project_adopt, and the difference is measurable in three places. `generate` rewrites the WHOLE `projects` scope under one global lock, so n adoptions as n calls cost n full passes over n projects, serialised — here every manifest is written first and the generator runs once. `sync_project_host` raises the system authentication dialog when a name is missing from /etc/hosts; its own comment argues that three subdomains must not ask three times, and eleven projects asking eleven times is that argument one level up, so the hosts write moved into a helper that takes every name at once. And a loop that stops on the first error leaves "some of them worked": every folder gets an outcome here. `skipped` is not `failed` — a folder that already carries a stackvo.json (the list can be a minute old) and a folder holding nothing but dotfiles are both ordinary. An unsafe name, a spec that does not validate or a manifest that cannot be written fails that folder alone. If the GENERATOR fails, every manifest this call wrote is removed and the call returns the error: the state it would otherwise leave — n projects listed and none generated — is exactly what project_register had to be invented to repair, and somebody who pressed one button should not have to know that. Names are deduplicated first, or the same name twice would take the same in-flight guard twice and the batch would report itself busy. Errors: INVALID_INPUT when the list is empty.

project_adoptable.why: `project_create` refuses when the directory already exists, so a folder cloned into projects/ could not be brought under management at all — the only way in was writing stackvo.json by hand. On the checkout this was written against, 11 of 21 directories under projects/ were in that state: real code, unmanaged.
project_adoptable.notes: Reads only, and needs no Docker. Each entry carries a detected runtime, server, document root and framework, plus the files that detection was based on — a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404, which is a failure with no error attached to it.

project_clone.returns: { operationId: OperationId, name: string, hasManifest: boolean }
project_clone.why: The only way a repository reached the workspace was the user cloning it in a terminal and then adopting the folder. The clone is the one step the app was not doing, and it is the first one.
project_clone.notes: StackVo authenticates NOTHING. No keys, no agent, no known_hosts, no tokens, no host trust — git and ssh read the user's own config, and a URL that works in their terminal works here. GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 and GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15' are set for one reason only: a windowless subprocess must fail rather than wait for an answer nobody can give. StrictHostKeyChecking is deliberately NOT disabled — silently trusting an unknown host is the one failure worth stopping for. No host is special-cased; a self-hosted forge on a company domain is the case this was built for. The URL is the first webview-supplied string in this codebase to reach a subprocess argv, so `git::parse` is an allowlist of two shapes (ssh/https URL, or scp-style user@host:path) rather than a filter: `ext::` transports execute commands, a leading `-` is read by git as an option, and file:// is not a network fetch. Emits scaffold:progress / scaffold:done deliberately — same step of the same flow, and the console already subscribes. Ends with code on disk. `hasManifest` says which follow-up the caller owes, and the two are opposites: a repository without a stackvo.json is adopted (detect, then write one), a repository with one is registered (the committed settings are the team's answer and are not overwritten). Cloning a repository that ships its manifest — the arrangement the file is commit-friendly for — used to end in "already has a stackvo.json" with nothing generated. Either way a clone never becomes a second way to create a project.

project_create.notes: Writes the manifest, runs generate, then builds. The build half is what makes it an operation rather than a mutation.

project_delete.notes: remove_files is NEW and MUST default to false. The current deleteProject() removes the project directory outright with no confirmation contract — a desktop app deleting user source code needs an explicit opt-in. The flag guards the user's CODE and nothing else: deleting a project always removes its container (web, worker sidecars, tunnel), every image tagged stackvo-<name>, generated/projects/<name>, logs/projects/<name>, its /etc/hosts line if StackVo wrote it, and its name from the certificate — all of which exist only because the project did. Docker-side cleanup is best effort and logged: a stopped engine is a fine moment to stop managing a project, and making the daemon a lock on deletion would be worse than a leftover image. Traefik needs nothing extra — project routing is compose labels, so it goes with the regenerated compose file. Named volumes likewise: a project service declares only bind mounts. Build cache is NOT touched; it is shared and global, and pruning it belongs to docker_prune.

project_devcontainer_plan.why: The competitor row read "the generator already renders compose, and .devcontainer/devcontainer.json is a small sibling of it" — and that was written without reading render_compose_service. What the generator writes is bound to THIS machine in five ways, every one load-bearing: absolute paths under the user's home, a `context:` relative to `generated/`, the shared `stackvo-net`, Traefik labels in a file with no Traefik in it, and the backing services in a different compose file rendered with values pulled from the OS keystore. Copied into a repository it cannot start anywhere. So this is a second rendering of the same manifest, not the first one relabelled.
project_devcontainer_plan.notes: A plan and not a write, because the destination is somebody's repository: `.devcontainer/` exists TO be committed, which is exactly why it should be readable before it is there. Nothing runs from generation either — agentctx writes into the project on every generate and says in the file that `.stackvo/` is not meant to be committed; this is the opposite, and a file that appears in `git status` because somebody pressed Start is a file they learn to `git checkout`. The Dockerfile is the GENERATOR'S own for PHP, not a second renderer — the whole value is that the container is the one StackVo builds, and it needs no adjustment because the PHP image never copies the source. The runtimes are the exception and it is release.rs's asymmetry from the other side: their Dockerfile does `COPY . .`, installs, builds and ends in a CMD, which is a snapshot of the application and the wrong thing to open a terminal in, so they get the toolchain, `sleep infinity`, and the install moved to postCreateCommand where it runs against the mount. Services are rendered from THEIR OWN packages' fragments through the same strict substituter the workspace uses — not a table of image names written here, because this application carries no service definitions, and because the mapping from `settings.ROOT_PASSWORD` to MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD exists only in that package's template (a compose file that starts mysql with no root password does not start). Six variables are answered differently and they are exactly the ones that name this machine: `file.*` becomes a relative path, `instance.logs` a named volume, secret settings a `${DEV_…}` placeholder, `network` the implicit `default`, `instance.domain` localhost, and `port.*` keeps the host number this workspace allocated — deliberately, because it is the one already in the author's database client. Container names are kept exactly (`stackvo-mysql-8-4`): the project's own .env names those hosts. Traefik labels are stripped, because they name a host that resolves nowhere and would quietly start binding on a team that does run Traefik. A rendered config file holding a placeholder is refused rather than written wrong — `${…}` is expanded by Compose in a compose file and is five literal characters in a my.cnf.

project_devcontainer_write.returns: string[] — the paths written, relative to the project
project_devcontainer_write.why: The other half. The plan is what the user reads; this is what puts it in the repository.
project_devcontainer_write.notes: Re-plans rather than taking the plan back from the caller: a plan that travelled to JavaScript and back is a plan the front end could have edited, and what it names is a path inside a directory this app writes to. Every file every time — these are rendered outputs, and a hand-edit that survived a regeneration would be a difference between the file and the manifest that nothing reports. A `.gitignore` holding `.env` is written whenever there are placeholders: the whole point of the placeholder is that the value does not travel, and the file the reader is about to create is the file that would undo it. Audited as `project_devcontainer_write`. Errors: NOT_FOUND when the project directory is gone.

project_dockerfile_preview.why: Runs the Rust generator port alongside the Bash one so its output can be compared before it replaces anything. `matchesBashOutput` is the differential check, live against the user's own projects rather than only against fixtures.
project_dockerfile_preview.notes: Strict mode is the behaviour change made visible: where Bash silently drops an incompatible extension, this refuses and names it. `skipped` always reports what compat mode would have dropped, so the difference is legible either way.

project_get.why: ProjectDetail.vue currently re-fetches the whole list and filters client-side.

project_hooks_approve.why: Approves this project's HOST commands exactly as they are now. The digest is sent back rather than recomputed server-side, and that round trip is the point: it is a receipt for the list the person actually read. MUST refuse when the manifest changed between the screen being drawn and the button being pressed — that refusal is what makes this consent rather than a checkbox. Container steps are never gated: the container already runs the repository's code.

project_hooks_plan.returns: HookPlan[] — one per event, in lifecycle order
project_hooks_plan.why: A hook is a command from a repository somebody cloned, so what would run has to be readable before it does.

project_hooks_revoke.why: Withdraws approval. Takes no digest — you may always revoke.

project_lan_share.why: `shop.loc` exists in exactly one place — this machine's /etc/hosts — so opening the site on a real phone has never been possible without editing a file on that phone. This writes the intent; `lan_status` derives the name.
project_lan_share.notes: Writes `lan_share` and nothing else. The hostname is NOT stored: sslip.io resolves an address out of the name arithmetically, so the name is computed from whatever this machine's address is at the moment it is asked for — a stored one would survive a DHCP lease and point at whichever machine took it next. Regeneration is still the caller's, exactly as it is for every other manifest change; a switch that quietly rebuilt the workspace would be doing an expensive thing behind a cheap-looking control.

project_local_read.why: A committed manifest is what makes a checkout reproducible and is exactly why there was nowhere to say “on this machine, PHP 8.3”. Reads the overlay beside it.

project_local_write.why: Text rather than a parsed object: this is a file somebody types, and a struct round-trip would reformat what they wrote. Empty text removes the file — “no overrides” and “an empty overrides file” are the same state and only one of them is something to wonder about in a directory listing. MUST reject `name` and `runtime`, and MUST validate the merged document rather than the fragment.

project_manifest_text.why: The manifest editor edits the FILE, not the reader's view of it. Manifest is spelled for this boundary — `documentRoot`, `lanShare` — and the file spells them `document_root` and `lan_share`, so a payload handed to a text editor and posted back through project_manifest_write silently dropped both: the document root became `public` and LAN sharing switched itself off. The file's own bytes have no such gap. Refused with the reader's error when the file does not parse, rather than offering to save over something this app never understood.

project_manifest_write.why: Editing an existing project is impossible today — the UI can only create and delete. MUST honour the write rules in project.schema.json (extensions last, one runtime block).

project_providers.why: And the largest gap the competitor review found: DDEV ships `ddev pull`/`ddev push` with recipes for Upsun, Acquia, Lagoon and Pantheon, Lando and Herd have their own, and the concept did not exist here at all — `grep -rn 'fn pull|pull_db|remote_db|rsync' src-tauri/src` returned nothing.
project_providers.notes: Both directions of every recipe, PLANNED, before anything is spawned — the review-then-apply shape this app uses for every act it cannot take back, and it matters more here than in most: the reader is about to hand somebody else's command their production credentials, and "it ran and something happened" is not reviewable afterwards. A direction a provider does not offer is returned NAMED rather than omitted, so a card showing one button for one recipe and two for another does not leave its reader guessing whether the recipe is short or the app is broken. Secrets appear BY NAME and never as values — the plan travels to a web view. Problems travel beside the plans rather than replacing them: three good recipes and one typo is three buttons and one sentence, not an error page.

project_register.why: project_adopt refuses a directory that already has a stackvo.json, and refuses correctly — it must not overwrite settings somebody chose. But that was only half an answer: the compose files, the hosts entry and the certificate had not happened either, and nothing else did them. The manifest watcher reports a change and regenerates nothing, on purpose.
project_register.notes: The other half. Reads and schema-checks the manifest that is already there, generates, syncs the hosts entry and the certificate, and writes nothing back — a committed manifest is the team's answer, and the Manifest tab is where it changes. Refuses when there is no stackvo.json, because that is adoption's job. Fixes the manual case too: a repository cloned into projects/ by hand with its manifest committed was skipped by project_adoptable and rejected by project_adopt, so it never came online at all.

project_requirements.returns: { declared: Array<{ id: string, known: boolean, enabled: boolean }>, suggested: Array<{ service: string, key: string }>, plan: Plan, preset: { path: string, name: string | null, description: string | null, plan: Plan } | null }
project_requirements.why: herd.yml, .lerd.yaml and .ddev/config.yaml all describe the whole environment and are committed, so a teammate clones and runs one command. stackvo.json carried the project and a preset carried the stack, and the two never met. `services` in the manifest is the missing half; this reports what the repository declares, what this machine gives it, and the diff.
project_requirements.notes: `preset` is the project's `stackvo.preset.json`, if it ships one — the half a manifest cannot carry: `services` says WHICH services, a preset says which VERSIONS and the shareable settings beside them. The path had no convention before this, which was the whole of what was missing: the export wrote a file, the import read one, and between them somebody had to say where they had put it. It is beside `stackvo.json` now, so a clone brings it. Reported, never applied — `preset_apply` is the same plan-then-apply shape hosts_plan/hosts_apply uses, and a file that arrived with somebody else's clone must not rewrite your stack because you opened a page. A preset that will not parse reads as no preset rather than taking this whole answer off the screen. Reads only. `declared` comes from the manifest — the statement a colleague agreed to — and `suggested` from the project's own .env, which is a guess and is kept separate for that reason; suggestions already declared are dropped. A suggestion carries the KEY that implied it and never the value, because that file holds credentials. `plan` is produced by the same planner preset_plan uses, so an unknown service id is rejected there by name rather than becoming a SERVICE_<JUNK>_ENABLE key. See src-tauri/src/detect.rs `services_from_env` for what counts as evidence.

project_requirements_apply.why: Turns the declaration into an enabled stack, through the plan-then-apply path a preset import already uses rather than a second one with its own rules.
project_requirements_apply.notes: Writes .env and stops, exactly as preset_apply does: the returned plan says needsRegenerate and regenerating is a visible step with its own progress. Never disables anything — a project declares what it needs, and one project not needing Redis is not a statement that another project's Redis should stop. Never writes a version: there is one SERVICE_<NAME>_VERSION per workspace, so a project pinning one would change every other project's database. Re-plans inside the call, so a .env changed between the review and the click is not overwritten with a stale diff.

project_requirements_declare.why: Writes the `services` list into stackvo.json, which is the file that gets committed — the point of the feature is that the next person to clone does not have to be told.
project_requirements_declare.notes: Reads the manifest, replaces one list and writes it back, so a field this version of the UI does not know about cannot be lost on the round trip. Ids are trimmed, lower-cased and de-duplicated the same way manifest::read normalises them. An unknown id is a WARNING and not an error: an invalid manifest is a project the app refuses to build, and a typo in an optional field must not take a project offline.

project_scaffold.why: The create half of P0-1 (detection/adoption shipped first). Runs the framework's own installer in a throwaway container — composer create-project, wp-cli, create-next-app — so nothing is installed on the host and only the bind-mounted project directory survives.
project_scaffold.notes: Ends where adoption begins: the UI follows with project_adopt, which detects runtime/server/document root from what the installer actually wrote — the same machinery as a git clone. Nine installers, every command pinned non-interactive — each flag measured against a real container rather than read off a README (nuxi needs both --template and --force; sv needs --no-add-ons; astro needs --yes). The JavaScript ones pass --no-install: the node Dockerfile installs for the container's platform, and a host node_modules in the image is the arm64-in-amd64 mistake NODE_DOCKERIGNORE exists to prevent (a prompt inside an operation console is a hang, not a question). On unix runs --user uid:gid so files land owned by the user, not root. Refuses a non-empty directory; a failed install that wrote nothing removes the husk so the retry is not blocked. Seventeen installers now, across PHP, JavaScript, Python and Ruby. Composer projects carry --ignore-platform-reqs because the installer container is not the machine the code runs on (CakePHP wants ext-intl, the composer image has none, and StackVo's PHP image does); Rails needs the full ruby image rather than slim, which cannot compile websocket-driver. Twenty-nine templates in two kinds: an installer container where the ecosystem has a scaffolder, and **written files** where it does not — Gin, Echo, Flask, FastAPI, Sinatra and Rocket are each 'write two files and let the language build them', so pulling an image to write thirty lines would be a download for nothing. Their dependencies are not skipped, they move: the project's own Dockerfile already runs pip/go build/bundle/cargo for the container's platform. Every written template binds 0.0.0.0 on the port lang_defaults gives its runtime — a test asserts it over code lines only, because the comments explaining the loopback trap were tripping the check.

project_sidecars.returns: DeclaredSidecar[] — one per declared container, in the order the manifest lists them
project_sidecars.why: A repository may declare a container of its own, which answers 'can I have Ollama or Qdrant' with 'write a sidecars block'. Both were true and neither was reachable: the block was parsed, validated and rendered into the project's compose file, and NOTHING showed it. `hooks` — the sibling block, from the same manifest — has had a pane since it was written. So the answer an ADR points at was a feature nobody could find, which is the same as not having it.
project_sidecars.notes: Reads the manifest and nothing else; a project with no `sidecars` key answers with an empty list rather than an error, because declaring none is the ordinary case. The two derived names are the whole reason this is a command rather than a field the view reads off the manifest it already has: `container` is what the application connects to (`stackvo-<project>-<id>`) and `volume` is what `docker volume` calls the state, and both are derived by `sidecar::container_name` / `sidecar::volume_name`. Deriving them in JavaScript would be a second copy of a naming rule whose whole purpose is that two clones of one repository cannot collide. Nothing here reaches the host: a sidecar has no host port and no host path by construction (project.schema.json), so there is no address to report and the reply says so by not carrying one.

project_components.returns: DeclaredComponent[] — one per declared component, in the order the manifest lists them
project_components.why: ServBay and FlyEnv both run many languages and in both the unit is a SITE: one directory, one runtime, one hostname. A repository holding api/ in Go, web/ in Next.js and worker/ in Python is three sites there — three entries to create, three to start, three to remember are related — and nothing in the tool knows they are one thing. Nothing in this category treats a monorepo as a single subject, and a local binary cannot: a directory has one runtime because the binary serving it has one. Every piece of the other answer was already here — eight runtimes, a Dockerfile renderer for each, Traefik routers generated per hostname — and what was missing was a manifest that could say so.
project_components.notes: Reads the manifest and nothing else; a project with no `components` key answers with an empty list rather than an error, which is every project that existed before the field. The containment is sidecar.rs's and carries over exactly: NO HOST PORT (a published port would be two clones of one repository fighting over the same number, and a declaration asking for one is refused BY NAME at parse time), the `path` stays inside the project (`..`, an absolute path and `.` itself are all refused — a build context is what Docker reads everything under), the container is NAMED FROM THE PROJECT using sidecar::container_name itself rather than a copy of it (they share one namespace on the machine, so an id used by both is a manifest warning rather than two declarations quietly producing one container), and it shares the project's compose PROFILE so `--profile project-shop` brings the whole repository up — the “one up” half of the item. PHP is deliberately not a component runtime and is refused by name with the reason: a PHP part needs a web server, a document root and a php.ini overlay, which the project's own runtime already renders, which does not generalise to several inside one project, and over which differential fixtures are frozen. A component domain does NOT go into `aliases`: an alias is another name for the project's OWN container and reaches its Traefik rule, while a component domain names a different container — merging them would route api.shop.loc to the PHP app. They meet in Manifest::extra_hostnames, which is what /etc/hosts and the certificate read, so both get an entry and a SAN with no change to either module. Two components on one domain is refused where the message can name both, and the FIRST one stands because file order is the only tie-break that is not arbitrary. A broken component is a WARNING beside the ones that parsed, the trade manifest already makes for hooks and sidecars. Everything is gated on the block being non-empty, so a single-runtime project renders byte for byte what it always did — the property fixtures_differential.rs freezes. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/component.rs.

project_validate.why: Pre-flight the new-project form against project.schema.json + php-extensions.json before anything touches disk. Today a bad extension name is only discovered when the Docker build fails minutes later.

projects_idle.why: Reports the idle time even with the threshold off — the number is worth seeing before somebody chooses what to set it to.

project_verify.returns: { project: string, checks: Array<{ id: string, subject: string, state: 'ok' | 'missing' | 'different' | 'unknown', detail?: string }>, ready: boolean }
project_verify.why: Every tool in this category does the setting-up half of onboarding and none does the checking half — which is the question somebody actually has an hour after cloning: not "how do I set this up" but "I did set it up; why does it still not work?". The repository already declares what it needs; what was missing was the sentence back.
project_verify.notes: Nothing new is measured. Four of the five facts come from `projects_list` — whether the manifest validated, whether the image was ever built here, whether the generated tree is older than the manifest, whether the domain resolves — and the fifth from the instance table, so a second derivation of any of them cannot disagree with the first. Every check carries a stable `id` and the UI holds the label and what to do about it, the arrangement preflight states for the same reason: a check gains a translation by being added to a locale file rather than by having English compiled into the binary. A declared service has three failure modes and they are three different sentences: in the catalogue but not installed (`service`, missing), installed but switched off (`serviceOff`, different, with the versions that ARE there named — "install it" would be the wrong instruction), and a name this build has never heard of (`unknownService`, unknown). `unknown` deliberately does NOT hold `ready` back: a check this app declined to make is not evidence that something is wrong, and a verifier that says not-ready for a question it did not ask is one people learn to override. A version the declaration does not pin is reported as ok with the version found beside it rather than judged — saying which version SHOULD be there needs a lock file, which is a separate item. Also reachable as `stackvo verify <project>`. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/verify.rs.
