When the project has a stackvo.lock (project_lock), a declared service is held against the version AND the package digest it was locked at, which adds three answers this could not previously give: `lockedVersion` (the wrong version is running), `lockedPackage` (the right version out of a different package — the substitution a version list cannot see) and `lockExtra` (the lock names a service the manifest no longer declares, so the repair is to re-lock rather than to install anything). Without a lock the behaviour is unchanged. A lock file that is there and will not parse is an ERROR rather than being read as "no lock": somebody wrote it and is entitled to be told it is not being used, and the weaker answer would look identical on screen. THE LARAVEL HALF, added later and needing no new measurement: `composer.json`'s `require` block states what the project needs of the PLATFORM, and detect.rs already turns a constraint like ^8.3 into 8.3 — it has used that to CHOOSE a PHP line at adoption all along, and the two were simply never compared again afterwards. `phpVersion` holds that against the manifest's php.version, and the failure it catches is frequent and expensive: composer.json says ^8.3, stackvo.json says 8.2, the image builds without complaint and `composer install` dies inside the container with a platform requirement error that names PHP and does not name the file that has to change. `phpExtension` is the second half — each `ext-*` in `require` against php.extensions, ONE ROW PER MISSING NAME because the repair is per extension and the name is the whole of it. `require-dev` is deliberately not read: a dev requirement is a tool for the test suite, and failing a project's readiness on one would call a working installation broken. A constraint with no major.minor in it (`*`, a bare `^8`) is `unknown` rather than a guess — first_version says itself that a bare major is not a version this app can pin. A project with no `php` block in its manifest gains no platform lines at all, whatever its composer.json says. The detail carries BOTH numbers even on a pass, because a green tick whose subject cannot be reconstructed is not worth reading.

project_lock.returns: { path: string, locked: Array<{ service: string, version: string, source: string, sha256: string }>, skipped: Array<{ service: string, reason: 'notinstalled' | 'off' }> }
project_lock.why: stackvo.json declares what a project needs AROUND it — "services": ["redis", "mysql"] — and names no versions, which is right: a repository should not have to guess what the person cloning it will have installed. verify.rs wrote the cost of that down in as many words: two machines can both satisfy `redis` while running 7.0 and 7.2, so a version the declaration does not pin was reported as ok with the version found beside it rather than called a match nothing checked. This is the file that closes it — the same division every ecosystem settled on, the manifest is intent and the lock is fact, and both belong in the repository because the second is what makes the first reproducible.
project_lock.notes: Written when somebody asks, NEVER on its own, and that is the whole design: a lock the app refreshed quietly would record whatever the machine drifted to, would therefore always agree with the machine and could never disagree with it — a check that cannot fail is worse than no check. project_verify only ever REPORTS against the file; nothing here installs, switches on, or changes a version. `sha256` is the digest of the package MANIFEST as the registry stated it at install time, copied from instances::PackageRef rather than recomputed, and it is the field that makes this a lock rather than a version list: a re-published 7.2 is a different 7.2, which is the substitution a version list cannot see. Deliberately NOT locked: the runtime and the server (stackvo.json already carries php.version and server, and a second copy of a fact is how two copies disagree), and the images this application itself runs (a property of the machine, not of any one project — one cloudflared, ten projects — and already lockable through the policy file's imagePins). It cannot lock what is not installed or is switched off, and it names which and why rather than writing an entry it invented: a lock file that quietly covers three of five services is one somebody believes covers five. Refused on a manifest that does not validate — a lock is a claim about what a declaration resolved to, and one nobody could read has not resolved to anything. Output is sorted and newline-terminated so the same workspace re-locked twice is byte-identical; a lock whose diff is noise is one people stop reading in a pull request, which is the only place it does its job. A lock written by a newer build is refused rather than read as far as it goes. Also reachable as `stackvo lock <project>`. Not audited: it writes one file, inside the project directory the caller named, that the caller asked for and can delete — the audit trail is for acts nobody can undo by looking at a directory. See src-tauri/src/lock.rs.

bisect_status.returns: { running: boolean, commit?: string, subject?: string, steps?: number, culprit?: string, drift: Array<{ id: 'runtime' | 'service' | 'serviceOff', subject: string, wanted: string, found?: string }> }
bisect_status.why: git bisect moves the code and nothing else. Three months ago the project declared PHP 8.3 and locked redis at 7.0; this machine runs 8.4 and 7.2 — so every step through that range runs OLD CODE AGAINST A NEW ENVIRONMENT and the commit the search finally accuses may be innocent. Nothing in this category does anything about that because nothing in this category knows what environment a commit wanted. This app does: stackvo.json has always travelled with the repository and, since project_lock, stackvo.lock does too — and both are readable AT A REVISION without touching the working tree.
bisect_status.notes: Answers on a repository with no bisect running — `running: false` and nothing else — because the pane asking has to be able to open before anything has started. Whether one is in progress is asked of git's own BISECT_LOG file rather than by running `git bisect log`, which exits non-zero when there is no bisect: an error that means "no" is an error this would have to special-case by message. Not audited: nothing moves. It reports the difference and does not install it, which is the decision the whole feature turns on: bringing the environment along would mean replacing containers whose volumes hold the developer's data, twenty times over a ten-step search, to answer a question about a diff. octane_status.returns: { server: string, octane: boolean, autoReload: boolean, watched: string[] }
octane_status.why: Octane boots the application ONCE and keeps it in memory, so an edited file changes nothing — a route added to routes/web.php does not exist until the workers are replaced, and the developer reloads the page, sees a 404, and goes looking for the mistake in their own code. generator.rs has written octane:start entry points all along; this is the consequence nobody said.
octane_status.notes: `server` is resolved through the ONE derivation — the manifest's value or the workspace default — so this and the generator cannot disagree about what serves the project. `octane` is true only for swoole, roadrunner and frankenphp: nginx, apache and caddy serve through PHP-FPM, which reads the file on every request, so there is nothing to reload and the button is not offered — a no-op with an explanation nobody would find is worse than no button. `watched` is Octane's own default watch list, reported so the pane can say what a save has to touch rather than describe it. See src-tauri/src/octane.rs.

octane_auto_reload.why: Laravel's own answer is `octane:start --watch`, and its price is installing Node and chokidar INTO THE IMAGE — a second file watcher, inside a container, polling a bind mount this application is already watching. Attaching the reload to the watcher that is already running adds nothing to the image, which makes it strictly better than the documented route rather than merely different.
octane_auto_reload.notes: OFF BY DEFAULT, and the default cannot be anything else: a reload that arrives while a request is being served kills that request, and somebody has to decide that is a trade they want. DEBOUNCED BY SECONDS rather than milliseconds — a `composer install` touches thousands of files and one reload per file is a server that never finishes booting; the watcher's own 400ms debounce answers a different question ("did the editor write this file three times"). Stored as a PREFERENCE rather than a manifest field: the manifest travels with the repository and describes what the project IS, while "reload my workers when I save" is what one developer wants on one machine — a colleague should not inherit it from a git pull. The whole map is sent in one key because prefs_set merges shallowly. Not audited: nothing on the machine is changed, and the act is undone by the same switch. See src-tauri/src/octane.rs.

octane_reload.why: The one action that makes an edited file real under Octane, without adding a file watcher to the image.
octane_reload.notes: `octane:reload` rather than a restart: the server replaces its workers and the socket stays open, so nothing outside notices beyond the requests already in flight. Refused when the project is not running — Docker's own "No such container" reads as a broken button rather than as a project that is not started. See src-tauri/src/octane.rs.

dusk_plan.returns: { installed?: string, image: string, declared: boolean, running: boolean, envFilePresent: boolean, envFile: string, isolatedDatabase: boolean }
dusk_plan.why: The mechanism was already here — imports.rs recognises Sail's `selenium` service by name and the manifest has supported sidecars since W-01. What is missing is the half no docker-compose.yml fixes: Dusk drives a browser and that browser has to open https://<domain> from inside a container that does not know this machine's certificate authority. A test that falls over on a certificate warning is a failure that reads as an application bug, and the developer goes looking in their own code.
dusk_plan.notes: `image` follows the ARCHITECTURE this build runs on: `selenium/standalone-chromium` on arm64 and `selenium/standalone-chrome` elsewhere, because Google publishes no arm64 Chrome and that image has no arm64 manifest — on Apple Silicon it either refuses to start or runs under emulation, and a browser under emulation is a suite that times out for a reason nobody finds. Always tagged, never `latest`: an untagged image moves under whoever pulled it last month. `envFile` is the CONTENT that would be written to .env.dusk.local, returned so it can be read before it is written — Dusk loads that file in place of .env for a run, so it is the right place for a driver URL that only means anything while the sidecar is up, and it is never overwritten. The driver URL names the sidecar's CONTAINER rather than localhost: localhost inside the project's container is the project's container, and a sidecar has no host port at all so two clones of one repository cannot fight over 4444. `isolatedDatabase` answers the reason people will not run Dusk locally — it hits a real database rather than a transaction that gets rolled back — and this app's own answer is a worktree with a database of its own; it is REPORTED, never done for somebody. Nothing runs a test suite. See src-tauri/src/dusk.rs.

dusk_apply.why: Declaring the browser container and writing Dusk's environment file, so that `stackvo artisan dusk` has something to talk to.
dusk_apply.notes: The sidecar goes into stackvo.json through the same type the manifest READER produces, so a block written here is one the reader accepts — assembling JSON at the call site is how a manifest gains a block only its writer can read. `.env.dusk.local` is written ONLY when it is not already there: that file overrides the project's .env for the length of a run, and overwriting somebody's copy would silently change what their suite tests. The project's DuskTestCase is NOT touched — the driver, the window size and the Chrome flags are the repository's code, and this app does not write PHP into somebody's tests. Audited. See src-tauri/src/dusk.rs.

dusk_trust.returns: Array<{ id: 'copy' | 'bundle' | 'nss', command: string, ok: boolean, output: string, optional: boolean }>
dusk_trust.why: The browser is in a container that does not know this machine's CA, and a Dusk test that dies on a certificate warning reads as an application bug rather than as a missing certificate.
dusk_trust.notes: THREE results rather than one boolean, because the CA has to reach two places inside that container and they fail separately: the system bundle, which is what curl and the JVM read, and the NSS database, which is what Chromium reads. The NSS step needs a tool that is not in every image, so it is `optional` and reported as itself — a step that says `certutil: not found` is a sentence somebody can act on, where "trust failed" is not. A REQUIRED step that fails stops the ones after it: an update-ca-certificates over a file that was never copied would report success over nothing. Run as root (-u 0) because the image runs as seluser and neither the bundle nor the certificate directory is writable by it — a docker exec against a container this application declared, on this machine, not a privilege granted to anybody else. IT HAS TO BE RE-RUN WHEN THE CONTAINER IS RECREATED: this writes into the container's writable layer, which is a property of the approach rather than a bug in it, and it is not hidden. Refused when the sidecar is not running. Audited. See src-tauri/src/dusk.rs.

dashboards_report.returns: { readEnv: boolean, boards: Array<{ board: 'horizon' | 'telescope' | 'pulse', installed?: string, url?: string, observations: Array<{ id: 'queueNotRedis' | 'storageSqlite' | 'ingestSharesTheQueuesRedis', key?: string, value?: string }>, needs: Array<{ id: 'horizonSnapshot' | 'telescopePrune', job: { label: string, cron: string, exec: string[], enabled: boolean }, scheduled: boolean }>, workers: Array<{ kind: 'horizon' | 'pulse' | 'pulsework', running: boolean }> }>, scout?: { installed: string, driver: 'meilisearch' | 'typesense' } }
dashboards_report.why: Telescope, Horizon and Pulse all ship a web dashboard, all three open in `local` with no authentication, and this app already serves the project on its own domain over a certificate the browser trusts — so https://shop.loc/horizon works TODAY and nothing anywhere says it exists. A link would have been the cheap half and not the useful one: each of the three goes quietly empty for a reason the developer cannot see, and every container is green while it happens.
dashboards_report.notes: Horizon needs the queue connection to be `redis`, and its metrics graphs stay flat until `horizon:snapshot` runs every five minutes — a scheduled job, offered here and added through scheduler_save, which is the schedule's only writer. Telescope needs `telescope:install` and `migrate` to have run — stated as a precondition and NOT reported as a state, because that is a question about a database this does not query — and a daily `telescope:prune`, or `telescope_entries` grows until the disk notices. Pulse's storage refuses SQLite; with Redis ingest it wants a Redis connection separate from the queue's; and `pulse:check` is a LONG PROCESS, so it is a worker sidecar (worker.rs gained Kind::Pulse, and Kind::PulseWork for the ingest) rather than a schedule entry — a schedule line for it would start a second copy every time it fired. THE LIMIT, and it is the reason nothing here is a verdict: this app reads `.env` and `composer.lock` and does not read `config/*.php`, so a project that has run `config:cache` can make both of them lie. Every observation therefore carries the KEY it read and the VALUE it found, and the caveat sits beside the row rather than at the top of a pane — a warning at the top of a screen and a row at the bottom are two things a reader has to join up themselves. A check that calls something broken without having measured it is the check people learn to ignore. `readEnv` says whether a `.env` was found at all, so "nothing was read" and "nothing is wrong" are different answers. Redis Cluster is deliberately not claimed: Horizon does not support it and the key that would say so cannot be read without guessing what config/database.php does with it, so it is in the help document instead. A scheduled job is matched on the artisan command rather than on its label, so renaming one does not make this offer it again. `url` uses each dashboard's own default path; a project that moved it moved it in a file this does not read, and the pane says so beside the link. `scout` is the purest form of this card's pattern and is present only when BOTH halves are true — laravel/scout in composer.lock AND a SCOUT_DRIVER of meilisearch or typesense — because either alone is the wrong sentence: Scout on the `database` driver has no index to fill, and a Meilisearch running for something else is not this note's business. Switching the service on is a Market click; what nothing said is the NEXT step, and an empty index returns nothing for every search while every container is green. It is a SENTENCE AND NOT A BUTTON: `scout:import` takes a model class name this application cannot know, and a button that filled in a guess and ran it is exactly what quickcmd's catalogue refuses — so it points at the mechanism that does exist, a project's own `commands` block in stackvo.json. No network. Nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/dashboards.rs.

boost_status.returns: { packages: { boost?: string, mcp?: string, ai?: string }, container: string, hasRoutes: boolean, servers: Array<{ id: string, server: { kind: 'boost' } | { kind: 'local', handle: string } | { kind: 'web', path: string }, command?: string, url?: string, files: Array<{ id: 'mcp' | 'cursor' | 'vscode', label: string, path: string, state: 'absent' | 'unregistered' | 'container' | 'hostPhp' | 'other' | 'unparseable', entry?: string, command?: string }> }> }
boost_status.why: `php artisan boost:install` writes a `.mcp.json` into the project holding `php artisan boost:mcp` — a command line that assumes a php on the HOST. There is none here and there will not be one: tooling.rs records that as a decision (a version is a property of a project, not of a directory a shim guessed). So Laravel's own installer leaves a configuration that cannot start, and the person who notices sees the failure in their assistant rather than in the tool that wrote it. No competitor can fix this, because in no competitor is the server inside an image.
boost_status.notes: Three of the project's own files are read and nothing else. `composer.lock` — already parsed for deps_report, so the two cannot disagree about what is installed — says whether laravel/boost, laravel/mcp and laravel/ai are there. `routes/ai.php` says which servers this project registered: the first quoted string after `Mcp::local(` is a handle and after `Mcp::web(` is a URI path, and a registration whose first argument is a constant or a variable is SKIPPED rather than guessed at — an invented handle produces `artisan mcp:start <something>` failing in somebody's assistant. `hasRoutes` is reported separately so "no servers" can be told apart from "the file this reads is not there". The per-project client configurations say what stands today, and a registration is matched by WHAT IT RUNS rather than by what it is called, because boost:install picks its own entry name and a person may have renamed it. `state: 'hostPhp'` is the break named: the entry starts a php on this machine. `state: 'other'` is a command this does not recognise — reported and left alone, because somebody wired it deliberately. `state: 'unparseable'` means the file is not JSON this can edit and every button is withheld; agents.rs carries that rule and it is the same rule on the same kind of file. A `Mcp::web()` server has no command and no files: it is an ordinary route inside the application, so it is already served on the project's own domain over the certificate the browser trusts — `url` reports where, and there is no certificate to extend, no hosts entry to write and no second router. No network. Nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/boost.rs.

boost_register.returns: string (the absolute path of the file that was written)
boost_register.why: The registration that boost:install writes cannot start here, and the line that can is the passage into the container this application already owns: `docker exec -i stackvo-<project> php artisan boost:mcp`.
boost_register.notes: Read, replace one entry, write back — agents.rs's three rules borrowed whole: a file that does not parse is REFUSED rather than rewritten, everything else in the file survives including keys this code has never heard of, and the previous contents are kept beside it as `.stackvo-backup`. An entry that already runs this server keeps the name it had — renaming it would leave two servers in somebody's client rather than one working one — and only a file with nothing registered gains an entry under a name of this app's choosing. `docker exec` rather than `stackvo artisan` for two reasons: the CLI resolves which project it means from the directory it was started in and an assistant starts its servers from wherever it happens to be, and `docker` is a hard requirement of this application while the `stackvo` binary is not necessarily on PATH. `-i` and no `-t`: MCP over stdio is a pipe, and a TTY would put line discipline in the middle of a JSON-RPC stream. A `Mcp::web()` server is refused: it is a route, not a process, and an entry that starts nothing is worse than no entry. Audited. See src-tauri/src/boost.rs.

egress_report.returns: { rows: Array<{ container: string, image: string, registry: string, mirrored: boolean, reach: 'outside' | 'contained' | 'unknown', networks: string[], sent: number, received: number }>, registryPrefix?: string, registries: string[], contained: number }
egress_report.why: An administrator who pointed every pull at the organisation's mirror with policy.registryPrefix has a follow-up — WHO BYPASSED IT — and the same person wants to know which containers on this laptop can reach the internet at all. Neither question had an answer here and neither has one anywhere else in this category: a local binary has no containers, so it has no network namespaces to separate one program's traffic from another's.
egress_report.notes: Two exact answers and one honest number. Whether a container can route out is a PROPERTY OF THE NETWORK asked of the daemon, not an inference from behaviour: a Docker network created with `internal: true` gets no gateway installed, so a container whose every network is internal cannot route out. The asymmetry is deliberate — one non-internal network is enough for `outside` because one gateway is all a packet needs, and nothing short of EVERY network being KNOWN internal earns `contained`; a network the daemon would not describe leaves the answer `unknown`, never `contained`, because a containment claim resting on a failed lookup is the one wrong answer this report must not give. The registry host is the first component of the image reference under Docker's own rule (images::registry_of, which policy::names_a_registry now also asks — two implementations of one rule is how a mirror and a report come to disagree about which references are already qualified). A reference naming no host is reported as `docker.io` rather than as none: that is where it is pulled from, and "none" would omit the one host most worth naming. `mirrored` compares against the prefix's HOST, not the whole prefix — a mirror written `registry.corp/proxy` puts `registry.corp` in front of a reference, and demanding the path back would report every correctly mirrored image as a bypass. `sent`/`received` are Docker's per-interface counters and count ALL traffic, the StackVo network between containers included, so they are a floor on "did anything leave this container" and never a measure of internet traffic; they are read with one_shot (bytes are counters, not a percentage, so the two-reading shape container_stats needs for CPU would turn a thirty-container report from one second into a minute), and a stopped container reports zero because Docker has no counters for it. IT DOES NOT SAY WHERE ANYTHING CONNECTED TO: Docker keeps no connection log, and answering that needs a packet capture inside the container's network namespace or a proxy in front of it — neither of which this app installs quietly on somebody's machine to fill in a report. That refusal is named on the screen rather than left as a gap, for the reason compliance.rs gives about its own `unmeasured`. Networks are inspected once per NETWORK rather than once per container — a workspace has thirty containers and three networks. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/egress.rs.

deps_report.returns: { locks: string[], total: number, direct: number, hosts: Record<string, number>, findings: Array<{ id: 'insecureSource' | 'noIntegrity' | 'otherIndex', subject: string, detail?: string }>, advisories?: Array<{ package: string, ids: string[], direct: boolean }> }
deps_report.why: pkg.rs verifies every file of every service package against a manifest digest before it runs, refuses a moving tag, and checks a signature over the index it came from. Meanwhile the project sitting beside it pulls four hundred libraries out of composer.lock and package-lock.json and nothing in this application has ever looked at them — which is the wrong way round: the service packages are a catalogue this project publishes and can vouch for, and the dependencies are somebody else's code, in far greater quantity, running with the developer's own permissions. No competitor looks at a project's dependencies at all.
deps_report.notes: No network, ever. Three findings come out of what the lock file already says. `insecureSource` is one row per package fetched over plain http:// — market.rs refuses exactly that for this app's OWN catalogue, and a project doing it for four hundred libraries is the same hole at scale; it is named rather than counted because whoever is on the path chooses what arrives. `noIntegrity` is a COUNT of packages the lock carries no hash over — counted rather than listed because on a lock written by an older tool that is every package, and four hundred identical rows is a screen nobody reads. `otherIndex` names any host other than the ecosystem's own, with a count: a private mirror is not a fault, but a supply chain nobody wrote down is one nobody is watching. `locks` names the files that were read so "no findings" can be told apart from "no lock file was found" — a project this cannot see is not a clean project. `advisories` absent means nobody asked; an EMPTY array means the query ran and found nothing, and the two must never look the same. Direct vs transitive comes from composer.json / package.json, because composer.lock does not record it — and the distinction is the one the whole report turns on: a direct dependency is a version you choose, a transitive one is a version somebody else chooses for you. Dev dependencies are included and not marked apart: they are installed on this machine and run in the same container, and "it is only a dev dependency" is a sentence that has introduced real incidents. A leading `v` is stripped from a composer version because that is composer's tag spelling and a query for v3.5.0 matches nothing. A lockfileVersion 2 file carries both the flat `packages` map and the old nested `dependencies` tree; the flat map is read when present and the tree only when it is not, so nothing is counted twice. Only composer.lock and package-lock.json are read — the two this application's own runtimes reach for most and the two that are JSON. yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, go.sum and Cargo.lock are named as absent rather than guessed at: a parser written from memory against a format nobody measured is how a report starts quietly missing half a project. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/deps.rs.

deps_advisories.returns: { locks: string[], total: number, direct: number, hosts: Record<string, number>, findings: Array<{ id: 'insecureSource' | 'noIntegrity' | 'otherIndex', subject: string, detail?: string }>, advisories?: Array<{ package: string, ids: string[], direct: boolean }> }
deps_advisories.why: pkg.rs verifies every file of every service package against a manifest digest before it runs, refuses a moving tag, and checks a signature over the index it came from. Meanwhile the project sitting beside it pulls four hundred libraries out of composer.lock and package-lock.json and nothing in this application has ever looked at them — which is the wrong way round: the service packages are a catalogue this project publishes and can vouch for, and the dependencies are somebody else's code, in far greater quantity, running with the developer's own permissions. No competitor looks at a project's dependencies at all.
deps_advisories.notes: THIS ONE LEAVES THE MACHINE, and it is a separate command for that reason rather than a flag on the one above. What is sent is the NAMES AND VERSIONS of the project's dependencies, to api.osv.dev, as one POST per thousand packages — no identifier, no project name, no path, no file contents. That is a real disclosure, so it is written in PRIVACY.md in those words rather than described as "checking for updates", and privacy_claims.rs holds the document to it. A failure is an ERROR and never an empty list: "nothing was found" and "I could not ask" must not look the same on a security screen, and `advisories: null` is what the report already means by the second. Chunked at OSV's documented batch ceiling rather than truncated — a report that silently stopped at a thousand packages would be a clean result for a large project, which is the worst answer available. Results are matched to queries POSITIONALLY, which is the only correspondence the API defines, so a length mismatch is refused as a protocol change rather than read as an empty answer. Only OSV's ids are reported (GHSA-…, CVE-…): an id is what somebody searches for, and a severity word this build derived itself would be a judgement it is in no position to make. Direct dependencies sort first, because the two have different repairs and the one somebody can act on today belongs at the top. Not audited: nothing on this machine is changed, and the consent decision is on the screen before the press, which is where it belongs. No network, ever. Three findings come out of what the lock file already says. `insecureSource` is one row per package fetched over plain http:// — market.rs refuses exactly that for this app's OWN catalogue, and a project doing it for four hundred libraries is the same hole at scale; it is named rather than counted because whoever is on the path chooses what arrives. `noIntegrity` is a COUNT of packages the lock carries no hash over — counted rather than listed because on a lock written by an older tool that is every package, and four hundred identical rows is a screen nobody reads. `otherIndex` names any host other than the ecosystem's own, with a count: a private mirror is not a fault, but a supply chain nobody wrote down is one nobody is watching. `locks` names the files that were read so "no findings" can be told apart from "no lock file was found" — a project this cannot see is not a clean project. `advisories` absent means nobody asked; an EMPTY array means the query ran and found nothing, and the two must never look the same. Direct vs transitive comes from composer.json / package.json, because composer.lock does not record it — and the distinction is the one the whole report turns on: a direct dependency is a version you choose, a transitive one is a version somebody else chooses for you. Dev dependencies are included and not marked apart: they are installed on this machine and run in the same container, and "it is only a dev dependency" is a sentence that has introduced real incidents. A leading `v` is stripped from a composer version because that is composer's tag spelling and a query for v3.5.0 matches nothing. A lockfileVersion 2 file carries both the flat `packages` map and the old nested `dependencies` tree; the flat map is read when present and the tree only when it is not, so nothing is counted twice. Only composer.lock and package-lock.json are read — the two this application's own runtimes reach for most and the two that are JSON. yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, go.sum and Cargo.lock are named as absent rather than guessed at: a parser written from memory against a format nobody measured is how a report starts quietly missing half a project. Not audited: nothing is changed. See src-tauri/src/deps.rs.

projects_suspend_idle.why: Returns NAMES, not a count: this is a background action whose whole risk is being surprising, and “3 suspended” is a number somebody then has to match against a list. MUST skip a project something else holds rather than queueing behind it — a sweep that waited behind a build would stop the container the moment the build finished.

provider_consent.why: A provider command is declared by a repository and reaches the network with the developer's credentials. That is hooks.rs's threat model word for word, so this borrows its answer: consent is per project, keyed on a digest of what would run.
provider_consent.notes: PER DIRECTION, and its own file rather than hooks': agreeing to run `composer install` in a container is not agreeing to send a database to production, and a single record would have made the second free once the first was given. The digest is RE-DERIVED here rather than taken from the caller — a digest that travelled to JavaScript and back is one the front end could have sent for a different command than the one on screen, and this is the exact approval standing between a cloned repository and somebody's credentials. It covers the image, every word of the command, the plain environment, the secret names and the direction, so editing any of them asks again; `about` is prose and is deliberately outside it, because rewording a description should not withdraw an approval. Audited as `provider_consent`.

provider_run.why: The verb. Everything else in this group decides whether it may happen.
provider_run.notes: A pull does NOT import anything itself: it produces a file and hands it to db_restore, which takes a copy of what it is about to replace — so pulling staging over the wrong database is recoverable for the same reason restoring the wrong file is, and reusing that path rather than writing a second importer is what makes that true rather than claimed. A push does not dump anything itself either; db::dump writes the file the recipe sends. The plan is MADE AGAIN here rather than taken from the caller: the screen that offered the button may be minutes old, and an approval revoked in between must not still be spendable. Secrets are read out of the keystore once and arrive as `-e NAME` with no value, which tells Docker to copy each one from this process — so no secret is ever an argument, and none of it is in `ps`, a shell history or a crash report. The scratch directory is this application's own, mounted at /stackvo, and is removed whatever happens; what comes back is checked with symlink_metadata and refused unless it is a regular non-empty file, because a container that can write into a mounted directory can write `dump.sql -> /etc/passwd` and turn a data import into an arbitrary host read. An empty dump is refused too: restoring one over a database is the same act as dropping it, and it is the shape a failed remote command leaves behind. ONLY a push is audited — a pull changes this machine and the app is full of things that do. There is deliberately no scheduler: nothing here may push on a timer. Errors: FORBIDDEN when an administrator switched it off, PERMISSION_DENIED for missing consent or a missing secret (naming which), INVALID_INPUT for a direction the recipe does not offer.

provider_secret_set.why: A recipe names what it needs and never carries it. The manifest is committed.
provider_secret_set.notes: Into the OS keystore, scoped per project AND per provider: two projects both wanting `SSH_KEY` are two different credentials, and a shared entry would hand one team's key to another project's recipe. Audited by NAME — there is nowhere in the record to put a value. DDEV mounts the developer's ssh agent into the container that runs the pull; that is coherent for a tool with curated recipes and wrong here, because a repository-declared container gets no host path and an ssh agent is a host path that signs things.

provider_recipes.why: The provider mechanism was finished and the catalogue was empty, so using the feature meant learning a file format from source — DDEV ships three recipes in every project and this shipped none. These are starting points written into the project's own stackvo.json, not integrations: every host name, database and project id in them is a placeholder.
provider_recipes.notes: Takes no workspace and answers the same for every project, because the catalogue is in the binary. Each card carries the image and every word of both directions, so the list and the approval screen describe the same thing — a list naming recipes without showing what they run would put the consequence one click further away than the click that commits to it. `edit` is never empty. Three shipped: mysql-remote and postgres-remote (both directions, password from the keystore through MYSQL_PWD/PGPASSWORD so it is never an argument) and upsun (pull only — its CLI's db:sql takes a query, not a file). SSH+mysqldump is NOT shippable and the reason is measured: a repository-declared container gets no host path, so no agent socket and no key file, and ssh authenticates with neither an environment variable nor an argv. Pantheon likewise: no Terminus image on any registry checked, and `terminus backup:get` answers with a URL that then has to be downloaded — a second command, therefore a shell.

provider_recipe_add.why: Closes the empty-field problem the recipe catalogue exists for: the user picks a starting point and it lands in their own stackvo.json, rather than being copied out of documentation.
provider_recipe_add.notes: Nothing is approved by being added. The recipe goes through the same consent digest as one somebody typed, and since every shipped recipe carries a placeholder host the version that gets approved is by definition not the version that was added — the digest covering that edit is what makes them two acts. Written through manifest::write, the same serialiser the form save uses, rather than by splicing an object into the file: a second writer for one file diverges, and the first divergence shows up as a project that opens with a Problem nobody wrote. Refuses a name the project already declares rather than replacing it — the copy on disk has been edited by definition, and overwriting it would discard a host name somebody looked up, in response to a button labelled add.

pty_open.v1Change: PtyTarget is NEW: { kind: 'container', name } or { kind: 'host', cwd }. node-pty could only reach containers because it ran inside one; portable-pty on the host can open a real host shell in the project directory.

qr_encode.returns: { version: number, size: number, rows: string[], text: string }
qr_encode.why: Two features hand out an address whose whole point is that it is opened on ANOTHER device — the LAN name from lan_status and the public URL from tunnel_status — and both are long, both contain either a dashed IP address or four random Cloudflare words, and the only way to get one onto a phone was to type it. That is the moment somebody gives up and uses the desktop browser's device emulation instead, which is not the same thing and is exactly the class of bug it fails to show.
qr_encode.notes: Byte mode, error-correction level M, versions 1-10 — 213 bytes, against a tunnel URL of about sixty. Written here rather than taken as a dependency because a QR code is a closed specification with published vectors: it cannot acquire new cases later, so the usual argument for a maintained dependency does not apply. It is NOT verified by its author's own expectations: examples/qr_probe.rs hands each symbol to macOS's own CIDetector — the decoder behind the camera — and passes a row only when the text read back is byte-identical. That measurement found the one real bug: the first format-information copy was written along row 8 instead of down column 8, and every other check passed while no decoder on earth would read the result. Returns the module matrix as one string per row rather than a picture, so the caller draws it; the front end renders an SVG with a four-module quiet zone, black on white whatever the theme is, because scanners expect dark modules on a light ground and the failure mode of an inverted code is a phone that simply sits there. INVALID_INPUT for empty text or more than a version 10 symbol holds — never a truncated symbol, which is indistinguishable from a complete one until somebody scans it. See src-tauri/src/qr.rs.

query_log.why: The largest product gap this stack had: three competitors sell query logging and N+1 detection, and this stack could not say what the database had been asked. The row also said it needed a collector inside the container — for MySQL and MariaDB that is wrong, and this is why.
query_log.notes: All four databases this app runs, each switched on at runtime with no agent, no rebuild and no code in the application. MySQL and MariaDB point their general log at a TABLE with two SET GLOBAL statements; Mongo profiles per database; Postgres takes three ALTER SYSTEM statements and a reload, which pin the switch, an epoch-stamped line prefix and the destination format. Reading Postgres back means asking the server where it writes — pg_current_logfile() — rather than assuming the container's stdout: every StackVo Postgres package ships logging_collector = on, which takes stderr away from the stream and puts it in a file under the data directory. Anything that is not a database answers supported:false rather than an error, because 'not this kind' must not read as 'something broke'. Verified against this workspace's live mysql:9.7, mariadb:12.3, postgres:14 and mongo:8.0 by examples/querylog_probe.rs. See src-tauri/src/querylog.rs.

query_log_clear.why: Start again from here — what somebody presses before reloading the page they are investigating. Without it every read is the whole session and the one request under study is buried.
query_log_clear.notes: A deletion on three of the four: MySQL truncates mysql.general_log, Mongo drops system.profile. Postgres deletes nothing — the log belongs to the server and this app must not rewrite it — and used to answer with a no-op, which is the same reply as success and was hidden by hiding the button. It now writes a watermark statement, and the reader drops everything above it. 'Cannot delete' was never the same as 'cannot start again'.

query_log_record.why: The log records every statement unsampled and costs write throughput, so it is an instrument you switch on, look at, and switch off — never a default.
query_log_record.notes: One command with a boolean rather than two, because the pair is one decision and the interesting failure is leaving it on. Stopping also clears: what the log holds is statement text, and in a development database an INSERT carries the row. MySQL truncates the table and Mongo drops the collection; Postgres cannot, because the log is the server's own file, so stopping writes the same watermark query_log_clear does and nothing this app shows reaches back past it. Nothing is written to disk by the app and nothing reaches a diagnostics bundle — on Postgres the server itself keeps what it wrote, which the pane says while recording.

quick_command_run.notes: **The fixed catalog is the security model.** The frontend sends an ID, never a command; the argv is built on the Rust side from compiled-in words, so there is no code path by which the webview can name a program to execute — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open uses, for the same reason: a project pane that accepted an arbitrary command string from its own frontend is a remote shell with extra steps. Every command is spawned as an argv ARRAY, never through a shell, so a project called `a; rm -rf ~` is a container name that does not exist rather than a second command. Two kinds, because they behave differently: interactive commands (tinker, wp shell) need a TTY and a human, so they open the user's own terminal and return null — an in-app REPL would be a second, worse one next to the one they have configured; one-shot commands stream through the operation console. `-it` is added only for the interactive ones, because Docker refuses `-t` when stdin is not a TTY. Refuses when the container is not running, so the failure is "the project is not running" rather than Docker's "No such container". The id may now name a command the project declared in its own stackvo.json as well as one compiled in. The webview still never names a program — `quickcmd::resolve` is the only place either becomes an argv, and a declared command reaches `docker exec` through the same function a built-in does. FOUR ROWS ADDED LATER ARE CHECKS, which the catalogue had none of: `pint` (`vendor/bin/pint --test` — the reporting shape, never the bare command, because a formatter that rewrites the tree behind a button is a diff nobody asked for; a non-zero exit code IS the answer), `test` (through `artisan test`, so it runs whichever of Pest or PHPUnit the project has rather than this app picking one), `wayfinder` and `boost-skill`. Three of the four are offered on the PACKAGE that provides them — `vendor/bin/pint`, `vendor/laravel/wayfinder`, `vendor/laravel/boost` — and not on `artisan`, because every Laravel project has artisan and most have none of these, so an artisan-gated button would produce `Command … is not defined` in an operation console. `wayfinder` is the one row in the catalogue with a PRE-STEP: `php artisan route:clear` runs first, as two argv ARRAYS in sequence rather than one `sh -c "a && b"` — never a shell string is a rule, not a habit — because wayfinder:generate reads the route list and a cached one makes it generate against yesterday's routes, which Laravel's own documentation writes down as a trap; if the pre-step fails the second command does not run, since generating against an uncleared cache produces WRONG output under a green console. A declared command never carries a pre-step: that field is a claim this repository makes about somebody else's framework, and a project making claims about itself has the `commands` block. `pennant:purge` is deliberately absent — it deletes stored feature flag values, and a one-click destructive button in a catalogue whose security model is "the frontend only sends an id" is the wrong shape; its place is behind a confirmation like containers_stop_all's, or nowhere.

machine_commands.why: Four rivals sell "add your own command" on the front page — DDEV drops a file in `.ddev/commands/`, Lando has a `tooling:` block, dde and Laragon each have their own — and this application had exactly one way to do it: edit a repository somebody else owns. `<root>/commands.json` is the layer above the project, and this reads it.
machine_commands.notes: The SAME schema as a manifest's `commands` block, the same argv rule and the same container boundary — read by the same parser, deliberately not a second shape and deliberately not a second threat model. It is the union of two decisions already taken: a file on disk may declare a command, and a declared command runs in the project's container and nowhere else. There is no `host` form here either; a step that has to run on this machine is a hook, approved against a digest first. `exists` is reported separately from an empty `commands` because an absent file is the ordinary case and not an error, and the pane says something different for each. `problems` are `Finding`s under the `COMMAND` code — the same code a manifest's bad block produces, because it is the same parser reporting the same rule. Shadowing is NOT reported here: a machine-wide row is only shadowed relative to a project that declares the same id, and this command has no project. `quick_commands` marks every row with the file it came from, which is where that shows.

crash_reports.returns: Array<{ name: string, path: string, bytes: number }>
crash_reports.why: The application could crash, write a perfectly good report, and never mention it. So "I would like to report this" never started — not because reporting is hard, but because nobody knew there was anything to report.
crash_reports.notes: Nothing leaves the machine, and that is not an omission: PRIVACY.md promises no telemetry, no crash reporting service and no server behind the app, and says anything future would be opt-in, off by default, and described there BEFORE it ships. This is the local half — the reports already travel in a diagnostic bundle, and this is what tells somebody one exists to send. Returns only the reports newer than the marker `crash_reports_seen` writes, compared by NAME rather than by count: a report pruned away (10 are kept) would make a count go down and a newer crash then go unmentioned. Newest first; the file name carries the UTC timestamp, so it sorts without a stat — an mtime is rewritten by a backup restore.

crash_reports_seen.why: So the notice does not repeat every launch.
crash_reports_seen.notes: Separate from reading them because the two are different moments: the window asks on open and marks when the person has actually seen the line. Marking on read would dismiss a notice nobody looked at, which is the same as not having one. Best effort — a marker that cannot be written means the notice appears again, which is a repeated line rather than a lost crash.

quick_commands.why: P3-19 was "a tinker quick action — the PTY exists, so it is nearly free". It is, and on its own it is also one button. What is worth building is the set it belongs to: artisan tinker, artisan migrate, composer install, npm install, wp shell. Each of those today means opening a terminal, remembering the container name and typing `docker exec -it stackvo-<project> …`.
quick_commands.notes: Offered only when the marker file exists — driven off the same Fingerprint adoption uses, so "does this project have artisan" is answered in one place. Offering a command the project cannot run is worse than omitting it: the failure arrives as `artisan: not found` in an operation console, which reads as a broken app rather than as a button that never applied. `because` names the file the offer is based on. Deliberately ABSENT: migrate:fresh, migrate:reset, db:wipe and composer update — the first three drop the user's data behind a button four characters from the safe one, and the last rewrites a lock file. Those are things to type deliberately in the terminal that is one click away. The list adds the four frameworks this app scaffolds and did not offer a row for: Symfony (bin/console), Django (manage.py), Rails and plain Ruby. Each is the same shape — a fixed id, an argv and a marker file only that framework writes. Rails is detected on `bin/rails` rather than on a Gemfile, which is Sinatra and Jekyll as often as it is Rails, and it runs through `bundle exec` rather than the binstub: a binstub is only executable if its permission bit survived the checkout, and `bundle exec` needs the gem rather than the bit. Doctrine's migrate carries --allow-no-migration because it exits non-zero with nothing to run, which the console would draw as a failed operation. This is NOT the workspace unlock: that is a command the WORKSPACE declares, and every row here is still compiled in. The list is the built-in catalogue filtered by the project's marker files, then whatever the project's own stackvo.json declares under `commands`, marked with `declared` so a caller can say which is which. Declared entries are container commands only — there is no `host` form, which is why this needed no approval flow. A THIRD LAYER comes last: the commands INSTALLED PACKAGES bring — the DDEV add-on shape, where installing ddev-redis also gives you `ddev redis-cli`, with the one thing DDEV does not have, which is that every byte of it was verified before it was read. A package may name a command for the reason a project may name one in its own container and a SIDECAR may not: the package already chose the image, already wrote the compose fragment and already decides what that container runs, and it arrived through the whole chain — a signature over the registry, the registry's hash over the manifest, the manifest's hashes over every byte beside it, re-checked on EVERY read rather than only at install. The containment that is still built rather than inherited: only ENABLED instances are offered (a command against a container that is not meant to be running is a button whose failure is `No such container`), the command never reaches the host, and the container name is DERIVED from the instance rather than declared, so a package can no more name somebody else's container than it can name a host port. Ids are prefixed with the instance (`redis-7-2:redis-cli`) because two versions of one service are two instances and an unprefixed id would resolve to whichever was listed first — and because a prefixed id cannot collide with a catalogue id or a declared one, a project cannot shadow a package's command by declaring the same string. See src-tauri/src/quickcmd.rs.

release_build.notes: **Verification is not optional and not a separate button.** The safety property here — no .env in the image, no active debugger — is exactly the kind that is easy to state in a Dockerfile and quietly wrong in the result, so the built image is RUN and asked. Proven both ways on a real project: with the ignore file, zero env files; without it, all five of that project's .env.* land in a layer and the check names every one. `hasApp` catches the other silent failure — a build whose context was empty produces an image that starts and serves nothing, which otherwise looks like a success. The ignore file is written BESIDE the generated Dockerfile as `Dockerfile.dockerignore`, which BuildKit reads in preference to the context's — confirmed to work before anything depended on it — so building somebody's image writes nothing into their repository. The tag is validated before it reaches a command line: lowercase only, because Docker rejects an uppercase repository with an error that does not say so.

release_load.returns: string[] (the image names the daemon adopted)
release_load.notes: `docker load` — the return trip `release_save` never had, and the half of an air-gapped install that was missing. Takes no project name and needs no workspace: a bundle is loaded on the machine that received it, which is exactly the machine that may have neither. A missing file is answered NOT_FOUND here rather than being handed to Docker, which calls it an invalid archive and sends the user looking for a corrupt bundle instead of a wrong path. The names come from `docker load`'s own stdout because nothing else knows them — the file name is whatever somebody called it, and one stream can carry several images. An image with no tag is reported by id rather than dropped: it did load, and an empty answer reads as an empty bundle.

release_plan.why: P3-20 — what `laradock ship` does. The analysis calls it the long-horizon differentiator because the container lineage makes it possible and no native-binary competitor can follow. It is also the item with a real question inside it, answered by looking at what the images actually contain rather than by assuming.
release_plan.notes: **The dev image is not a production image**, measured on this checkout: a PHP project's image holds NO application code — /var/www/html contains one file, index.nginx-debian.html, because the source arrives through a bind mount — and it has Xdebug loaded. Exporting it ships a web server with nothing to serve and a step debugger that dials out on every request. A NODE image is the opposite: its Dockerfile does COPY . . and npm install, so it already holds the code and the build. Hence two strategies: `layer` (build FROM the dev image, add the source, remove the debugger inis) and `retag` (nothing to add; rebuilding would replace a Linux node_modules with whatever the host has). `excluded` carries every ignore pattern WITH ITS REASON, because an exclusion the user cannot explain is one they work around. `warnings` names what the result will be true of — no .env, vendor as it is on disk, Xdebug's binary still present though inactive — before the build rather than after.

release_push.why: MUST re-check on the way out — the plan the caller was shown crossed the IPC boundary and came back, and a check that only runs on the way out is not a check.

release_push_plan.why: MUST re-run the verification rather than remember it from the build: the interval between building and pushing is exactly where somebody could retag something else onto the name.

release_recipe.why: A deployment recipe for the built image. Returned as TEXT, not written: where it belongs is the user's decision. MUST carry no source mount, no debugger, no database container, and variable NAMES with empty values — a recipe with credentials in it is a .env wearing a different extension, and this file is meant to be committed.

release_save.notes: `docker save` to a tarball — the artefact you hand to something that is not this machine.

repl_history.why: The snippet you ran ten minutes ago, back in the editor. Without it the workbench is a text box that forgets, which is the terminal REPL's weakness rather than an improvement on it.
repl_history.notes: The code, never the output. A snippet is what the person wrote and is the thing they want back; the output is the application's DATA — a row, a customer, a token — and querylog states the rule this follows: what came out of somebody's database is not written to disk by this app. Kept in the app's own config directory beside hook-consent.json, never in the project, because a file written into a checkout turns up in somebody's git status. A re-run moves a snippet back to the top rather than adding a copy.

repl_history_clear.why: Forget them. A snippet can hold a customer's id or a token somebody pasted in, and a history with no way to clear it is one people learn not to use.

repl_run.why: Run the snippet against the booted application and hand back everything about the run — both streams, the exit code, the duration.
repl_run.notes: **The webview picks a runner, it never names a program.** `laravel` means `php artisan tinker --execute` and nothing else; an id outside the table is refused before anything is spawned, and so is one the project has no files for. The snippet is ONE argv element and always the LAST, so a snippet containing `; rm -rf ~` is a string rather than a second command — the rule hooks and quickcmd state as their security model. It runs in the project's own container, which already runs that repository's code, and there is no host runner: a snippet that has to run on this machine is a hook, approved against a digest first. Two limits, guarding different failures: `timeout` INSIDE the container stops the snippet (killing a docker exec client does not stop what it started), and this process's own clock stops the wait. `limited` records which — measured present in php, node, python, ruby and wordpress-cli images, but "every image I checked" is not "every image". Success is read from the exit code and never from "stderr was empty": a PHP fatal is written to stdout, measured. Laravel's --execute does not echo the last expression the way the interactive REPL does, so the pane says to dump().

repl_runners.why: Held as a decision rather than a task, because quickcmd refused an in-app REPL in writing — "a second, worse REPL next to the one they already have configured" — and reversing a refusal is not something a commit does quietly. The refusal stands for a LINE repl and this is not one. A snippet is twenty lines you edit: write a query, run it, change line three, run it again. In tinker that is retyping. `tinker` still opens the user's own terminal, and the two are split by what the person is doing rather than ranked.
repl_runners.notes: Offered from the same Fingerprint the quick commands use. Two tiers, and each row says which it is: `booted` means the application is loaded (artisan tinker, wp eval, manage.py shell, bin/rails runner), and false means the language on its own (php -r, node -e) — a pane that showed them alike would let somebody debug for ten minutes before finding out their models were never loaded. Laravel is offered only where composer.json also declares laravel/tinker, because --execute is Tinker's flag and a --no-dev install does not have it. See src-tauri/src/repl.rs.

args.key: string (SPX report key — the request this is about)
args.service: string? (database service id; omit and the database half is absent rather than empty)

request_explain.why: The three instruments already existed and each was its own pane: SPX says where the code's time went, the query log says what the database was asked, the timeline says what else happened. Reading them about ONE request meant opening three panes and comparing clocks by eye. No new measurement was needed — a common request key was, and a recording is one.
request_explain.notes: The key is a php-spx REPORT: the only artefact here that names a request (`GET /checkout`), says when it started and says how long it took. Everything else is joined to it BY TIME, and the payload never pretends otherwise — timeline's refusal to attribute a statement to a request still stands and TimelineMoment.request is still null on every query moment. What replaces the reader's eye is a STATED window plus `overlaps`, which names every other recording claiming part of the same wall clock. The window has two bases and the payload says which. For a recording THIS APP started, it is `observed`: the host clock on both sides of the request, kept by spx_record_request and spx_record_command, which needs no premise about what `exec_ts` means. Otherwise it is `derived` — `exec_ts ± 1s + wallTimeUs`, where php-spx files exec_ts as WHOLE SECONDS and the tolerance is that truncation rather than an allowance for clock drift. The derived half rests on `exec_ts` being the START of the run, which is REASONED AND NOT MEASURED; `examples/explain_probe.rs` asks a live container. `wallTimeUs` is MICROSECONDS despite php-spx naming the field `wall_time_ms` (measured — see spx_report); reading it as milliseconds opens a window a thousand times too wide and attributes the whole session to one page load. IMPLEMENTORS: compute the split over the WHOLE hotspot list, not a top-N — a request whose driver frames each sit below the cut is exactly the one the split exists for, and a trimmed list reports it as pure PHP. Three absences are survived and each is reported as its own finding rather than as an empty list: no trace half (`traceRead: false`), a log that was not recording (`queriesUnrecorded`) and a recording log with nothing in the window (`queriesOutsideWindow`). A key that names no report IS an error — answering it with an empty explanation would present "nothing is known" as an answer about the request. See src-tauri/src/explain.rs.

args.service: string? (database service id; omit for dumps only)

request_timeline.why: The row read 'dump/mail/log three separate screens, no correlation'. What the code thought it had (dd()) and what it actually asked the database for are two halves of one question, and reading them meant comparing clocks by eye across two panes.
request_timeline.notes: Dumps correlate: the bridge writes the request they happened in, so several from one page load group together and the group is named. Queries do NOT — MySQL's general log records the statement and the connection and nothing about which HTTP request caused it, and guessing from adjacency would be wrong on the first concurrent request and wrong silently. They are placed by time and left ungrouped, and the screen says which is which. Attributing a query to a request needs the application to say so, which is code inside somebody's project — the thing this feature exists to avoid needing. A database that cannot be reached yields the dumps alone rather than an error. See src-tauri/src/timeline.rs.

routes_list.why: A route the renderer skips MUST still appear here, or the screen shows a route the proxy does not have.

routes_save.why: Replaces the whole list and regenerates. Whole-list rather than add/remove/edit: the file is a handful of pairs in one table, and three commands over one small document is three chances for the file and the screen to disagree about order. MUST check every route before writing any, so one bad row fails the save rather than writing half of it, and MUST refuse a duplicate domain — two routers on one name is a coin toss the user cannot see.

args.target: string (rules target id: claude | agents | cursor | copilot | windsurf | gemini)
args.project: string? (project directory name; omit for the workspace root)

rules_apply.why: The write half of rules_status. Puts the guidance an assistant needs — which tool answers which question, that generated files are overwritten, that a writing tool can stop the whole stack — into the file that assistant already reads.
rules_apply.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: only the region between `<!-- stackvo:rules:begin -->` and `<!-- stackvo:rules:end -->` may be written. Everything else in the file MUST come back byte for byte — this is the user's own CLAUDE.md — and a file with no markers is APPENDED to, never replaced. A copy is kept beside it as `.stackvo-backup` first. Front matter (Cursor's `alwaysApply`, VS Code's `applyTo`) is written only when the file is created, because a user who narrowed it meant that. Audited: this writes instructions into a file the user owns and usually commits. A `project` that is not a directory under the projects root is refused rather than joined.

args.project: string? (project directory name; omit for the workspace root)

rules_remove.why: The undo. A feature that writes into somebody's repository and cannot take it back out again is one they do not press the first time.
rules_remove.notes: Removes the marked region and nothing else; the file itself stays, even when the block was all it held — it is the user's file and may hold nothing else only by coincidence. Removing from a file that has no block is not an error.

args.project: string? (project directory name; omit for the workspace root)

rules_status.returns: Array<{ id: string, label: string, scope: 'workspace' | 'global', path: string, exists: boolean, installed: boolean, current: boolean }>
rules_status.why: agents_install makes the MCP tools reachable; it does not make them used. An assistant that has never seen this stack reads the source, guesses at nginx and edits a generated file, because nothing told it stackvo_doctor answers that question in one call. Every rival ships this half — ServBay files 'AI Rule' beside its MCP documentation, EnvKit installs a skill, Lerd writes context files — and this repository had no answer to it. This is the read half: which rules files exist, which carry a StackVo block and which carry an older one.
rules_status.notes: Reads only, and works with no workspace selected — the global rows are about the machine. Six rows, one per FILE rather than per client, because Codex and Zed both read AGENTS.md and two rows writing one path would disagree about whether the rules are installed. `installed` means the file carries the marked block; `current` means that block is this version's wording, which is what distinguishes an update from a fresh install. See src-tauri/src/rules.rs.

scheduler_jobs.why: worker_start('scheduler') runs Laravel's own scheduler as one all-or-nothing process, and nothing on screen says which entry last ran. This is the table instead: every job in stackvo.json with its last run read from disk, plus whether anything is actually running them — a schedule with no sidecar up is a list of intentions, and the screen must not let that read as scheduled.

scheduler_log.why: Where the reason lives. The exit status a job records is xargs's rather than the command's — every failure is 123 — so the number answers whether it worked and this answers why. Empty rather than an error when the job has never run.

scheduler_run.notes: Runs it the way a tick would: the sidecar sources its own script and calls run_job, so a manual run writes the same log and the same last run. A second execution path would be a second set of bugs, and the first symptom would be a manual run that logged nothing. Needs the scheduler to be running.

scheduler_save.notes: The whole list, not add/edit/delete verbs: the schedule is one value in stackvo.json and one generated directory, and three verbs would be three chances for the two to disagree. Refuses a cron expression outside the portable subset (*, a, a-b, */n, a-b/n and lists of those) and two jobs whose labels slug to the same log. A running sidecar is recreated rather than left to notice: the tick loop rereads disk every minute, and 'eventually' means a deleted job firing once more after it was deleted.

scheduler_start.notes: A sidecar from the project's own image with --restart unless-stopped, on the same terms as a worker: Docker is the supervisor, so a schedule keeps firing while this app is closed. The tick loop is POSIX sh rather than cron or supercronic because the image is the project's and this app does not add packages to it. Refuses when the project has no built container, and when nothing in the schedule is enabled.

scheduler_stop.notes: Removal, not just stop: with unless-stopped, a merely-stopped container is one engine restart away from coming back. A sidecar that was already gone is the state being asked for, not a failure.

secret_move.why: On a company machine ~/.stackvo/.env is backed up, synced and DLP-scanned, and it holds database passwords in plain text. This moves one into Keychain / Credential Manager / Secret Service and leaves `keychain:<entry>` in its place.
secret_move.notes: One key at a time and never automatic, because it has a consequence: the Bash CLI reads .env directly and would use the string `keychain:…` as the password. Writes the keystore first and the .env line second, and removes the entry again if the file write fails — the other order loses the password. Moving an already-moved key succeeds silently rather than failing, so a double click is not an error. Errors: INVALID_INPUT for a key that is not a credential, NOT_FOUND when there is no value to move, PERMISSION_DENIED when the keystore will not open. Audited as `secret_move`. This does NOT remove the value from generated/docker-compose.dynamic.yml, which is rendered with the real password — see src-tauri/src/secrets.rs.

secret_restore.why: The way back. A user may only discover the CLI incompatibility after moving a key, and without this the only way out is hand-editing .env with a value the app will not show them.
secret_restore.notes: Writes the .env line first and deletes the keystore entry second — deleting first and failing to write would destroy the password. The only caller of env_writer::apply_verbatim, which is what stops the ordinary write path from undoing a move nobody asked to undo. Audited as `secret_restore`.

secrets_status.returns: { available: boolean, keys: Array<{ key: string, moved: boolean, resolvable: boolean, set: boolean }> }
secrets_status.why: The Settings pane has to draw a row per credential saying where it lives, and it has to know before it offers a Move button whether this machine has a keystore at all — a headless Linux box with no Secret Service is a real machine somebody runs this on.
secrets_status.notes: Reads the .env text, NOT a loaded Env: loading replaces a keychain: reference with the value it points at, which is exactly the fact this reports. `available` is probed by reading an entry nothing ever writes, so asking leaves nothing behind. No value ever appears in the response — `env_reveal` remains the one deliberate way a password crosses the boundary. See src-tauri/src/secrets.rs.

args.name: string? (project; without it only .env is read)

leaks_scan.returns: { findings: Array<{ id: string, source: 'env' | 'tracked', subject: string, line?: number, fingerprint: string, preview: string, inHistory: boolean }>, scanned: number, skipped: number, truncated: boolean, envTracked: boolean, envInHistory: boolean }
leaks_scan.why: secrets.rs moves a password out of .env and into the OS keystore, which is the direction somebody takes AFTER they know there is a problem. The other one — "there is an AWS key in your .env that is not in the keystore", and harder, "that key is in a file git is tracking" — did not exist, so nobody found out until the repository was already public.
leaks_scan.notes: Matches the VALUE, not only the key name, and that is the whole design: Env::is_secret matches a key by suffix, which is right for masking and not enough here — preset.rs already wrote the reason, that "a key added upstream tomorrow called SERVICE_FOO_APIKEY would sail straight through". So every rule is a vendor-assigned prefix with a known alphabet and length (AKIA…, ghp_…, xoxb-…, sk_live_…, AIza…, SG.…, a PEM private-key header). The key-name rule is kept as a second, independent net. There is deliberately NO entropy heuristic and no long-random-string rule: those fire on minified JavaScript, on a hash in a lockfile and on a base64 image, and a scanner people learn to ignore is worse than no scanner — a miss costs a finding, a false positive costs the feature. A PEM header is matched only for the block types that are actually private keys, so a certificate and a signature are not findings. Nothing puts a secret on a command line: `git log -S<value>` would make the value an argument and therefore visible in `ps`, so the tracked files are read and matched in-process and the only thing reaching git's argument list is `ls-files`. `git ls-files` rather than a directory walk, which is not an optimisation — a walk would read node_modules and every build directory, and what is TRACKED is exactly what leaves the machine. `envTracked` outranks every other finding: it means every value in that file is in the history whatever its shape. `envInHistory` is asked separately and is the one people get wrong — untracking the file today does not take it out of the history, so a repository where this is true and `envTracked` is false is one somebody has already half-fixed. Both are asked BY PATH (`git log --all -- <path>`), never by value: `git log -S<secret>` would put the secret in the argument list where `ps` shows it to every process on the machine, and a path answer is stronger anyway — a file committed and later deleted is still in the history with everything that was in it, which a value search would miss the moment somebody rotated half of it. Each tracked finding carries `inHistory` from the same question. One finding per file, because a private key is fifty lines and fifty findings would bury every other file. Bounded at 2000 files and 512 KB each, with what was skipped and whether the cap bit reported rather than dropped — a scan that passed over four hundred files and said nothing reads as a clean repository. The value is NEVER carried in a finding — a report that quotes the secret is a second copy of it, in a place people paste into chat windows — and "never print it" on its own leaves somebody with a finding they cannot act on, so each one carries what every scanner in this field carries instead: a `fingerprint` (the first twelve hex characters of the value's sha256, so two rows with one fingerprint are one secret in two places, which is the difference between rotating one key and rotating two) and a masked `preview` (the first and last four characters, and only for a value of at least sixteen — below that it is masked whole, because four characters at each end of a short password is the password). The fingerprint is taken from the matched RUN and not the line, so the same key written `AWS_KEY=…` in one file and `key: "…"` in another is one secret rather than two. Not audited: nothing is changed, and nothing leaves the machine. See src-tauri/src/leaks.rs. THREE OF THE RULES ARE MODEL PROVIDERS' — OpenAI's sk-proj-, Google's AIza and Anthropic's sk-ant- — and the third was added last because it was the only common provider this table could not see: laravel/ai puts one of the three in the .env of every application that installs it. It is not a worse finding than the others, and no severity is derived from it; what is different is that having one says the application sends EVERY REQUEST IT MAKES to a service outside this machine, so the pane puts one sentence beside it pointing at egress_report — which asks Docker which containers can reach the internet rather than inferring it. The grouping lives in leaks::MODEL_PROVIDER_RULES; nothing about what is scanned or reported changes.

env_untrack.returns: { untracked: boolean, ignored: boolean, gitignoreWritten: boolean, exampleWritten?: string, exampleKeys: number, stillInHistory: boolean, needsCommit: boolean }
env_untrack.why: A finding people cannot act on is a finding they turn off, and this repair is easy to get half right: the common half-fix is deleting the file in a later commit, which takes it out of the working tree and leaves every value in the history.
env_untrack.notes: The standard repair, in the standard order. `git rm --cached` — NOT `git rm`, which would delete the running stack's configuration — with `--ignore-unmatch`, so a file that is already untracked is a success rather than an error: the caller pressed a button that says untrack it, and it being untracked is what they asked for. Whether it is ignored is ASKED with `git check-ignore` rather than parsed, because `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude` and a global excludes file all take part and this app is not the authority on any of them; the line is appended only when the answer is no, with a leading newline when the file does not end in one — otherwise `.gitignore` would gain `something.env` rather than a line of its own. `.env.example` is written only when there is none: overwriting somebody's example with a generated one throws away the comments and grouping they wrote for the next person. The example keeps every comment and blank line, because an example file is documentation, and every assignment keeps its key and its `=` and nothing else; `export FOO=bar` keeps its `export`, since some projects source the file from a shell. `stillInHistory` and `needsCommit` are the two halves this does NOT do and reports instead: untracking does not rewrite history, so a file that was ever committed still has every value in it and they have to be rotated, and `git rm --cached` writes the index — the removal leaves the machine when somebody commits and pushes it. UNSUPPORTED when the project is not a git repository. Audited as `env_untrack`, because it writes into somebody's repository and because it is done in answer to a credential having been committed, which is exactly the kind of act somebody has to be able to date afterwards. See src-tauri/src/leaks.rs.
