server_config_get.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_get.notes: The raw file including its comments. Only nginx and caddy are accepted; the other servers have no generated config file for a snippet to be added to.

server_config_set.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_set.notes: Written atomically. Takes effect on the next generate: the directives are rendered into each project's server config, not into a file the server reads directly.

service_connection.why: The services sheet showed a container name, a port table and a credentials block, and left the reader to assemble a URI. The obvious assembly — `mongodb://stackvo-mongo:27017/` — cannot work from the host, because that name only resolves on the Docker network. Null for a service nobody connects to with a string.
service_connection.notes: Two addresses come back, not one: `fromHost` is 127.0.0.1 and the published port, `fromContainer` is the container name and the port inside it. `fromHost` is null when a running container publishes nothing, rather than an address that would fail. The password is bullets unless `reveal` — the same act `env_reveal` is, and percent-encoded on the Rust side so a password containing `@` cannot rename the host. See src-tauri/src/connect.rs.

service_db_clients.why: The picker beside `service_open_in_client` has to be built from what is on this machine, not from a list of clients somebody might have. Empty for most services, which is the answer rather than a failure: a service with no connection string has nothing to open, and an AMQP or SMTP address is not one a desktop database client takes.
service_db_clients.notes: Which protocols a client opens is read from the application rather than declared here — on macOS from the bundle's own CFBundleURLTypes. That is not a detail: Redis Insight declares only `redisinsight`, so a table written from the name would have offered it for `redis://` and produced a button that launches an app which ignores the address. An installed client that does not declare the scheme is omitted rather than greyed out — it is not missing, it is not applicable. The first entry is always the system handler, with the empty id. See src-tauri/src/apps.rs.

service_dependencies.notes: Kept for completeness; services_list already returns required/optional/unmetDependencies per service, so the front end has no reason to call this separately.

args.client: string (id from service_db_clients; empty = the system handler)

service_open_in_client.why: The correct connection string has existed since connect.rs was written and the sheet has offered to copy it since; what was missing was the step that pastes it, which everybody was doing by hand.
service_open_in_client.notes: Always the host address — the container one is a name on a Docker network that no client on this desktop can resolve, which is the confusion connect.rs exists to remove. Refuses when the container publishes nothing rather than inventing 127.0.0.1. The URI carries the real password, because a URI with bullets in it is one that fails to connect, so this is `reveal` in the sense of env_reveal and is recorded in the audit trail as one — the service and the client, never the URI. The cost is that the secret is an argument to `open` and so visible in `ps` while that process lives; the alternative is a temporary file with the same reachability and a lifetime nobody controls. Copying the string is still there for a shared machine.

service_reveal.why: The value behind one masked credential on the services list, whichever place this workspace keeps it.
service_reveal.notes: Dispatches the way every other reader of service state does — the instance table when there is one, `.env` when there is not. `key` is the manifest setting key for an instance (`ROOT_PASSWORD`) and the `.env` key for the legacy path (`SERVICE_MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`), which is what the row carries in each case. The detail sheet called `env_reveal` directly before this existed, and after a handover that reported "not set in .env" over a password that does exist.

site_save.why: Whole document rather than per key: three settings in one small file, and three commands over one document is three chances for it and the screen to disagree - the same reasoning routes_save gives. MUST refuse a key that is not a POSIX variable name and a value carrying a line break: the overlay is YAML, where a newline in a scalar ends it and everything after is read as configuration somebody else wrote. Regenerates, because the directory listing lands in a GENERATED server config while the variables and the agent land in a compose overlay - two different paths for one save.

site_settings.why: Three settings in one document, because they are one kind of thing: a per-project setting the generator cannot read from the manifest (project.schema.json is additionalProperties:false and frozen), kept in .stackvo/site.json so it travels with the project. listingSupported and agentAvailable are answered by the machine rather than assumed by the screen: Apache and Swoole have no configuration file for a directory index, and an agent cannot be forwarded when none is running - a control drawn for either would do nothing.

spx_build.why: An extension has to match the exact PHP version, ABI and thread-safety of the binary that loads it, and SPX is built from source.
spx_build.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: the build runs in a THROWAWAY container of the project's own image (`docker run --rm`), never against the running container \u2014 that would mean apt-get inside somebody's live php-fpm, which lasts until the next recreate. Output is keyed by PHP version. A failed build MUST clear the copied extension: `built` treats its presence as proof of a usable build, so leaving a half-copied one turns 'try again' into a mount that stops PHP starting. Needs network and a few minutes; it belongs in the operation console.

spx_clear.why: Sampling is cheap enough to leave on, which is exactly why the directory fills.
spx_clear.notes: Reports only. The built extension is not touched \u2014 it is per PHP version and shared.

spx_delete.why: One report is a pair of files and deleting one of them leaves the other unreadable.
spx_delete.notes: The key comes back from a screen and ends up in a path. SPX's own keys are alphanumerics, dashes and underscores; anything else MUST be refused rather than resolved.

spx_options.why: php-spx's OWN default sampling period is 0, which means it records every call — a tracing profiler with the cost this feature exists to avoid. StackVo defaults to 100 microseconds so the claim on the pane, the profiler you can leave on, is true; 0 is still the right answer for counting a fast function exactly, so it stays reachable.
spx_options.notes: Separate from spx_set because it is a different decision: the switch says whether the extension is mounted, this says what it does when asked to record. IMPLEMENTORS: these reach a recording THIS APP starts — the cookie on a recorded request, the environment of a recorded command — and they MUST NOT be written into the extension's ini instead. MEASURED in php-spx's PHP_RINIT: the ini source is read only when access was NOT granted, meaning a request carrying no key and therefore not being profiled. A recording always carries one, so `spx.http_profiling_sampling_period` and its siblings are never consulted for it, and a pane wired to them would have had controls that appeared to work and did nothing. A recording started in SPX's own control panel uses that panel's own controls. MUST refuse a period above 1000000: a sampling period longer than a second samples a page load once.

spx_record_command.why: The slow thing is often not a page. A queue worker, a migration or a test suite is where minutes go, and none of them can be profiled from a browser.
spx_record_command.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: the id is resolved through quickcmd, so the frontend still names an id and never a program — that rule is this feature's whole security model. `SPX_REPORT=full` is NOT optional: php-spx defaults to `full` for a request and to `fp`, a flat profile on stderr, for the command line, so a CLI run without it profiles perfectly and writes no file. Interactive commands MUST be refused: a recording has to finish, and `artisan tinker` ends when a person types exit.

args.name: string (project)
args.path: string | null (a path on the site, default "/")

spx_record_request.why: Recording used to need a browser: SPX's control panel is the documented way in and its switch is a cookie only a person can set. The same trigger is a plain request header — php-spx's README profiles a page with `curl --cookie "SPX_ENABLED=1; SPX_KEY=…"` — so the app can send the request itself. That is what makes profiling reachable from a terminal, and from an assistant that cannot open a browser.
spx_record_request.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: the HOST is the project's own domain from its manifest and MUST NOT come from the caller. The path MUST be refused unless it starts with a single `/`: a value opening with `//` is a protocol-relative URL and would send the request, with the profiler key on it, to somebody else's host. Redirects MUST NOT be followed — a framework answering `/` with `/login` would otherwise write two reports for one button. The workspace CA is added as a trusted root rather than turning certificate verification off, and the client MUST opt out of the system proxy for the reason mail.rs documents. SPX writes the report during the request's own shutdown and says nothing about it in the response, so the new report is found by diffing the directory — which means one recording of a project at a time, or two races each claim the other's. The HTTP status belongs in the failure message: a 404 is a path that reaches no PHP at all, and 'recorded nothing' on its own sends people looking at the profiler for it.

args.name: string (project)
args.snapshot: { service: string, name: string }? (K-5 — the snapshot to restore before the second run)

request_replay.returns: { before: Report, after: Report, wallTimeUs: number, peakMemory: number, restored?: string }
request_replay.why: The commonest loop in performance work takes four steps today: change the code, open the site, find the page, come back and hunt for the new recording among twenty. explain.rs opens by saying no new measurement is needed and it is right about this too — the recording that names a request, the sender that can issue one with the profiler on, and the observation window a query log is joined against all exist. What was missing was the act.
request_replay.notes: Runs THE SAME request `spx_record_request` does — the two share one function rather than two implementations, because they would drift on exactly the details that make a replay comparable to the original: the profiler cookie, the redirect policy, and the observation window `request_explain` later joins statements against. Takes the same `spx:record:<project>` in-flight guard, so a replay and a manual recording cannot each claim the other's report. Returns BOTH reports so the difference is read where it came from, plus the deltas; there is deliberately no `faster` field, because one run against one run is not a benchmark — a cold opcache and whatever else the machine was doing are inside it — and a boolean would invite a conclusion the measurement cannot carry. UNSUPPORTED, with the reason, for anything but a GET: a recording names the request LINE and nothing else, so a POST re-sent without its body and its session is a different request and is usually answered with a redirect or a 419, and a result that looks like an answer and is not is worse than a refusal. Same for a CLI recording — replaying it would mean running the command again, which is a different act. NOT_FOUND for a key this project has no recording under. Deliberately NOT audited: it is the same act spx_record_request performs, that one is not audited either, and audit.rs states the bar — a trail that records routine traffic is one nobody reads. See src-tauri/src/explain.rs. With a capture window armed (capture_arm) and a session captured for THIS recording, a POST becomes replayable and the request is sent with its captured cookies and body. Without one the refusal above stands word for word, because it is still true. The match is by request line AND clock together within 2 seconds, nearest wins — matching on the line alone would attach one visitor's basket to another visitor's recording of the same page. Only the "not a GET" refusal is lifted; a CLI run and an unsendable path are still refused. K-5 — BINDING THE REPLAY TO A SNAPSHOT. The old refusal for a POST was lifted once a session could be captured, and what took its place is a request that DOES THE THING AGAIN: a second order, a second charge, a second row. That is not a reason to refuse it — somebody replaying a POST is doing it on purpose — it is a reason to offer the one thing that makes pressing it twice safe, which this application already has. `snapshot` names a database snapshot to restore BEFORE the second run and never after: restoring afterwards would discard what the replay did, which is the thing somebody replayed a POST to look at. The restore takes its own SAFETY COPY first, the same net db_restore puts under an ordinary restore — pressing a button on a profiling screen must not be the irreversible act — and a failure at any step STOPS the replay, because sending the request anyway would run it from a state the caller did not choose and report a number under a premise that is not true. It is NEVER CHOSEN AUTOMATICALLY: this app cannot know which snapshot holds the state the original ran under, and picking one would be answering a question nobody asked with data it does not have. And what it buys is stated rather than implied — REPEATABILITY, NOT COMPARABILITY: the `before` recording ran against whatever state existed at the time and nothing recorded what that was, so a snapshot means the replay can be run again from a stated point, not that the two numbers are a controlled experiment. `restored` carries the name back so the second run's premise sits beside its numbers. The restore is audited as `db_restore`, like any other.

capture_status.returns: { armed: boolean, remainingMinutes?: number, expires?: string, maxMinutes: number, bridge: boolean, captured: number, recent: Array<{ request: string, method: string, cookies: number, bodyBytes: number, contentType?: string }> }
capture_status.why: explain::replayable refuses a POST BY NAME with the reason: only the request line was recorded — not its body, its headers or its session — and a POST replayed without them is a different request, usually answered with a redirect or a 419 rather than the page. That refusal was not a gap in the code, it was what the code knew. But K-4's own example sentence is the one that needs the other half: "this bug only happened in that basket". A basket is a session, and replaying it means recording the request's cookies and body — which means writing somebody's session token and their form input to disk. So the feature is THE ASKING, not the storing.
capture_status.notes: `recent` describes at most the last five and NEVER quotes: `cookies` is a count of names and `bodyBytes` is a size, so the screen can say what would be sent without being a second place the credential exists. Not audited: nothing is changed, and reading a count is not the act somebody has to account for. Four rules, each a refusal rather than a default. spx_report.returns: { key: string, wallTimeUs: number, callCount: number, functions: number, events: number, truncated: boolean, hotspots: Array<{ function: string, calls: number, exclusiveUs: number, exclusivePercent: number, inclusiveUs: number, inclusivePercent: number }> }
spx_report.why: A report row could say a request took 900ms and nothing about which function held it. That answer is in the trace half of the pair and was readable only in SPX's own web UI — which needs a browser, a key and a person.
spx_report.notes: Reads only. The trace format was established by recording against a real image: `[events]`, one line per call entry and exit carrying CUMULATIVE metric totals, then `[functions]` naming them by index LAST — so time is attributed by the gap between consecutive events to whatever is on top of the stack, and names are applied after the replay. Absolute times are DERIVED from the metadata's own total by share, so they cannot drift from the figure shown beside them in the list — and that total is in MICROSECONDS even though php-spx calls the field `wall_time_ms`. MEASURED against a script written to burn a known 180ms: the metadata said 182837 and the trace's own cumulative total for the same run said 182837191, which is nanoseconds. Rendering the field as milliseconds is wrong by a factor of a thousand and still looks plausible. IMPLEMENTORS: cap the events replayed and the bytes decompressed, and report `truncated` rather than presenting a prefix as the whole run. Inclusive time MUST be added only when the outermost frame of a recursive call leaves, or a function that calls itself counts its inner calls twice.

spx_set.why: The switch. Writes `projects/<name>/.stackvo/spx.json` and re-renders the compose overlay so the reply describes something that is already true.
spx_set.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: switching on without a build MUST be refused rather than stored. An overlay that mounted an empty directory over the extension path stops PHP starting at all, which is a far worse failure than a button that says no. The mount reaches an already-running container only when it is recreated, which `active` reports.

spx_status.returns: { supported: boolean, enabled: boolean, built: boolean, phpVersion?: string, image?: string, active: boolean | null, running: boolean, controlUrl?: string, xdebugConflict: boolean, reports: Array<{ key: string, recordedAt: number, cli: boolean, request?: string, command?: string, wallTimeUs: number, peakMemory: number, callCount: number, mutates: boolean, bytes: number }>, bytes: number, directory: string }
spx_status.why: php-spx samples, so it can be left on during a real page load where Xdebug's profiler costs several times the request \u2014 the case Xdebug's profiler cannot cover, and the one Herd and Lerd both ship. The extension is NOT in contracts/php-extensions.json and cannot be: SPX is not on PECL, and the contract's `special` install method is documented as v1-MUST-REJECT. So it never enters the manifest, the Dockerfile or that contract; it is built into a directory this app owns and mounted, the way the debug bridge is.
spx_status.notes: Reads only. `built` is per PHP VERSION, not per project \u2014 the artefact is a function of the interpreter, so two projects on 8.4 share one build. `active` asks the running container whether the mount is there, which is a different question from `enabled`: mounts are fixed when a container is created. `wallTimeUs` is MICROSECONDS: php-spx's metadata calls the field `wall_time_ms` and it is not milliseconds — measured, see spx_report. `xdebugConflict` is true when Xdebug is also recording; two profilers hooking one engine is unsupported in both projects and the symptom is wrong numbers rather than an error, so it is reported rather than prevented. See src-tauri/src/spx.rs. `mutates` says whether sending this recording again would WRITE — everything that is not a GET, and never a CLI run. Not a judgement about the application's own routes (a GET can write too, and nothing here can know that), but the one distinction the request line does carry, and the one that decides whether the second run of a replay is the same act as the first. It is computed where the line is parsed so nothing downstream — the window, the pane, an assistant — re-derives it from a string, and it became worth stating when a captured session made a POST replayable: the old refusal stopped being true, and what took its place is a request that does the thing again.

stripe_key_set.returns: boolean (whether a key is now stored)
stripe_key_set.why: A credential needs somewhere to go that is not a file in the workspace, and this app already decided where that is.
stripe_key_set.notes: One command for both directions: `null` clears it, because a screen that could only ADD a credential is one people are right not to give one to. A key beginning `pk_` is refused here rather than by the CLI three seconds later inside a container — a publishable key is the one somebody has open in a browser tab, and it fails with an authentication error that says nothing about which key was pasted.

stripe_start.why: An operation because the first start pulls the Stripe image.
stripe_start.notes: Refuses when the project container is not running: the CLI would otherwise accept the events, fail to deliver each one and report the failures back to Stripe, filling the dashboard with delivery errors for a project that was simply not started. Removes any previous listener before starting — the container is not `--rm`, so a crashed one still holds the name. An empty `events` list means every event, which is the CLI's own default and the right one for "does anything arrive at all". `path` is a path inside the application and a URL is refused. `stripe listen` opens an OUTBOUND connection, so nothing has to be reachable from the internet — which is why this is not the tunnel with a different label: a quick tunnel's URL changes on every start, so the endpoint has to be re-registered in the dashboard each time and the signing secret changes with it. The API key is kept in the OS keystore by secrets.rs, one entry per project (two accounts must not share one, or one account's events are forwarded into the other's application, which looks like it is working). It reaches the container through `-e STRIPE_API_KEY` and never as an argument: argv is visible in `docker inspect`, in the host process list and in this app's own operation console, which streams the command it ran. The sidecar deliberately does NOT use `--rm`, unlike the tunnel's: an invalid key makes the CLI print its complaint and exit, and a removed container takes the log with it — so the pane showed no listener, no error and no reason for the single most likely failure this feature has. Found by examples/stripe_probe.rs, which also caught itself reporting success on Docker's own "No such container" message.

stripe_status.notes: `signingSecret` and `failure` are read from the container's log on every call rather than cached, so an app restart or a crashed listener stays truthful. `hasKey` is a boolean and there is no command that reads a key back — the pane can replace it or clear it and never display it. stripe_stop.why: Turning it off has to be as easy as turning it on.
stripe_stop.notes: Removes rather than stops: the signing secret is in that container's log and it is dead the moment the listener is, so leaving it behind would leave a stale secret on screen for the next person to paste.

supervisor_check_run.why: Takes the check rather than an id so a form can try what is on screen before it is saved — the same reason supervisor_test takes a server record. Never fails: a probe that could not be made is a failing check, not an error.

supervisor_check_save.notes: Replaces the check already on that process rather than adding a second. Returns the checks for the server it was about, not all of them. Probes run during the snapshot poll — there is no scheduler here and no automatic restart: a local tool that silently restarted php-fpm would be hiding the thing somebody opened it to see.

supervisor_checks.why: supervisord reports that a process is up. It has no idea whether the thing inside it is answering — a php-fpm out of workers, a queue worker wedged on a lock and a web server serving 502 are all RUNNING, and that is the state somebody is staring at when they open this. One check per process, because a process either answers or it does not.

supervisor_control.notes: One command for the whole matrix rather than twelve, because supervisord treats it as one: the verb and the scope pick the method name and every combination takes the same arguments. `restart` is two calls and not a method — supervisord has no restartProcess, and the stop half is allowed to fail because stopping something already stopped is a refusal and the expected first step.

supervisor_log.why: Where a FATAL says why. The last N bytes, which is the shape supervisord's own web interface uses; paging back through a log is a separate feature and is not pretended at.

supervisor_project.why: StackVo's own generated image for an nginx or caddy project runs supervisord as its command, with php-fpm and the web server under it — so every such project has had a supervisord in it the whole time and nothing could talk to it. Nothing is configured and nothing is stored: a project names its container. `reach` separates the ways this can be empty, because they look identical on screen and send somebody to different places — no supervisord in the image at all, an image built before the config grew a socket (rebuild), or a container that is not running.

system_accent.returns: { available: boolean, name: string|null, hex: string|null }
system_accent.why: The desktop's own accent colour, so the app can match it instead of shipping a brand colour that clashes with everyone's system theme.
system_accent.notes: macOS reads AppleHighlightColor via `defaults` and maps it to the eight colours the OS itself draws with. Elsewhere `available` is false and both fields are null — Windows keeps its accent in the registry, and saying "unknown" beats returning a wrong blue. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

template_override.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
template_override.notes: Copies the shipped file into the workspace so it can be edited, and returns its absolute path. Refuses when a copy is already there — that file is the user's edit. Only paths in templates_list are accepted.

template_revert.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
template_revert.notes: Deletes the workspace's copy; the version in the binary takes over on the next render. Destructive and not undoable — the front end confirms first.

templates_list.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
templates_list.notes: Every template compiled into the binary, with whether this workspace has a copy on disk. Installing writes none, so a copy means somebody chose to override it.

terminal_open_external.v1Change: Always works. The HTTP version returned HTTP 400 with 'Terminal cannot be opened from containerized environment' — it could never succeed in the shipped configuration.

args.tool: string (host tool id — only `mkcert` has a download today)

tooling_install.why: mkcert is a host requirement this app could report and never obtain: without it the stack runs and every browser warns. It is one static binary its author publishes, which makes it the one tool in the catalogue where fetching is the right answer rather than a second copy of `docker pull`.
tooling_install.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: the SHA-256 is compiled into the build, one per platform, and is NOT fetched. A checksum served beside the file it describes is not a check — whoever can replace one can replace the other. Nothing is written until the digest matches; a mismatch is FORBIDDEN and MUST NOT be offered as a retry. The file is written beside its target and renamed, because a half-written executable on PATH is worse than none. 0755 on unix. Over 64 MiB is abandoned mid-download. There is deliberately no update verb: an idempotent install that follows upstream is how a pinned digest stops being a pin. UNSUPPORTED for a tool with no download, or a platform the publisher has no build for. Audited as `tooling_install`.

tooling_path_apply.why: The `yerd path install` half, which this app had no equivalent of. Links `stackvo` and `stackvo-mcp` into the directory the app owns and writes one line into one shell's startup file.
tooling_path_apply.notes: IMPLEMENTORS: only the region between `# stackvo:path:begin` and `# stackvo:path:end` may be written; everything else in the file MUST come back byte for byte, and a file with no markers is APPENDED to, never prepended — the lines above ours are the ones the user put there deliberately. A copy is kept beside it as `.stackvo-backup` first. The directory goes FIRST on PATH, so a managed tool wins over a half-removed system one. Both halves run together: a PATH entry pointing at an empty directory is the version where `stackvo` still says "command not found". The linking half is best-effort — a checkout with no build of the CLI still gets its PATH entry. A startup file larger than 1 MiB is refused rather than rewritten (FORBIDDEN), with the line to paste in the hint. Audited as `tooling_path_apply`. macOS bash reads `.bash_profile` and Linux bash reads `.bashrc`; one file per shell, never both.

tooling_path_remove.why: The undo. A feature that edits somebody's .zshrc and cannot take it back out is one they do not press the first time.
tooling_path_remove.notes: Removes the marked region and nothing else. The links in binDir STAY: somebody who removes the PATH entry has said where they want `stackvo` looked up from, not that they want it deleted — and agents_install may by then have written that path into six assistants' configuration files. Removing from a file that has no block, or no file at all, is not an error.

tooling_remove.notes: Removes only the copy in binDir. A system copy — Homebrew's, the distribution's — is never touched, which is the whole distinction `source` reports. NOT_FOUND when this app did not install one.

tooling_status.returns: { binDir: string?, onPath: boolean, currentShell: string?, own: Array<{ id: string, about: string, built: string?, linked: string? }>, shells: Array<{ id: string, label: string, path: string?, exists: boolean, installed: boolean, current: boolean, line: string? }>, tools: Array<{ id: string, label: string, program: string, why: string, source: 'managed' | 'system' | 'missing', version: string?, path: string?, offers: string?, publisher: string?, availableHere: boolean }> }
tooling_status.why: Every rival ships a Tooling page — Yerd's installs composer, node, bun, the Laravel installer and wp-cli onto the host and shims them onto PATH. Half of that page has no place here and half of it was missing entirely. The half with no place: those five run in the project's container at the version the project declared, and a host copy would be a second answer to "which composer runs" whose answer is wrong. The half that was missing: `stackvo` and `stackvo-mcp` are programs this repository builds, the README documents them, agents_install registers one of them with six assistants — and nothing put either where a shell would find it. This reads that state: the directory, the links in it, the four shells' startup files, and the four HOST tools this app itself shells out to.
tooling_status.notes: Reads only, and answers with NO WORKSPACE selected — putting a command on PATH is something done before a folder is chosen, so a pane that needed one would be unreachable from the state it fixes. `source` distinguishes a copy this app installed (`managed`, in binDir) from the user's own (`system`, elsewhere on PATH); a program that is on PATH but will not run is reported `missing`, because a dangling symlink and a half-deleted install both leave a file behind. `current` on a shell row means the block in that file names *this* build's directory — which is what separates "already done" from "done when the data directory was somewhere else". `built` is null when the CLI has not been compiled: neither binary is bundled with the app (see Cargo.toml), so the pane offers the build command instead of a button that would link nothing. See src-tauri/src/tooling.rs.

args.labels: Record<string,string>? (keeps the current catalog when omitted)

tray_relabel.notes: Re-label the tray and the native menu bar, and adopt the catalog they are drawn from. The tray is created during setup(), before the webview exists, so Rust carries a fallback table for the two languages this build was born with — but that table is a bootstrap detail, not the app's translation of its own tray. The front end sends the real strings on boot and on every language change, which is what stops a third language from being a change to tray.rs. A map rather than a named type on purpose: a struct would make every new menu entry a contract change on top of a code change. The keys are checked instead — a catalog missing any of them is refused with INVALID_INPUT naming the gaps, because a menu half in one language reads as broken rather than untranslated. The three counted labels (containers, more, runningSummary) arrive as templates carrying {count} / {running} / {total}: Rust knows the numbers, the language file decides where they go.

tunnel_auth_reveal.why: The one readable secret in this app, and deliberately: a Stripe key and a provider token are entered from elsewhere and never needed again, while this one is generated by StackVo and has to be typed into a browser on somebody else's phone. A password nobody can read is a password nobody can use.
tunnel_auth_reveal.notes: Returns the password in full. The pane keeps it hidden until asked and offers to copy it beside the link it belongs to.

tunnel_auth_set.returns: TunnelCredentials | null (what is now in force)
tunnel_auth_set.why: A quick tunnel is a public, unauthenticated door into an application running on somebody's laptop, and the Share pane could only warn about it. This turns basic authentication on for one project.
tunnel_auth_set.notes: One command for both directions, like tunnel_token_set: `null` clears it. An empty password means GENERATE one — a field somebody has to fill in is a field that gets `test123`, and this one sits behind an address on the public internet. The credential goes to the OS keystore, one entry per project (a token is a machine's, a tunnel password is a door's — two projects sharing one means the link handed out for one opens the other). Authentication is enforced by an nginx container of StackVo's own between the sidecar and the project, NOT by the provider: four of the nine can do basic auth themselves, three cannot, and the four that can spell it four different ways. The guard is measured by examples/tunnel_guard_probe.rs against real containers — no credentials 401, wrong credentials 401, right credentials the application's own bytes — and it refuses to start at all when no credential reaches it. Enforcement begins at the NEXT tunnel_start: a guard cannot protect a link that was handed out before it existed.

tunnel_identity.why: Two questions are asked of every link the moment it is pasted somewhere — who else can open it, and will it still be this address tomorrow — and the pane had an answer to neither. This is the state behind both, without the password.
tunnel_identity.notes: Never returns the password; tunnel_auth_reveal is the one deliberate way to ask for that. `authUser` present means authentication is ON — a credential in the keystore IS the switch, because a second flag that can disagree with the keystore eventually says protected about a tunnel that is not. `keystore` says whether this machine can hold a credential at all, so a switch that would fail when pressed explains itself before. `reserved` is one entry per provider, because a kept address is granted by one account on one service: an ngrok domain is not a tailnet hostname. See src-tauri/src/tunnelid.rs.

tunnel_name_set.why: B-7's other half: an OAuth redirect URI, a Stripe webhook endpoint and a QR code on a slide are all registered once and used later, and a quick tunnel's address changes on every start.
tunnel_name_set.notes: Refused for a provider that keeps nothing rather than stored and silently ignored — three of the nine hand out a new address every time. The name is validated against hostname rules HERE, before an image pull and a start would say the same thing minutes later; `dotted` in the provider's `reserved` shape decides whether the field is a whole domain (ngrok's `shop.ngrok-free.app`) or one label (localtunnel's `shop`). Stored per project AND per provider, beside the app's own state rather than in the project manifest: a reserved name is granted by one account on one service, so a manifest carrying one would travel to a colleague's checkout as a name their account does not hold. MEASURED with localtunnel, which needs no account: the same subdomain came back twice, ninety seconds apart — and started immediately after the previous tunnel closed, the same request came back as a different address with no error at all, which is why tunnel_status reports whether the name was actually granted.

tunnel_providers.why: The picker is built from the table that owns the invocation, in Rust. A list the front end kept would go on offering a provider the day one is removed, and offer it without the fact that decides whether it can be used at all — whether its token is in the keystore.
tunnel_providers.notes: hasToken is a boolean and never the token. `anonymous` marks the four providers that hand out a URL with no account; `verified` marks the ones a real tunnel was opened through in this repository, which is those same four — the rest carry the vendors' documented invocations and say so on screen. `sessionMinutes` is the free tier's cap where one is enforced, which somebody needs before they paste the URL into a dashboard rather than after. `reserved` describes what a provider can be asked to keep — its own word for it, whether the field is a whole domain or one label, and whether the client still prints the address it ends up on (false for exactly one: a named Cloudflare tunnel is routed from Cloudflare's configuration and cloudflared never learns the hostname). Nine providers now, not eight: `cloudflare_named` is the same client as `cloudflare` running a tunnel somebody already created, which is the other half of the trade the quick tunnel makes.

tunnel_start.why: Starts a tunnel-client sidecar on the stack's network, forwarding a public URL to the project's container. No host-binary competitor can attach to the container network at all. `provider` names one of the eight in tunnel_providers and defaults to cloudflare — the choice is real: an anonymous quick tunnel gets a URL in ten seconds and a new one on every start, which is right for "did the webhook arrive" and useless for a redirect URI somebody registers in a dashboard.
tunnel_start.notes: An operation because the first start pulls the provider's image, which can take minutes. Targets the project container directly: with SSL on, every Traefik project router listens on websecure only, and a public visitor cannot complete a TLS handshake against a hostname that exists in no DNS. Three providers also present the local domain as the Host header; the SSH-based ones cannot, and the pane says so. A provider that needs a token is refused here when none is stored, before the pull rather than after it, and the token reaches the container as an environment variable — never as an argument, which docker inspect and the operation console both print. When a credential is stored for the project, the sidecar is pointed at StackVo's own nginx guard on the stack network instead of at the project container, and that guard is what asks for the password — including for Tailscale, whose sidecar joins the guard's network namespace rather than the project's. A reserved name is sent through the flag the chosen client actually has (`--subdomain`, `--url=`, `--hostname=`, or zrok's reserve-then-share), and the name asked for is recorded on the sidecar as a label so the status call can check it against the address that came back. `cloudflare_named` is refused without a hostname: Cloudflare routes a named tunnel from its own configuration and cloudflared never prints the address, so starting anyway would leave the pane saying "connecting" for ever.

tunnel_status.why: Webhook testing (Stripe, GitHub) had no answer: myapp.loc does not exist on the internet. This reports every running tunnel sidecar and its assigned public URL.
tunnel_status.notes: The URL is read from the sidecar's own log on every call rather than cached — what the log says is what is actually live, across app restarts and container crashes alike. `url` is null while the client is still connecting; the UI polls until it appears. `provider` comes from the container's `stackvo.tunnel.provider` label and is null only for a sidecar started before the picker existed, which is a cloudflared one. `failure` is the client's own complaint, read from the same log — a rejected token is the likeliest failure four of the eight providers have, and the sidecar is deliberately not --rm so its log survives the exit that produced it. `guarded` is read off the sidecar's own label, so it describes the tunnel that is actually running rather than what the keystore holds now. `reserved` is the address that tunnel asked for and `reservedHonoured` is whether it got it — measured against a provider that quietly assigns a different name when the one asked for is still held, which is a tunnel that works and a dashboard entry that points nowhere.

tunnel_stop.notes: Removes rather than stops. The sidecar is kept after an exit so its log can say why it failed, so a container left behind here would go on showing a dead URL and a stale reason to the next person who opens the pane. Removes the project's tunnel guard as well, and unconditionally — reading the keystore first to decide would leave a guard running whenever the credential had been cleared in between.

tunnel_token_set.returns: boolean (whether a token is now stored)
tunnel_token_set.why: Four providers need an account token, and a credential needs somewhere to go that is not a file in the workspace — this app already decided where that is.
tunnel_token_set.notes: One command for both directions: `null` clears it. The entry is per provider and not per project, which is the opposite of stripe_key_set and deliberately so — a Stripe key is an account's, and two projects on one account cross-post events; a tunnel token is a machine's. A provider that takes no token is refused rather than given a keystore entry that would sit there for ever looking like configuration.

updater_offer.why: `tauri-plugin-updater` fetches a manifest, compares versions, verifies a signature and installs — that is the whole of it. It has no notion of a channel, no notion of a percentage, and no way to STOP: a release found to be broken cannot be recalled, because every running copy keeps asking the same endpoint and getting the same answer. Channels, staged rollout and rollback are therefore four extra fields in the manifest and one decision made BEFORE the plugin is asked, and this is that decision.
updater_offer.notes: Takes the manifest rather than fetching it, so the branches are testable — every one of them is a branch somebody's install depends on. Order is the design: `paused` wins over everything (an emergency stop a channel mismatch can override is not one), `supersededBy` is checked before the version comparison because its entire purpose is to defeat it, and the rollout wave is last because a wave only means anything for an update that would otherwise be offered. The bucket is `sha256(installId : version) % 100` — stable for one install and one version, so an update cannot appear and disappear between checks, and independent between versions, so the same unlucky 1% is not first every time. A manifest with none of these fields is offered to everybody, which is what `latest.json` looks like today. The install id never leaves the machine; the response carries the bucket so a person can check the arithmetic, and not the id.

updater_status.returns: { configured: boolean, hasPublicKey: boolean, endpoints: number }
updater_status.notes: Whether this build can verify an update. Tauri checks a bundle's signature against the public key compiled into the app; with an empty `pubkey` every check fails inside the plugin with a message about signatures, which reads like a server fault and is a build fault. Read from tauri.conf.json via include_str! so the answer describes the binary, not the working tree.

updates_check.notes: Needs tauri-plugin-updater plus a signing key and a release endpoint — i.e. a release pipeline, not just code. Deferred to Phase 4 alongside signed builds. Declared here so the surface is complete and the gap is visible.

websurface_start.returns: { address: string, token: string, tools: number }
websurface_start.why: The loopback API is OFF until somebody asks. Not because loopback is dangerous by itself, but because a listener nobody knows about is a listener nobody turns off — and the honest default for a surface answering questions about somebody's workspace is that it is not answering them.
websurface_start.notes: The token comes back ONCE, to the caller that started it. It is never written to disk and `websurface_status` does not carry it: a status call that did would hand it to every later caller, and the first of those is the surface itself. Starting while one is already up is a CONFLICT rather than a second surface — a caller that asked to start something and silently got somebody else's token would have no way to know. Port 0 by default so the OS picks; a fixed port is one something else on this machine may already hold, and a surface that fails over a collision is one people work around by choosing another fixed one.

websurface_status.returns: { running: boolean, address: string | null, tools: string[] }
websurface_status.notes: The address and what would be served, never the token. `tools` is the intersection of two policies computed rather than listed: a tool reaches the wire only if it does not write AND its contract command passes the keystore rule, so a tool added to the MCP table joins this list only when both agree.

websurface_stop.notes: `false` when nothing was running. Aborting the accept loop drops the listener, which closes the port; an in-flight request on its own task is not waited for — it holds a token that was already checked, and a stop that blocked until every connection finished is a stop somebody presses twice.

window_close_action.notes: Carries out the choice the close dialog collected, optionally storing it as closeBehaviour. Four behaviours exist including "ask"; the extra "quit" (close, leave the stack running) is meaningful here because the containers are Docker's and outlive the app.

worker_options.why: Which workers this project can offer, from its files alone: artisan offers 'queue' and 'scheduler', laravel/horizon in composer.json adds 'horizon'. A Node project gets an empty list, not an error.

worker_start.notes: The sidecar runs the project's own image (same PHP, extensions, bind mount and network, so .env and the database resolve as the web container sees them) with --restart unless-stopped — self-healing is Docker's own supervisor, not reimplemented. queue:work carries --max-time=3600 on purpose: a worker holds the code it booted with, and an hour caps how long it serves yesterday's code. Refuses when the project has no built container.

worker_status.why: A Laravel app runs queue:work, the scheduler and Horizon beside the web server; locally they live in a forgotten terminal tab, which is why "my job never ran" is a support staple. This reports every worker sidecar with its restart count — the self-heal made visible; a large number is a crash loop, not a success story.

worker_stop.notes: Removal, not just stop: with unless-stopped, a merely-stopped container is one engine restart away from coming back.

workspace_get.why: The web UI never needed this — it ran inside the StackVo repo, so its root was `/app` by mount. A desktop app has to be told, or work it out. Returns the resolved root plus how it was resolved, so the UI can show the user which checkout it is driving.

workspace_pick.notes: Opens the native directory picker, then applies workspace_set. Returns null if the user cancels.

workspace_set.notes: Validates that the path contains core/cli/stackvo.sh and projects/ before accepting it, then persists it. Rejects with NO_WORKSPACE and an explanation rather than silently accepting a wrong folder.

args.name: string
args.options: { newBranch?: boolean, name?: string, database?: 'none' | 'create' | 'copy', instance?: string, minutes?: number }?

worktree_create.why: N — the item nothing else in this space does. `git worktree add` gives a branch its own directory; this gives that directory its own subdomain, its own database and its own environment, so two branches of one application run side by side.
worktree_create.notes: Plans first and refuses on the plan's own reason, so the command and the preview cannot disagree. Steps in order, each rolling back the ones before it: git worktree add (streamed as scaffold:progress / scaffold:done, the same events project_clone uses), then the manifest, then the database, then the record, then the generate. NOTHING IS WRITTEN INTO THE CHECKOUT THAT GIT TRACKS — the files in a worktree are the branch's. Identity goes into stackvo.local.json, the machine-local overlay that exists to be the file that is never committed, and which is added to the repository's .git/info/exclude (git's own per-clone ignore list, never .gitignore) when git says it is not ignored yet. A branch that carries no stackvo.json gets a full one derived from the parent's instead, with the parent's aliases and LAN sharing dropped so it cannot claim the same names. The environment — database credentials, APP_URL, STACKVO_WORKTREE_BRANCH — is app-owned, outside every checkout, and reaches the container through the compose overlay site.rs already renders. The database is a database on an instance that is already running, not an instance of its own: a branch is not a different engine. Emits project:creating / project:created, because a worktree IS a project and nothing downstream knows the word. Audited as worktree_create. After the database is created and copied, the worktree is given a database login of its own — a MySQL/MariaDB account granted on that schema alone — and the password is written to `worktree-logins.json` beside the table, NOT onto the record: `Table` is serialised both to disk and across this boundary into a webview, so a credential on `Record` would ship with it. Failure to create that account is reported as progress and is NOT fatal: refusing the whole worktree because a server would not GRANT would take away a feature that works today, and the app instead says which login the branch has. PostgreSQL and MongoDB get no account of their own and are reported as sharing the instance's — Postgres needs object-level grants applied inside the database after the copy plus default privileges for what the application creates later, which is a second design, and half of it produces a branch that cannot read its own tables. `minutes` is what turns a worktree into a sandbox: an expiry, clamped to seven days, recomputed at creation rather than taken from the plan — a plan made minutes ago on a screen somebody was reading should not spend part of the time it was asked for. Nothing acts on the date by itself and nothing ever will on a timer: an app that deleted a directory on a clock would eventually delete one with a morning's uncommitted work in it. What the date does is let the list say the time has passed, so removing it stays a decision somebody makes in one click.

worktree_env_set.returns: { env: Record<string, string>, effective: Record<string, string> }
worktree_env_set.why: A worktree's own environment variables. site_save cannot serve this: it writes .stackvo/site.json, which is inside the checkout, and on a worktree the checkout is a branch somebody else is working on.
worktree_env_set.notes: Keys and values go through the same checks the project overlay applies (site::checked_key / checked_value) — a POSIX variable name, and a value with no line break in it, because the overlay is YAML and a newline in a scalar is a second directive somebody else wrote. `effective` is what the container will actually be given: the derived database variables and APP_URL beside the typed ones, with DB_PASSWORD masked and the same password masked inside DATABASE_URL. The credentials are never stored in the record — they are derived from the instance on every render, so a password changed in Settings reaches every worktree at the next generate instead of leaving a stale copy. A typed variable of the same name still wins, which is what makes the derived ones a default rather than a decision.

worktree_list.why: Every worktree in the workspace, so the projects list can say `branch of shop` on a row instead of showing two unrelated siblings. Asking per project would be one command per row.
worktree_list.notes: Each row carries what is true right now beside what was recorded: `exists` for the directory, `dirty` for uncommitted work (null when git could not answer — the same third state `projectLocalRead` reports for ignore rules), and `orphaned` when the registration outlived the checkout. Reads two files and asks git per row; no Docker call, so it answers with the engine down. `isolated` says whether the branch reaches its database with a login of its own; it is DERIVED from whether a login is held for that name rather than stored on the record, so the file that holds the password is the file that decides the answer. `false` means the branch uses the instance's shared account and can therefore reach the parent's data, which is a true thing the screen has to be able to say. `expired` and `remainingMinutes` come from the record's `expiresAt`, judged against ONE clock read for the whole list — rows judged against their own `now` could report two of them on either side of the same second. `remainingMinutes` is `Some(0)` for a sandbox whose time has passed and absent for a worktree with no expiry: two different answers rather than one. The comparison is textual, which is correct only because the timestamps are fixed-width UTC — the same property audit.rs relies on.

worktree_plan.why: A worktree creates a directory, a hostname, a container and a database at once, and the only moment any of those can be argued with is before they exist. The same plan-then-apply pair as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and db_move_plan/db_move_apply.
worktree_plan.notes: No side effects — safe to call on every keystroke in the branch field. A refused plan still carries the name, path, hostname and database it *would* have produced, because a dialog that blanks out when it says no makes the reason harder to act on. `refused` is one sentence naming the cause: git missing, the project not a repository or itself one, no `domain` to build under, a branch git will not accept, a branch already checked out elsewhere (git allows one working tree per branch), a directory or hostname already taken, or a database instance that is absent or stopped. `warnings` is for what proceeds anyway: a parent with a `*.` alias means two Traefik routes match the new name, MongoDB has no CREATE DATABASE, and a database of that name already existing means it will be used rather than created. `expiresAt` is the moment a `minutes` option would produce, worked out in the preview so the screen shows the moment rather than the duration — "in 120 minutes" is arithmetic the reader has to do, and "at 14:32" is the answer they were doing it for.

args.name: string
args.options: { force?: boolean, dropDatabase?: boolean, deleteBranch?: boolean }?

worktree_remove.why: The way back. A worktree left behind is a directory that looks like a project, a branch git will not check out anywhere else, and a database nothing points at.
worktree_remove.notes: Four things can go and three of them are separate decisions the screen asks first: the checkout always, its uncommitted changes (`force`), its database (`dropDatabase`) and its branch (`deleteBranch`). Order is the reverse of creation with one exception — the containers go first, because Docker holds the tree open through its bind mount and git refuses to remove a worktree files are being written into. The database is dropped before the checkout: one that will not drop should leave the worktree there to try again from, rather than leaving a database nothing points at. `db::drop_database` refuses the instance's own database and the engines' system databases whatever the record says. Deleting the branch is best effort and never fatal — the worktree is already gone by then, and refusing to finish over an unmerged branch would leave the removal half done. project_delete reaching a worktree through the ordinary Delete button forgets the record and prunes git's registration, and deliberately leaves the branch and the database alone: `removeFiles` is that command's only licence to destroy anything. Audited as worktree_remove. The worktree's own database account is dropped whatever was decided about the data, and its stored password is forgotten with it: keeping `dropDatabase` off means “leave my data alone”, not “leave behind an account that can reach it”. A failure there is logged and does not stop the removal — an account with nothing left to reach grants nothing.

worktree_passport_keys.why: Passport signs tokens with storage/oauth-private.key and that file is in .gitignore, so a fresh worktree does not have one and every token request comes back as a stack trace about a missing file.
worktree_passport_keys.notes: GENERATES a new pair inside the worktree's own container; it does NOT copy the parent's. Copying a signing key into a second environment is the exact opposite of what a worktree's database isolation exists for — the branch would be able to mint tokens the place it branched from accepts. A key that is already there is REFUSED rather than overwritten: `passport:keys` overwrites, and overwriting invalidates every token issued under it, so somebody who really wants a new pair says so in the terminal where the consequence is theirs. Refused with a sentence when laravel/passport is not in that worktree's composer.lock, and when the project is not running — Docker's own "No such container" reads as a broken button rather than as a project that is not started. Audited. See src-tauri/src/worktree.rs.

worktree_support.why: N. Everything a project can say about worktrees before a dialog opens: whether git is here, whether the directory is a repository, which branches exist and which of them are already checked out somewhere, which database instances a branch could be given a database on, and the worktrees this project already has. One call rather than five, because the answer decides whether the button is even drawn.
worktree_support.notes: `reason` is a sentence, not a boolean — 'not a git repository', 'itself a worktree', 'no domain in its manifest'. `linked` is git's own answer (a linked checkout has its own git dir and a shared common dir), which is a different question from `record`: `record` means this app made it and therefore knows what it gave it. Branches come back newest-commit-first, because the branch somebody wants a worktree for is almost always one they touched this week. Instances that are stopped are listed and marked rather than hidden: 'why is that greyed out' has an answer on the row, 'why is the list empty' does not. `isolated` is the same fact `worktree_list` reports, for this project: whether its database login is its own. False for a project that is not a worktree at all. `grantArgs` is the registration that would give an assistant this branch and nothing else, rendered from a Grant rather than assembled on screen so what is copied is what the server enforces. It carries `--for` only while there is time left; for a sandbox whose expiry has passed it is EMPTY rather than an unlimited grant, which is what dropping a zero `--for` would silently produce. `auth` is what a branch's OWN HOSTNAME breaks — a bug this feature produced by working. Sanctum's SPA mode ties a session to a list of hostnames (`sanctum.stateful`, `SESSION_DOMAIN`) and the new host is in neither, so signing in on a branch returns 419 or 401 with nothing on screen saying why and the developer blames their own code; Passport keeps its signing keys in `storage/oauth-private.key`, which is in .gitignore, so a fresh worktree does not have one and every token request is a stack trace about a missing file. TWO VALUES ARE WRITTEN ONLY WHERE THEY CHANGE SOMETHING, and that is the measurement rather than a preference: `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS` is written only where the project PINS a list of its own, and the branch host is APPENDED to it — where the project pins nothing, Sanctum's own default already follows APP_URL, which worktree.rs has just pointed at this branch, and writing a list there could only take hostnames away; `SESSION_DOMAIN` is written only where the project pins a domain that does not COVER the branch host (`.shop.loc` and `shop.loc` both cover `feature-x.shop.loc`), because Laravel's own default is the current host and is already right. Both go in BEFORE the record's own variables in worktree::env_for, so a value the user typed still wins — the line env_writer already holds. `passportKeysMissing` is answered only where laravel/passport is in the WORKTREE's composer.lock, not the parent's. The repair is worktree_passport_keys, and the parent's key is NEVER copied.

xdebug_set.why: One switch instead of three manual steps: adding the extension to the manifest, configuring the client host and port, and telling the IDE where the code is mounted.
xdebug_set.notes: Writes `php.extensions` in the manifest and re-renders `generated/docker-compose.xdebug.yml`. The extension is COMPILED IN, so enabling it needs a rebuild before it takes effect — `needsRebuild` says so rather than letting the toggle look finished. Writing the manifest canonicalises it the same way project_manifest_write does (`webserver` becomes `server`); that is the contract's rule for writers, not a side effect of this command.

xdebug_status.why: Step debugging is the thing Docker makes hardest and the thing a PHP developer needs most. `xdebug` was already in the extension catalog with per-version pecl pins, so it could be compiled in by hand-editing stackvo.json — and then it still would not connect, because nothing set xdebug.mode or told it which host the IDE is on. This reports all three layers separately: listed in the manifest, present in the built image, and live in the running container.
xdebug_status.notes: `active` is read from the running container's environment rather than assumed from the manifest. The two disagree in a case users hit: `stackvo up` from the CLI does not layer the overlay this app writes, so it recreates the container without the Xdebug environment and debugging stops working with nothing on screen to explain it.

events._note: Names are preserved from Socket.io so the Vue listeners keep working, with ONE deliberate change: the terminal events move from dash to colon separators for consistency. That is a 4-line change in the terminal component.

app:close_requested.notes: The window was asked to close and closeBehaviour is "ask". Rust prevents the close and emits this; the front end shows the choice dialog and answers with window_close_action.

build:built.note: The IMAGE finished building. `project_build` has three stages — generate, build image, recreate container — and this marks the end of the second. The UI shows 'starting container…' between this and build:success.

build:success.note: The container is up from the fresh image; the whole operation is done.

certs:changed.why: The certificate was reissued, so anything showing coverage or an expiry has to re-read it. Traefik picks the new file up on its own; the UI has no way to know without being told.

compose:progress.why: `docker compose up/down` writes its progress to stderr line by line. The old UI held the HTTP request open for the whole run (proxy_read_timeout 600s) and showed nothing until it ended.

container:state_changed.why: Sourced from the Docker events stream. Today the UI polls on a visibility-gated timer (useVisiblePolling); a push stream removes the polling entirely.

db:progress.notes: The tools write progress and warnings to stderr; stdout is the dump itself and never reaches the UI.

devserver:changed.why: Turning dev mode on changes the compose overlay, which changes what the container is and what an `up` would recreate — so anything showing the project's configuration is out of date.

engine:status_changed.why: Drives the whole-app connected/disconnected state and the tray icon.

folder:appeared.notes: A directory that was not there when the watch started now is. The project directory is a park, and cloning a repository into it used to be silent — the answer to "why is my new site not listed" was "reopen this dialog", which is the part a park exists to remove. The watcher was already receiving those events and dropping them: its manifest reader accepts `<projects>/<name>/stackvo.json` and nothing else, which is right for its own question and misses every git clone. Announced on the folder becoming NEW TO THE WATCHER rather than on a timer: a clone writes for as long as the repository takes and every second of it is a create event, so a time window would either repeat the same folder a dozen times or be long enough to miss the next one. A folder that is removed is forgotten, so cloning over the same name announces it again. Decides nothing — the UI refetches, which is the only thing that can tell an adoptable folder from one that arrived with its manifest committed.

logs:line.notes: `container` is the container for a container stream and the project for the cross-project fanout — one stream has one origin, a fanout has one per line, which is why it is carried per event rather than settled when the stream opens. `source` is omitted entirely on a single-source stream, so those payloads are byte-identical to what they were before the fanout existed.

logs:sources.why: The fanout follows at most 60 files. Emitting what it dropped is the difference between a view that is honest about its coverage and one that silently implies it sees everything. Re-emitted after every rediscovery, so a file appearing at midnight moves the number on screen.

octane:reloaded.notes: The watcher saw a save under one of Octane's own watched paths and replaced that project's workers. Emitted whether or not it worked, because a reload that silently did not happen is the same experience as the bug the feature removes — an edited file that changes nothing. Only for projects where octane_auto_reload was turned on, which is off by default: a reload arriving mid-request kills that request. Debounced by seconds, so a composer install is one reload rather than four thousand.

manifest:changed.why: fs-watcher on projects/*/stackvo.json. Enables 'config changed — regenerate?' instead of the user remembering to run `stackvo generate`.
manifest:changed.notes: Debounced 400ms — editors write a file several times per save. The app does NOT regenerate on its own; it offers the action, because rebuilding a container under someone who is mid-edit is worse than the staleness it fixes.

perf:changed.payload: { project: string, path: string, enabled: bool }
perf:changed.why: A layer moved. The container is still reading the old arrangement until it is recreated, which is the same 'written to disk, not to the container' state xdebug:changed reports.

php_ini:changed.why: Creating or removing the file changes the compose overlay, which changes what a `up` would recreate — so anything showing the project's configuration is now out of date.

preset:applied.why: Importing a preset rewrites service enablement and versions across .env, so the services list, the enabled/disabled chips and the pending-regenerate state are all now out of date.
