site:changed.why: A per-project setting was written. The container is still the old one until it is recreated, which is the same state xdebug:changed and perf:changed report.

stripe:done.why: The listener is up, or it is not — what it then says about the key is read from its log.

stripe:progress.why: The image pull, streamed into the operation console.

supervisor:alarm.why: Emitted by a background loop rather than by a pane, which is the whole point: a notification matters when nobody is looking, and a poll that only runs while its tab is open can only tell somebody what is already in front of them. Edge-triggered — a process sitting in FATAL is not news every twenty seconds, it was news once — and the first look after start records without announcing, because a process that was already broken did not just break. Running projects only: a stopped one has no container to exec into.

tunnel:progress.why: The first tunnel_start pulls the cloudflared image; the pull's own lines belong in the operation console like every other long-running docker invocation.

usage:over-budget.payload: { project: string, date: string, cpuMinutes: number, gbHours: number, budgetCpuMinutes?: number, budgetGbHours?: number }
usage:over-budget.notes: One project has passed a budget set for it in preferences. Emitted from the stats sampler, ONCE per project per day: the sampler runs every sixty seconds and a project that is over at two o'clock is still over at half past, so a notice per round would be four hundred by the evening — and the feature somebody switches off within the hour is the one that would have told them tomorrow. The key is `<date>/<project>`, so tomorrow's first breach is an event again without anything having to clear the set at midnight.

xdebug:changed.why: The toggle changes the manifest and the compose overlay, so anything showing the project's configuration or its pending-regenerate state is now out of date.

AdoptBatch.operationId: string? — the single generate this batch ran; absent when it had nothing to generate

AdoptOutcome.name: string
AdoptOutcome.reason: string? — why, whenever it is not `adopted`
AdoptOutcome.note: `skipped` covers the two ordinary conditions a batch meets and a single adoption does not: a folder that is already managed, and a folder with nothing in it but dotfiles. Colouring either of those red would teach people to ignore the colour. `code` sits beside `reason` rather than instead of it: the two skips are conditions this command decides and the UI has to render in the reader's own language, so they need something stable to switch on, while a failure's reason is an error message from somewhere else with nothing to switch on. Matching the English prose in JavaScript would have turned a sentence somebody could improve into a wire format nobody could see was one.

Adoptable.name: string
Adoptable.note: `has_files` ignores dotfiles: a directory holding nothing but a `.DS_Store` is empty for this purpose, and offering it for adoption as if it had code in it is how a real checkout looked before this was handled. `compose_file` is reported but NOT resolved — resolving costs a `docker compose config` per project, which is not something to spend on a list that loads on every visit; migrate_scan does that for the one the user picks.

App.name: string
App.note: One launchable application on this machine. `id` is the stable key stored in preferences and never the display name, which is localised and moves between versions. An entry that is not installed is returned with `available: false` rather than omitted, so a picker can grey it out — a list that drops them reads as lack of support. At most one entry per list carries `default: true`: the one that would be used when the preference is unset. Every list ends with `id: 'custom'`, named 'Other…', always `available: true` and never `default: true`: it is the one entry whose availability cannot be checked, because what it points at is a command line in `preferences.json` that has not been typed yet — and an automatic fallback onto a command nobody chose would be worse than no fallback.

Bundled.versions: number — versions whose files were carried; lower than the index's total when something was withdrawn
Bundled.files: number — files written, index and package.json included
Bundled.bytes: number — their total size, so the person choosing a stick knows
Bundled.skipped: string[] — versions deliberately not carried, each with its reason. Empty is the normal case; a non-empty list is a fact the person carrying the bundle should read before they walk away from the network
Bundled.signed: boolean — whether registry.json.minisig travelled with it. A machine whose policy sets requireSignature refuses a bundle without one, and this is where that is cheap to find out

CertPlan.note: `domains` is the exact SAN list mkcert will be invoked with, so what the user approves is what lands — the same relationship `preview` has to the hosts file. `remove` names domains the certificate still covers that no project asks for any more; they disappear on the next reissue and are listed so that is not a surprise. `rejected` names domains dropped as invalid rather than silently omitting them.
CertPlan.reloadedNote: Writing the certificate is not enough to change what a browser gets. Traefik's file provider watches generated/traefik/dynamic, and the certificates are not in it — routes.yml only points at them, and a certFile is read while the dynamic configuration is parsed. So cert_apply rewrites the watched files with their own bytes to force a reparse. Observed on a real checkout: Traefik up two days, serving a certificate a day older than the one on disk. False after an apply means the new certificate is on disk but not yet served.

CertStatus.trust: Array<{ id: 'system' | 'firefox', trusted?: bool, detail?: string }>
CertStatus.note: `covered` is read from the certificate's subjectAltName, not from the project list. `missing` is wildcard-aware: `*.stackvo.loc` covers `api.stackvo.loc` but not `shop.loc` and not `a.b.stackvo.loc`, because a wildcard matches exactly one label. `ca_trusted` is null when the platform gives no cheap way to ask, which is not the same as false; it is the SYSTEM store, which is what every existing caller means by it. `trust` is the fuller answer, store by store, and it exists because of Firefox: Firefox does not use the operating system's store, it carries its own (NSS) per profile, and mkcert installs into that one only when `certutil` is present — it warns and carries on when it is not. So the ordinary state on a fresh laptop is a trusted system store, a working Safari and Chrome, and a Firefox that refuses every page, which one boolean reported as `true`. A store's `trusted` is null for "this machine would not say", which for Firefox means Firefox is not installed here — not a problem anybody has to fix. The three failing states are kept apart because their repairs differ: certutil missing (install nss and trust again), the CA absent from a readable store (trust again), and a store that could not be read at all. `stale` is true when anything is missing or the certificate has expired — it is what the UI badges. `rejected` names the domains dropped for being unparseable: `certs.rs` refuses one bad manifest rather than costing every other project its certificate, and naming them is the point — `CertificatesPane` reads this array without a guard, so a contract that omitted it described a UI that would throw. `error` is set when the certificate file exists but could not be read, which is why `covered` being empty is not on its own an answer: "covers nothing" and "could not be asked" are different states and the pane shows different things for them. `notAfter` is Unix epoch **seconds**, not a formatted date — the frontend multiplies by 1000 and hands it to `Date`; it was declared as a string here for a while and the generated types said so, which is exactly the kind of drift this file exists to prevent.

Checkout.note: The `origin` remote, verbatim, read out of .git/config rather than by running `git remote get-url` — this is called once per project on every list, and a subprocess per row turns a directory listing into twenty forks on a page that reloads whenever a container changes state.

CompanionRow.name: string — the manifest's handle, and the suffix of the container name
CompanionRow.containerName: string — stackvo-<instance>-<name>, derived exactly as render::context derives it
CompanionRow.image: string — the reference actually pulled, digest-pinned when the manifest pins one

Connection.note: `masked` is false both when `reveal` was asked for and when the service has no password at all, so the UI only offers the eye where there is something behind it. `passwordKey` names the .env key rather than carrying a value — it is the same key the credentials list reveals, and the two must agree about which secret is in play.

ContainerDetails.name: string
ContainerDetails.note: Read from one `inspect`. `gateway` is the first non-loopback gateway — the detail page shows one. `imageSize` is bytes on disk for the image this container runs, not the container's own writable layer. Nearly everything is nullable because a created-but-never-started container has no state to report, and reporting zero for it would be a number somebody reads as measured.

CpuStats.note: `loadAverage` is the 1/5/15-minute triple and is null on Windows, which has no equivalent. `breakdown` is null until two samples exist — the counters are cumulative, so one reading cannot produce a percentage — and null for good on a machine where it was measured to disagree with `percent`. It is reported when it can be trusted and withheld when it cannot, rather than drawn next to a number it contradicts.

DbInstance.note: Separate from DbTarget rather than a field added to it: `db_targets` answers “which engines can this workspace dump”, one row per engine, and four callers read it that way. One row per instance would give all four a list twice as long for a question none of them asked. Stopped instances are included and marked — a list that hid one would leave somebody wondering where the instance they just created went.

DbMovePlan.note: Dumping and restoring are two calls this app already had; what it did not have is an answer to “will this work”. Same engine is allowed. MySQL↔MariaDB is allowed WITH a warning — the same dump format in practice and genuinely different servers, and refusing it would refuse a thing that usually works. Crossing families is refused: a mysqldump file is not Postgres input and never becomes it, so accepting the request would empty the target and then fail on thousands of syntax errors. A downgrade is warned about because it is the direction that breaks quietly and does so partway through a restore that has already replaced the data.

DbMoved.bytes: number — the size of the dump that crossed, the only number that says anything actually moved

DbTarget.note: `extension` is the suggested file extension, and it differs by engine rather than being cosmetic: mysql and postgres dump to plain SQL a person can read and edit, while mongodump produces a gzipped BSON archive that only mongorestore can read. `database` is null for mongo, where the dump covers the whole server.

DeclaredPort.name: string — the manifest's handle: main, console, smtp
DeclaredPort.host: u16? — what the container publishes when there is one, the recorded allocation when there is not

DeclaredSidecar.id: string — the key the manifest gave it
DeclaredSidecar.about: string — one line the repository wrote, so a reader knows what the extra container is for
DeclaredSidecar.command: string[] — argv, empty when the image's own command stands
DeclaredSidecar.container: string — `stackvo-<project>-<id>`, the hostname the application connects to
DeclaredSidecar.note: A sidecar, NOT a service: it is rendered into this project's own compose block, comes up and goes down with the project's profile, and never enters instances.json. There is no host address beside `container` and that is by construction rather than by omission — project.schema.json refuses a host port and a host path — so the only way in is from inside the project's own network. The two derived names are why this is a command rather than a field read off the manifest the view already has: deriving them in JavaScript would be a second copy of a naming rule whose whole purpose is that two clones of one repository cannot collide.

DependencyRow.capability: string — what the manifest asks for, so MariaDB can answer 'sql'
DependencyRow.service: string? — the one service that will do, when only one will
DependencyRow.provider: string? — the installed instance answering it, null when none does
DependencyRow.running: bool — false whenever there is no provider; the two are told apart by `provider`

Detected.server: string? — null unless something in the folder actually named a web server. A folder of PHP files says nothing about which server should run it, so there is nothing to detect; DDEV's `webserver_type` is the one input that does say. It was a bare string spelling 'nginx' at every site, which read as a finding and was a default in a module that cannot see SUPPORTED_SERVERS_DEFAULT — so `detected_spec` resolved the setting first and imported a DDEV project configured for Apache as whatever the setting named
Detected.note: `evidence` names the files the answer was read from, and `confidence` says how much to trust it. `guess` means nothing recognisable was there and the fields are defaults the user is expected to correct — presenting that as an answer is the failure this distinction exists to avoid. `server` is null rather than defaulted for the same reason, one level down: what the folder declares wins and the workspace setting answers for a folder that declares nothing, which is the rule every other field here already followed.

DevServerStatus.note: `tool` is read from package.json with the FRAMEWORK checked before its bundler — Nuxt and Next both pull one in as a dependency, and the wrong order tells a Nuxt project to edit a vite.config.js it does not have. `command` prefers the `dev` script over `start`, because `start` in a Next project serves a production build, which is the mode this feature exists to get out of. `mounted` is read from the RUNNING container, never inferred; `stackvo up` from the Bash CLI layers three compose files, not six, and will recreate the container in production mode. `host_allowed` is null when there is no config file to look in, which is NOT the same as false — it is checked as text, because parsing JavaScript to decide whether a key is present is a much larger promise than "does the file mention it", and the answer is only ever used to decide whether to show the snippet.

DevcontainerPlan.secrets: string[] — the `${DEV_…}` names the reader has to fill in
DevcontainerPlan.skipped: string[] — services or config files that could not be carried, with why
DevcontainerPlan.notes: string[] — true things a reader would otherwise discover by failing
DevcontainerPlan.note: `DEV_` is the placeholder prefix and it is chosen, not arbitrary: template.rs lists the eight prefixes the workspace renderer substitutes, and a placeholder starting with STACKVO_ would have been replaced on the way out — silently, with an empty string, leaving a compose file in a repository with no password in it and no error anywhere. A test asserts the prefix is one that renderer leaves alone.

DiskStats.note: Totals are cumulative since the sampler started; the rates are bytes per second, derived from the gap since the previous sample.

DnsCheck.name: string — the probe name, under the suffix and in no hosts file
DnsCheck.tcp: DnsProbe — asked the responder over TCP
DnsCheck.system: DnsProbe — asked this machine, the way a browser would
DnsCheck.public: DnsProbe — whether the rest of the internet still resolves
DnsCheck.ok: bool — udp and system together, which is the pair that means 'this works'
DnsCheck.note: Four probes rather than one verdict because the repair differs: a responder that does not answer is this app's fault, a machine that does not ask it is the resolver file's, and public names failing matters more than the feature does. `public` is informational on its own — an offline machine fails it — and is only ever decisive as a before/after comparison inside dns_resolver_install, which undoes its own change when public names stop resolving.

DnsProbe.detail: string — what came back, in words, for a screen that has to explain a failure

DnsStatus.mechanism: string — resolver | network-manager | dnsmasq | systemd-resolved | nrpt | manual
DnsStatus.writable: bool — whether this app can apply the change itself, or only report it
DnsStatus.tld: string — the last label, which is what a resolver is pointed at
DnsStatus.tcp: bool — the second socket, reported separately because a port can be half-taken
DnsStatus.file: string? — the file this mechanism writes, where it has one
DnsStatus.configured: bool — whether this machine currently asks us for the suffix
DnsStatus.instruction: string — the file this app would write, or the line the user must place
DnsStatus.reload: string? — what is reloaded after the write, spelled out rather than done quietly
DnsStatus.foreign: string? — a file already at that path that is not ours, and what it says
DnsStatus.stale: string[] — resolver files this app wrote for a suffix the workspace has since left
DnsStatus.broken: bool — the machine asks us and nothing answers, which is the state where every name under the suffix fails
DnsStatus.note: The responder answers ONE suffix and refuses everything else — it never forwards, has no upstream and holds no cache, because an open forwarder on a machine is a thing that can be pointed at and a development tool has no business becoming the resolver for anything it did not create. `listening` is read from whether the socket is bound rather than from a preference: a setting saying yes over a port something else took would be a screen that lies. `mechanism` is detected rather than derived from the platform — on Linux WHICH file to write is a question about the machine (NetworkManager's dnsmasq, a standalone dnsmasq, systemd-resolved), and a guessed path is worse than no feature because it rearranges name resolution on a machine this app was wrong about. `manual` is the honest answer when none of them is found. `foreign` MUST be reported before the switch is pressed and the file MUST be copied aside rather than replaced — /etc/resolver/test is a path dnsmasq, Valet or a colleague's script may own, and taking a suffix away from another tool with no way back is not a thing to discover afterwards. `stale` exists because macOS's mechanism is one file PER SUFFIX: changing DEFAULT_TLD_SUFFIX leaves the old file pointing at a responder that now REFUSES that TLD, which is worse than never having written it — before, those names went upstream and failed honestly. `broken` is asked of the socket rather than of this process's own flag: a responder whose thread died and one in another copy of the app are both cases where the flag and the machine disagree, and the machine is right.

DockerfilePreview.skipped: [{extension, reason}] — what the Bash generator drops without telling anyone

Doctor.dns: { suffix: string, port: number }? — null in every ordinary state, INCLUDING the feature being off. Set only when the machine's resolver points at a local responder that is not answering: the one DNS failure nothing else on screen reports, where the app, the containers and the proxy all look healthy and every project domain fails to resolve.
Doctor.extensionsNote: **Added after reading `tools/validate-contracts.mjs`'s output instead of its summary line.** Three of that tool's four errors on this checkout are C-06 — all one root cause, `imap` removed in PHP 8.2, sitting in two project manifests AND in the stack's default extension set — and every one is local and fixable. The desktop app reported none of them, because the doctor knew about ports, disk and hosts and nothing about extensions. It matters more than a lint: the Bash generator SKIPS A BAD EXTENSION SILENTLY, so nothing fails and nothing is logged, and the symptom is a fatal `Call to undefined function imap_open()` at runtime with nothing connecting it to a build that reported success. `isDefaultSet` entries come first because they are the worse case — a project created right now, with nothing customised, cannot build. The default PHP version is itself contested (DEFAULT_PHP_VERSION vs SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES_PHP_DEFAULT, CONFLICTS.md C-12), so BOTH are checked rather than one being picked: an extension failing on either is a problem whichever key wins. Project rows reuse manifest::normalize's own C-06/C-07 findings rather than restating the rule.
Doctor.note: ports.requiredBy is the compose service that publishes the port, read from the generated files — which is the enabled set, because the generator only writes enabled services. ports.state: ok = free or held by the stack itself; warn = a docker backend holds it but the engine could not say whose container; fail = a named conflict. generated.state: warn = an input (.env or a manifest) is newer than the oldest generated compose file, detail names it; fail = never generated.

DumpsStatus.note: **There is no on/off switch, and that is deliberate.** The overlay sets VAR_DUMPER_FORMAT and VAR_DUMPER_SERVER for every eligible project and leaves them set, because with the variables set and nothing listening `dump()` renders into the response exactly as it does today — ServerDumper falls back, verified in a running container. A state file for a setting with no observable off-state would be ceremony. Two things had to hold for this to reach a WEB request rather than only the CLI, and both were checked in the container: the official PHP image's docker.conf sets `clear_env = no`, so the container environment reaches FPM workers, and `variables_order` is EGPCS — the E is what puts it in $_SERVER, which is where VarDumper looks.

Endpoint.note: `host` is 127.0.0.1 for the host address and the container name for the internal one. Both are in the URI already; they are carried separately so a client that takes a host and a port in two fields can be filled in without parsing the string back apart.

EngineStatus.note: `platform` is derived from the socket path and is a label, never a branch: nothing in this application does anything different because of it. `podman` covers rootless ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock, searched first) and rootful (/run/podman/podman.sock) — Podman speaks the Docker API on a unix socket, so the only thing it ever needed was the path. `podman-docker` installs Podman's socket under Docker's name and therefore reads as `engine`; that is a limitation of a path-based label rather than a failure, and it works. `version` and `apiVersion` mean different things and only the second is Docker's: Podman answers `Version: 5.1.1` — its own — and `ApiVersion: 1.41`, the Docker level it emulates. Neither is compared against a minimum anywhere, which is what makes a non-Docker engine work at all.

ExplainFinding.subject: string?
ExplainFinding.note: A kind and its numbers, never a sentence: the surfaces render these in their own words and two of them render in two languages, so a sentence built in Rust would be English in a Turkish window. Ordered most useful first — the ones that name a fix above the ones that qualify them. Thresholds: `nPlusOne` at 3 repeats (the same constant the query log pane uses, so one screen cannot call three an N+1 while another calls it four), `databaseBound` at 30% of the run in driver frames, `hotspot` at 20% of the run in one function's own body. `noDriverFrames` is the cross-check no single pane can make: statements landed in the window and the trace names no driver frame at all, which usually means php-spx's `builtins` switch is off and the wait is charged to whichever userland function called the driver.

ExplainSplit.note: The sum of the EXCLUSIVE time of every frame that is a database driver — `PDO::`, `PDOStatement::`, `mysqli`, `pg_*`, `SQLite3*`, `MongoDB\\Driver\\`. Exclusive rather than inclusive because inclusive would count a nested driver frame twice, and because the question is how long PHP spent waiting, which is time in the driver's own body. Framework layers (Illuminate\\Database\\Connection::run) are deliberately NOT counted — their own body is bookkeeping and counting them double-counts the driver frame beneath. Caches and queues are not counted either: they are not what the query log records, so their time could not be checked against anything on the same screen. `drivers` is the decomposition, so the share is auditable rather than asserted.

ExplainWindow.note: Seconds since the epoch. `observed` is the stretch THIS APP watched the request across — the host clock before it sent the request, and the host clock once php-spx's report was on disk — which brackets the run by construction whatever `exec_ts` turns out to mean. It is kept per report key in `logs/projects/<project>/spx-observed.json`, written by spx_record_request and spx_record_command, and pruned against the reports that still exist. `derived` is the fallback for a recording made in a browser: `exec_ts - 1` to `exec_ts + wallTimeUs/1e6 + 1`, where the second at each end is exec_ts's own truncation and NOT an allowance for drift. The fallback carries one premise this repository has not measured — that `exec_ts` is the START of the run rather than the moment the file was written during shutdown; if it is the end, a derived window sits one whole duration late and quietly. `examples/explain_probe.rs` asks a live container. A screen MUST say which basis it is showing, because the two are not equally trustworthy.

FanoutStream.note: `followed` < `total` means the 60-file cap bit and the oldest-modified files are not being watched. Reported rather than trimmed silently: a view that caps its own coverage and says nothing reads as "nothing else is happening".

FinishedEvent.subject: string
FinishedEvent.note: On failure `error` carries the last few output lines rather than a generic exit-code message — that tail is almost always the real cause.

Flame.frames: Frame[] — folded stacks; a function under two callers is two frames
Flame.total: number — microseconds accounted for, which is the width of the root row
Flame.records: number — entry and exit records read
Flame.stacks: number — distinct stacks the file held
Flame.truncated: bool — the file was longer than the reader's ceiling; this is the start of the request
Flame.pruned: number — paths too thin to draw, dropped and counted rather than silently missing
Flame.depthCapped: bool — the stack went deeper than 64 frames
Flame.note: Microseconds always, computed by this app from the trace's own timestamps — unlike a cachegrind report, whose unit is whatever the file declares and MUST be read from it. A trace costs far more than a profile to record (two lines per function call, hundreds of megabytes for one request), which is why the mode is trigger-started like profiling and why the tree is pruned before it crosses this boundary.

Frame.name: string
Frame.note: One box in the flame view, and the type is recursive because a call tree is. `value` is the cost of this BRANCH in the file's own time unit. `recursive` is true when this function is already on the path above it — the walk stopped there, which is different from a branch that cost nothing.

GeneratorReport.warnings: string[] — configuration problems the port can see and StackVo does not report, e.g. C-20

HandoverNote.kind: string (resolvedMovingTag | portMoved | adoptedVolume | settingHasNoHome | unknownService | versionNotInstalled | nothingToInstall | noFreePort). `versionNotInstalled` is NOT 'unpublished': the catalogue handover reads is the local package tree, so the honest sentence is 'not installed here', and the two ask for different things — one is a click in the Market, the other is a version that was never in the index.
HandoverNote.subject: string

HandoverPreview.missing: MissingPackage[] — packages the handover needs and this machine does not have

HookPlan.digest: string? — what an approval would be recorded against; absent when the project has no host steps
HookPlan.note: A plan, not a result: it says what would run for one event and what would not, before anything is spawned — the same review-then-apply shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and a preset import. A refused step is NAMED here rather than silently skipped at run time, because “nothing happened and nothing said why” is indistinguishable from a hook that ran and did nothing.

HookStep.command: string — display only; nothing parses it back
HookStep.blocked: string? — policy-off | policy-host | needs-consent; absent means it runs

HostsOverview.note: `stale` names domains inside StackVo's own block that nothing serves any more. Only managed lines are ever offered: a hand-written entry belongs to whoever wrote it, and a tool that tidies away lines it did not write is one nobody trusts with the file again.

HostsPlan.note: `preview` is the exact text that will be written — the same value the diff is rendered from, so what the user approves is what lands.

HtmlCheck.note: Percentages are of the client/feature combinations Mailpit tests (186 on the version measured against).

IdleProject.seconds: number? — since the last request; absent when the log has never mentioned this router
IdleProject.note: Container CPU is not the signal and neither is the network counter: php-fpm sits near zero whether it is serving or asleep, and network moves for health checks and DNS — one mistake stops something in use, the other never stops anything. The honest answer is the proxy's, which wrote down when it last routed to each router. A project the log has NEVER mentioned is not suspendable: that is the state of a stack that just came up, and stopping everything the first time somebody enables this would be the worst possible introduction to it.

Install.path: string — the installation root, or for Valet/Sail the directory that was pointed at
Install.sites: Array<{ name: string, path: string, domain: string | null, bytes: number, partial: boolean, detected: Detected, taken: boolean, services?: string[] }>
Install.note: L. `domain` is what the OTHER tool serves the site at, when the other tool says so: Laragon writes a vhost with a ServerName, Valet and Herd derive one from their own tld, a DDEV project's config.yaml names it and the machine's project_tld supplies the suffix, and a Sail project's .env may carry an APP_URL. XAMPP and MAMP have nothing to read, so it is null and adoption asks. Sail's localhost defaults are treated as no domain rather than imported as one.

InstancePlan.id: string — the id this would take
InstancePlan.refused: string? — why a second instance is not allowed, or null
InstancePlan.settings: InstanceSetting[] — the manifest's, with defaults as values and secrets unmasked
InstancePlan.ports: DeclaredPort[] — host is what the allocator would choose, or null when it could find nothing

InstanceRow.primary: boolean — holds the pre-package network alias

InstanceSetting.key: string — as the manifest spells it, no SERVICE_<ID>_ prefix
InstanceSetting.kind: string — the manifest's type: string | secret | int | bool | enum | instanceRef
InstanceSetting.isDefault: bool — the value in force is the manifest's own default
InstanceSetting.defaultValue: string? — the manifest's own default, so the form can put it back; null for a secret, whose default is never handed out unasked
InstanceSetting.required: bool — instance_apply_settings refuses to empty one of these
InstanceSetting.options: string[] — an offer, not a constraint. For an instanceRef it is the installed instances answering the capability it names
InstanceSetting.label: Record<locale, string>

LanProject.name: string
LanProject.note: `host` is null when the project asked to be shared and this machine has no address to build a name from — the switch is on and there is nothing to show for it, which is a state the screen has to be able to say out loud.

LanStatus.note: `address` is null both when there is no network and when this machine's address is PUBLIC — the second is a refusal, because handing out `shop.<public-ip>.sslip.io` would publish a development site under a name anybody can resolve. `suffix` is reported so the screen can say where the name comes from instead of showing a domain nobody recognises. `stale` is a name already written into a compose file or certificate that this machine would no longer produce — a laptop that changed networks — which is the one thing a derived address cannot tell you by being derived.

LandingStatus.note: `rendered` is an RFC 3339 timestamp, or null if the page has never been written. `running` and `rendered` are independent: the sidecar serves a FILE, so the container can be up while the page it serves is stale.

LocalOverride.note: `stackvo.local.json` is this machine's overrides for a committed manifest. `applied` is the dotted paths it currently supplies and `refused` the keys it may not carry (`name`, `runtime`) — both read back from the same merge the renderer runs, so the screen cannot disagree with what actually runs. `ignored` is git's own answer to whether the file would stay out of a commit, and is null when git had no answer: no git, or not a repository, which is not the same as “not ignored”.

LogFile.label: string
LogFile.note: `id` is `<root>:<relative path>` — `app:` for files the code wrote under projects/<name>, `server:` for files the stack wrote under logs/projects/<name>. It is a handle, not a path: it is what app_log_open takes, and it is the reason no absolute path is ever accepted from the frontend. `modified` is epoch seconds so the date is formatted in the user's locale rather than the backend's.

MailBody.note: `headers`: every header flattened to one row per value, sorted by name; Mailpit serves them from a dedicated route, MailHog inlines them.

MailMessage.subject: string
MailMessage.note: `date` is passed through unparsed: the UI formats it in the user's locale, and the two servers disagree about which field it lives in, not about the format. `snippet` is null on MailHog, which does not send one — deriving it from the raw body would render MIME boundaries as preview text. `bcc` is populated only by Mailpit, which derives it from the SMTP envelope; MailHog cannot tell a Bcc from a To, so there it is empty rather than guessed. MailHog's `cc`/`replyTo` come from headers as one joined string per entry.

MailStatus.note: `unread` is null rather than 0 on MailHog, which has no concept of a read message — a zero would render as "all caught up" on a server that cannot know. `available` is false when the checkout has neither catcher at all, which is different from having one that is switched off.

MachineCommands.path: string — where the file is, or would be. Shown so somebody can go and write one
MachineCommands.commands: Record<string, { exec: string[], about?: string, interactive?: bool }> — keyed by id, in file order
MachineCommands.note: The machine-wide half of the declared-command surface, at `<root>/commands.json`. Between the two declaring layers the PROJECT wins an id collision and the machine file is told: refusing a committed, shared file because of a personal one its author has never seen would be hostile, and overriding it silently is the button-that-lies failure the catalogue rule already refuses. An id already in the built-in catalogue is refused from either layer.

Manifest.name: string
Manifest.php: { version: string, extensions: string[], xdebug: boolean } | null
Manifest.node: { version: string, install: string, build: string | null, start: string, port: number, packageManager: string | null } | null
Manifest.lang: { version: string, install: string | null, build: string | null, start: string, port: number } | null
Manifest.schedule: unknown[] — commands this project runs on a timer; omitted when empty
Manifest.providers: Record<string, unknown> — named places this project's data lives; omitted when empty
Manifest.note: `stackvo.json` as the READER returns it: the file's fields plus this app's verdict on them. ProjectManifest is the file itself, defined by project.schema.json — the difference is `valid`, `errors`, `warnings` and `local`, none of which are ever written. `runtime` is canonical and absent-means-php. `aliases` are lower-cased, de-duplicated and never contain `domain`; a leading `*.` is the one entry that reaches the certificate and the router and cannot reach /etc/hosts. `hooks`, `commands`, `sidecars` and `providers` are keyed maps whose values are defined by project.schema.json — the FILE's spelling, so a step is `{"exec": [...]}` and a command's argv is `exec`; `schedule` is a list in the same spelling. Each is omitted entirely when empty. They are written that way because this payload is posted back through project_manifest_write: serialised any other way, every one of them was dropped on the first save. `local` names the dotted fields this machine's stackvo.local.json supplied and is empty for a manifest read straight from the committed file — `project_manifest_write` refuses a manifest whose `local` is non-empty, which is what stops one developer's overrides being saved into the file the team shares.

ManifestFinding.note: `path` is the location inside the manifest, so a finding can be shown against the field it is about rather than at the top of the form.

MarketPackage.name: Record<locale, string>
MarketPackage.keywords: string[] — search terms the index publishes, so mysql is findable by typing 'database' and by typing 'mariadb'
MarketPackage.multiple: boolean — whether two versions may run at once
MarketPackage.maintainer: string? — who publishes it. Every package names one and no screen showed it; a catalogue meaning to carry third-party packages has to say whose a package is

MarketStatus.fetched: boolean — false before the first refresh
MarketStatus.installed: number — version directories on this machine
MarketStatus.signed: boolean — whether the CACHED INDEX was signature-verified when it arrived. Not whether this build can verify: a machine that pins the official key still holds an unverified catalogue whenever the last refresh came from a directory somebody picked.
MarketStatus.signatureRequired: boolean — whether policy.market.requireSignature is set. Reported apart from `signed` because the pair is the story: required and not happening is a refusal a user needs explained.
MarketStatus.verifiedBy: string | null — the key id that verified the cached index. Null whenever `signed` is false. Present so the two states a user can be in — verified by the official key, verified by their organisation's mirror key — are distinguishable, which a bare boolean cannot do.
MarketStatus.offlineBundle: string | null — the bundle policy.market.offlineBundle points at, which wins over the path the user chose. Nothing is embedded, so this is the only way an air-gapped machine ever gets a catalogue.
MarketStatus.constrained: boolean — whether a policy says anything about the market at all, so the page can explain a refusal before it happens

MarketVersion.overridden: number — how many of this version's files this workspace has taken over (P). On the row rather than behind a click: it is the answer to 'why does this behave unlike the documentation', and somebody asking that will not open a sheet they have no reason to suspect.

MemoryStats.note: `free` is `total - used` and is the only figure that can sit beside `used` in one control without the two contradicting each other. `available` is what a new process could actually get, which on macOS and Linux is MORE than `free` — page cache is reclaimable and is counted in `used`. Drawing a donut from used+available once filled it to 60% while the label in its middle said 78%, on numbers that were both true.

Migration.note: `version` is null when the tag does not state one — `latest`, `alpine` and `stable` yield nothing rather than a pin, because importing `latest` as a version invents a decision the source file deliberately did not make. Image matching is on the repository with registry and namespace stripped, so docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch and elasticsearch are one entry, and it is exact rather than fuzzy: a project running ghcr.io/acme/redis-shim is not running Redis, and guessing that it is enables a service nobody asked for. A registry port is not a tag — localhost:5000/mysql has no version. Two compose services mapping to one catalog id collapse to one, or the same .env key would be planned twice with different versions. `evidence` names what each conclusion was read from, for the same reason Detected carries it: a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404.

MigrationPlan.note: `spec` is detection with the compose file layered on top, and the order is the point: detection reads the CODE and gets runtime, framework and document root; the compose file records what its author DECIDED — version, domain, extensions, services. Where both have an answer the compose file wins, because a guess loses to a declaration. `env` is the service enablement expressed as the same reviewed diff a preset import shows, rather than a second way of saying "turn these on".

MissingPackage.installable: boolean — whether the cached index offers it, which decides whether the UI can offer a button or only an explanation

Mount.note: `source` is a host path, or a volume name when Docker manages the storage — the two are not distinguishable from the string alone, which is why `kind` is reported beside it.

NetworkStats.note: Totals are cumulative since boot, unlike DiskStats — the counters have different origins and a UI that labelled both “since start” would be wrong about one of them. The rates are bytes per second across the gap.

PackageReport.resealed: string[] — files whose hash the manifest had wrong
PackageReport.note: C-1. A manifest states the sha256 of every file the package ships and pkg::verify checks them on every read, so editing a compose fragment leaves a package that refuses to load with a message about bytes rather than about the line somebody just edited. That bookkeeping — not the JSON — is what made authoring a package impractical. `resealed` is what sealing changed (or would change, from a lint); `problems` is what it refused. A report with problems means NOTHING was written: sealing is bookkeeping, not a way past the validator.

PerfLayer.enabled: bool — whether the setting says it lives in a volume
PerfLayer.exists: bool — whether that volume exists on the engine
PerfLayer.bytes: number? — what it holds, when the engine can say
PerfLayer.onHost: bool — whether the host still has a copy, which is what an editor indexes
PerfLayer.hostFiles: number? — files in the host copy, counted up to a cap
PerfLayer.gain: { workload: 'boot'|'write', times: number }? — what moving THIS directory measured; absent when nobody has measured it
PerfLayer.note: Measured with examples/perf_layer_bench.rs on the machine this shipped from: vendor in a volume is 3.8x on a framework boot and does NOTHING for writes; storage/framework is what buys the writes, at 2.8x. That is why this is a list of directories rather than one 'make it fast' switch — the win depends on which directory moves, and a single switch would be a guess about somebody's project. `gain` carries that per row and is the only place the figure is stated to a user: it used to be an AVERAGE of the two, in prose, in `perf.explain` in both locale files — which hid the very fact the design rests on, and put a measurement somewhere a translator had to restate it correctly without any way to know it was one. It is absent for bootstrap/cache and node_modules, which are offered and have never been through the bench; a row with no number is a row nobody measured, and lending it a neighbour's figure would be the average all over again. src-tauri/tests/perf_claims.rs holds perf::GAINS against the bench's own recorded output and fails if a locale grows the number back. NOT a synchronising layer: nothing on the host writes these directories, so nothing needs reconciling. A bidirectional sync (Mutagen's job) is deliberately not built here — see src-tauri/src/perf.rs for why a worse copy of it would be a liability rather than a feature.

PhpIniStatus.effectiveNote: What PHP in the RUNNING container reports right now, from one `docker exec php -r ini_get`. Null when nothing is running. Read rather than assumed because assuming was wrong: measured on a real stack, `php -i` says `Loaded Configuration File => (none)` — the official images ship no php.ini at all, so conf.d is not one layer among several but the only one — and `max_execution_time` is 0 under FPM, not the 30 the manual lists. The form uses these as placeholders, so it never shows a default the container does not have; it is also where an override is confirmed to have landed after a restart.
PhpIniStatus.note: `values` holds the four directives the form manages (memory_limit, upload_max_filesize, post_max_size, max_execution_time); `unmanaged` holds everything else the file contains, which is preserved verbatim on every write — the file is the user's and is safe to hand-edit and commit. `containerPath` is /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/zz-stackvo.ini: every PHP image the generator builds on (php:X-fpm, php:X-apache, php:X-cli for Swoole, and FrankenPHP, itself built on the official image) parses conf.d after its own php.ini, and `zz` sorts after the docker-php-ext-*.ini files the build writes, so what is set here is what PHP ends up with. Mounted read-only. `warning` is a legal but near-certainly-unintended combination — post_max_size below upload_max_filesize silently caps uploads at the smaller number, which is the classic "I raised the limit and it still fails".

PolicyImage.repository: string — the key a pin is written under
PolicyImage.usedFor: string — what this image is for, so the list reads as an inventory
PolicyImage.shipped: string — the reference this build carries
PolicyImage.effective: string — what will actually run, after the policy's pin and its registry prefix
PolicyImage.moving: bool — whether `effective` is still on a tag that can change under it
PolicyImage.pinned: bool — whether a policy pin produced `effective`
PolicyImage.note: One of the images this application runs and did NOT build: nine tunnel providers' runners, the landing page, the tunnel guard and the perf helper. Six ship on `latest`, which is exactly the tag `pkg::MOVING_TAGS` forbids a third-party package from using — so the rule was enforced against everybody except this application, and the day a broken `cloudflared:latest` is published every user's tunnels stop at once with no version to go back to. The tags are NOT pinned in the source, deliberately: choosing a pin means naming a version that exists, which is a release-time act against a registry rather than something a source file can assert. What changed is that there was nowhere to pin — these ten lived as literals in four modules, appeared in no interface, no .env and no policy file, and nothing could say which of them moved. `moving` is computed AFTER the pin, so a row an administrator has fixed stops being flagged; one that stayed flagged would be a screen that lies about a setting that worked.

PolicyMarket.constrained: boolean — whether the policy says anything about the market at all
PolicyMarket.registryUrl: string | null — a mirror the organisation runs; read by the HTTPS source
PolicyMarket.offlineBundle: string | null — a directory to install from with no network. Nothing is embedded, so this is the only way an air-gapped machine gets a catalogue, so it is a first-class install path rather than an enterprise extra
PolicyMarket.requireSignature: boolean — the one key in the block that is a lock rather than a note: it can only turn verification ON, and there is no value of it that turns a check off. Raises market::Trust to Signed, which refuses today because no key is pinned
PolicyMarket.allowedPackages: string[] — services that may be installed. EMPTY MEANS NO OPINION, not 'none'
PolicyMarket.allowedRegistries: string[] — registries an image may come from; a reference with no host counts as docker.io. Empty means no opinion
PolicyMarket.allowedSources: string[] — catalogue sources this machine may fetch an index from. An https entry matches on its HOST; a local path matches as a directory prefix on a boundary. Empty means no opinion
PolicyMarket.allowOverrides: boolean | null — whether a workspace may put its own copy of a package file in front of the published one (P). null is no opinion, which means allowed. Reported here because it is a rule that refuses an action, and this pane is where somebody who was just refused finds out which rule did it
PolicyMarket.additionalKeys: number — how many extra signing keys were supplied, not which

Preferences.editorCommand: string | null — an id from `appsAvailable().editors`, or 'custom'
Preferences.editorCustom: string | null — the command line to run when `editorCommand` is 'custom'. Split on quotes into argv and handed to the OS unexpanded; there is no shell, so $HOME, pipes and && are literal text. The path being opened is appended as the last argument
Preferences.terminalApp: string | null — an id from `appsAvailable().terminals`, or 'custom'
Preferences.terminalCustom: string | null — as `editorCustom`, with the command line the terminal should run appended as the last argument. The flag that takes it (`-e`, `--`, `/K`) belongs in this string, because it differs per emulator and guessing it wrong opens a terminal running the wrong thing
Preferences.browserCommand: string | null — an id from `appsAvailable().browsers`, or 'custom'. Empty means the system default
Preferences.browserCustom: string | null — as `editorCustom`, with the URL appended last
Preferences.dbClientCustom: string | null — as `editorCustom`, with the connection URI appended last. It has no `dbClient` companion because the client is chosen per service in the endpoint menu rather than stored: which clients are offered depends on the scheme that service speaks
Preferences.tourSeen: bool — whether the introduction has been shown. Absent means "not yet", which is what a fresh install is. It is a preference rather than a session flag because "once" has to survive a restart or it is not once, and Settings can set it back to false: a one-shot screen somebody skipped in their first minute is one they can never get back, which is the failure mode of every welcome flow with a single chance to land
Preferences.note: The whole preferences document, as `default_prefs` writes it. Rust never interprets `appearance`, `appearancePresets` or `favourites` — they are stored and handed back, which is why they have no shape here: giving them one would be this contract claiming to know something the code does not check. `theme` is the legacy top-level key and is carried into `appearance` on read rather than reset, so a user who chose light before the move does not silently lose it. `prefs_set` takes a PATCH, not this: it merges, and a caller that sent the whole document would overwrite keys a newer version of the app added. The four `*Custom` keys are the `Other…` row's half of the app pickers: detection cannot enumerate every editor, terminal and browser there is, and before them somebody running one that is not listed could select nothing at all.

Preflight.note: `detail` is what the machine said — a version, a path, the daemon's own error — and is deliberately not translated. `ready` ignores warnings: mkcert reports `warn` rather than `fail` because a stack without HTTPS still runs, it just serves a browser warning.

Preset.name: string?
Preset.note: `kind` and `version` are what make this a file format rather than "some JSON": `kind` is checked on load so a package.json is refused instead of read as an empty preset, and a `version` above what the app understands is refused rather than half-read — a newer preset may mean something different by a field this version already has, and applying the half we recognise writes a stack that matches neither machine. A service entry has exactly two fields; that is the mechanism by which no secret can be in one. `settings` is limited to DEFAULT_TLD_SUFFIX, SSL_ENABLE, DEFAULT_PHP_VERSION, DEFAULT_NODE_VERSION and DEFAULT_WEBSERVER, and the limit is re-checked on import — trusting the export side alone would let a hand-edited preset write any key it liked into somebody else's .env.

PresetPlan.name: string?
PresetPlan.note: `from` is null when the key is absent from .env entirely, which is different from present-and-empty. `unchanged` exists so "nothing to do" is distinguishable from "everything was rejected" — an empty `changes` list alone is ambiguous between the two, and they need opposite responses from the user. `kind` lets the UI group without parsing the key.

ProfileFile.note: `compressed` is read from the file's magic bytes. The overlay turns Xdebug's compression off, but a file written under somebody else's ini — or before profiling was turned on here — can still be gzipped, and the UI says so rather than the parser failing.

ProfileReport.creator: string
ProfileReport.note: `events` carries the units the file declares — do not assume microseconds. `summary` is the file's own total and is LARGER than `self_total`; the two are reported separately rather than conflated, and `percent` is a share of `self_total` so the column adds to 100. `functionCount` is how many distinct functions the file held before the top-60 cut. Measured on real output: 200,004 blocks aggregated to 5 functions, 10 MB parsed in under a second.

ProfilerStatus.traces: ProfileFile[] — read by profiler_flame, not profiler_read
ProfilerStatus.bytes: number — profiles AND traces; they share a directory and a disk
ProfilerStatus.note: Layered on XdebugStatus rather than duplicating it: the extension has to be compiled in for any mode, so `needsRebuild` and `active` mean exactly what they already meant. `mode` is one value and not a set because the three want different start triggers — stepping connects on the next request, profiling and tracing wait for a trigger so an idle stack does not fill a disk. `trace` is the third: it writes stacks, which is what a flame graph is built from, where a profile writes summed edges. The two lists are separate because they open different views. IMPLEMENTORS: xdebug.output_dir MUST exist before either mode records — Xdebug does not create it and writes nothing, silently, when it is missing.

ProgressEvent.subject: string
ProgressEvent.note: One line of a running process's merged stdout+stderr. Merged deliberately: docker compose writes progress to stderr and results to stdout, and separating them makes the log read out of order.

Project.name: string
Project.note: `manifestValid` is hoisted out of `manifest` so a list view does not have to dig; the findings themselves stay on `manifest.errors`, which is the only place they exist — this type used to declare a `manifest_errors: string[]` beside it that no payload has ever carried. `generatedStale` is measured from the manifest's mtime against the oldest of its generated outputs, NOT accumulated from `manifest:changed` events: the watcher cannot tell whose write it saw, so the app writing a manifest during project_create used to raise a “needs regenerating” badge on a project it went on to generate half a second later. Derived, it is also right on first load, which an event-driven flag never was for an edit made while the app was closed. `git` is null for a directory that was never versioned; `Some` with no `remote` is local history and no upstream, and the two are different answers to where a project came from.

ProjectLogFile.note: A LogFile with the project it belongs to. The id alone does not identify a file across the workspace — every Laravel project has an `app:storage/logs/laravel.log` — so the cross-project surface carries the pair, and app_log_open still takes them separately.

ProjectSpec.note: The create form's payload IS a project manifest. The old POST body used a flat shape (runtime, version, extensions at top level) that ProjectService then reassembled — and reassembled wrongly for node. v1 sends the manifest itself, so there is nothing to reassemble.

Provider.name: string
Provider.pull: string[] — empty when this direction is not offered
Provider.push: string[] — empty when this direction is not offered

ProviderPlan.digest: string — what a consent screen would grant
ProviderPlan.note: `blocked` is ordered cheapest-refusal-first, and the order is what the reader sees: being told to fill in three secrets for a direction an administrator switched off is three pieces of work for nothing.

ProviderSet.plans: ProviderPlan[] — both directions of every recipe
ProviderSet.problems: { provider: string, message: string }[] — recipes that could not be read, named

PushPlan.registry: string? — the host the tag names
PushPlan.authenticated: bool? — whether this registry is in the user's Docker config; null means the answer could not be read, which is NOT “not logged in”
PushPlan.note: An image is pushed only after it has been verified: a registry keeps layers, deleting a tag does not remove what was in it, and on a shared registry somebody has already pulled it. A tag naming no registry is refused too — `docker push myapp:v1` goes to Docker Hub under whichever account is logged in. Credentials are not this app's business: `docker login` is the user's, exactly as ~/.ssh/config is.

QueryEntry.note: `shape` is the statement with the parts that vary between iterations of a loop replaced by placeholders, so `WHERE id = 1` and `WHERE id = 2` are one shape. Two statements formatted differently are two shapes, which is honest: they came from different code.

QueryLogSession.note: `supported` is false rather than an error for anything that keeps no statement log — Redis, RabbitMQ, Memcached. The screen asks every database, and “this kind cannot” must not read as “something broke”. `repeats` holds shapes seen more than three times, most repeated first; three rather than two because two identical queries is a page reading a row and reading it again, and the ones that matter in practice are twenty and two hundred.

QuickCommand.about: string — the English one-liner. The window shows `quickCommands.<id>` from its locale and falls back to this
QuickCommand.because: string (the marker file, the declaring file, or `<service>@<version>` for a package's own)
QuickCommand.declared: bool — the project's own stackvo.json declared it, rather than this app shipping it
QuickCommand.instance: string? — the SERVICE INSTANCE this row runs in. Absent for every other row, which run in the project's own container. Present means a PACKAGE brought this command and it runs in that instance's container and nowhere else
QuickCommand.foreignAbout: bool — `about` is the package author's sentence in the language they wrote it, so the window marks it lang="" rather than claiming its own language for it
QuickCommand.note: `display` is the command as typed, so what runs and what is shown cannot drift. `interactive` decides where it goes — the user's terminal, or the operation console. `id` is the only thing quick_command_run accepts — and it is also the translation key, which is why there is no second name here to keep level. `hint_translations.rs` fails if a row is untranslated in either locale, or if a locale carries one the catalogue no longer offers.

RecipeCard.name: string — the key it is written under, and the locale key `providerRecipes.<name>` translates
RecipeCard.about: string — the English one-liner. The window shows the translation and falls back to this
RecipeCard.edit: { key: string, english: string }[] — what has to be changed before the recipe will work. A pair rather than a sentence because the window is bilingual: `key` is looked up as `providerRecipeEdits.<key>`, `english` is what the CLI, the MCP surface and the log get. Keyed rather than positional because both database recipes need the same instruction, and positions are not names

RelayConfig.note: What `mail_relay_set` accepts. The password is never in here — it goes to the OS keystore through the command's own `password` argument. `from` is the envelope sender: providers reject a From they do not own, and the error comes back from the relay as a number. `allowedRecipients` empty means anywhere, which is Mailpit's own default; it is offered because a development stack that can email any address somebody types is one typo away from a real customer.

RelayStatus.note: RelayConfig as it is stored, plus the two things a caller cannot know from what it sent: whether a password is held (`hasPassword`) and whether the OS keystore is the thing holding it (`keystore`). The same shape `mail_relay_get` returns, which is why `mail_relay_set` returns it — a setter that answered `void` would leave the pane redrawing from what it hoped it wrote.

ReleasePlan.note: `dockerfile` is shown before it is built — plan-then-apply, like the hosts file, the certificate and a preset import. A production image is the one artefact here that leaves the machine, so reviewing it is not optional politeness.

ReleaseResult.verification: { envFiles: string[], xdebugActive: bool?, hasApp: bool, clean: bool }
ReleaseResult.note: Read out of the BUILT image by running it, not inferred from the Dockerfile. `xdebugActive` is null for a node image — there is no PHP to ask, which is not the same as "no". `clean` is all three checks passing.

ReplRun.note: Success is `exit_code == 0`, never "stderr is empty" — a PHP fatal goes to stdout. `limited` false means the in-container limit was not available, so the snippet may still be running in there after this app stopped waiting; the pane says so rather than letting a leak look like a clean stop. Streams are cut at 256 KiB from the FRONT, because a stack trace's useful half is its last lines.

ReplRunner.note: `display` is the command as typed with the snippet left off, so what runs and what is shown cannot drift. `id` is the only thing repl_run accepts. `booted` is the difference between User::count() meaning something and meaning nothing.

ReplSnippet.note: The code, never the output — see repl_history.

RequestExplanation.note: One request, and everything three instruments recorded across it. `queries`, `hotspots` and the lists are capped at 25; `queryCount` and `functions` are the counts BEFORE the cap, so a screen can say what it is not showing. `queriesElsewhere` is the denominator that makes an empty `queries` readable — none in the window out of none recorded is a quiet session, none out of four hundred is a request that asked nothing. `requests` comes from the dumps, which DO carry the request they happened in; where it disagrees with `request` above, two requests were in flight. `builtins` is the profiler's CURRENT setting and describes now rather than the moment of the recording — it is context for the `noDriverFrames` finding and never a claim about this trace.

Service.id: string — the instance id (mysql-8-0) on the market model, the service id before it
Service.enabled: bool — whether it should run, which is not whether it is running
Service.built: bool — a container exists, running or not
Service.url: string? — the whole domain, suffix included
Service.health: string? — 'healthy' | 'unhealthy' | 'starting'; null when the image declares no healthcheck
Service.declaredPorts: DeclaredPort[] — every port the package declares, by handle, with the host number in force; empty before the migration
Service.aliases: string[] — the Docker network names this answers to, its own first; the second is the pre-package alias
Service.eolDate: string? — ISO date upstream support ends or ended
Service.companions: CompanionRow[] — containers shipped with this instance and not separately installable
Service.unmetDependencies: string[] — the subject of every required dependency that is unprovided or stopped

SidecarVolume.name: string — the handle the manifest gave it
SidecarVolume.path: string — where it is mounted inside the container
SidecarVolume.volume: string — what `docker volume ls` calls it

SiteSettings.note: What `site_settings` reads and `site_save` gives back, so the pane redraws from what was stored rather than from what it hoped it wrote. `listingSupported` and `agentAvailable` are about THIS machine and this project's server, not about the settings — a switch that cannot take effect is shown disabled rather than accepted and ignored.

SourceProbe.location: string — exactly what was asked for
SourceProbe.resolved: string — where the bytes were actually fetched from; differs when a GitHub repository URL was translated
SourceProbe.currentSequence: number | null — the cached index's sequence, when there is one
SourceProbe.goesBackwards: boolean — this index is older than the one already here, which market_refresh refuses (T-6, replay)

SpxHotspot.note: One function in a recording. Exclusive is time in its own body, inclusive is it and everything it called. Absolute times are derived from the metadata's own total by share, so they cannot drift from the figure shown beside the recording in the list.

Timeline.note: Oldest first: a timeline read downward is a request read forward. `requests` names the requests the dumps mentioned, in the order they first appear. `queriesRecording` false means the database half is ABSENT rather than empty — without it an unrecorded window and a window with no queries are the same picture.

TimelineMoment.note: `request` is the request id a dump named, null for anything the bridge did not attribute. `shape` is set on query moments only and is the same normalisation QueryEntry.shape uses, so repeats line up across the two. `request` and `job` are the two moments that are STRETCHES rather than instants, and each is placed at its end — the moment its duration and its outcome became knowable; their summary carries both.

UpdaterOffer.note: `detail` is the version for `update`, `{ bucket, percent }` for `waiting`, and the other channel's name for `otherChannel`. `bucket` at the top level is this install's hundredth for the manifest's version — returned so somebody who did not get an update they expected can compute `bucket < percent` themselves rather than guess.

UserRoute.target: string — http:// or https://, origin only
UserRoute.rewrittenFrom: string? — what the user typed, when normalisation changed it
UserRoute.error: string? — set instead of `notes` when the route no longer normalises
UserRoute.note: Traefik routes every project and every catalogue service and nothing else, so a dev server somebody started by hand has no way in. The whole difficulty is one string: `http://localhost:3000` is read INSIDE Traefik's container, where localhost is Traefik — the config loads, the browser gets a 502, and nothing says why. So localhost and 127.0.0.1 are rewritten to host.docker.internal and the screen says so; refusing them would be defensible and useless, because it is the address people have. Checked on the way out rather than stored checked, so a route written today does not keep today's answer after the rule changes.

Workspace.note: root is null when source is 'none'. `source` exists so the UI can say WHY it is pointing at a given checkout — silently guessing wrong would be worse than asking.

Worktree.name: string — the project name, which is also the directory name, and the identity everything else keys off
Worktree.parent: string — the project it was branched from
Worktree.branch: string — the git branch checked out into it
Worktree.domain: string — a subdomain of the parent's, so it stays inside any wildcard route or certificate the parent has
Worktree.path: string — absolute, and recorded rather than derived: the project tree can be moved, and a derived path would send `git worktree remove` somewhere git has never heard of
Worktree.database: { instance: string, name: string, seededFrom?: string } | null
Worktree.env: Record<string,string> — what somebody typed. The database credentials are NOT here; they are derived from the instance on every render
Worktree.note: N. Stored in <root>/worktrees.json, outside every checkout, because the files in a worktree directory are the branch's and this app writes nothing there that git tracks. `seededFrom` is the only record of whether a branch started with a copy of the data or an empty schema, which is the question somebody asks three weeks later.

WorktreePlan.newBranch: bool — whether the branch would be created rather than checked out
WorktreePlan.name: string
WorktreePlan.database: { instance: string, service: string, name: string, seed: bool, source?: string } | null
WorktreePlan.refused: string | null — one sentence naming why it cannot
WorktreePlan.note: Carries what it WOULD have produced even when refused: a dialog that blanks out on refusal makes the reason harder to act on, not easier.

WorktreeRow.exists: bool — is the directory still there
WorktreeRow.dirty: bool | null — uncommitted work a removal would discard. null when git could not answer, which is a third state and not a warning
WorktreeRow.orphaned: bool — the record points somewhere git no longer has a checkout, usually because the folder was deleted by hand

WorktreeSupport.repository: bool — is the project's directory a git repository at all
WorktreeSupport.linked: bool — is it itself a linked worktree, as git sees it. Different from `record`, which means this app made it
WorktreeSupport.effectiveEnv: Record<string,string> | null — what this worktree's container is actually given, present only when `record` is. DB_PASSWORD is masked, and so is the same password inside DATABASE_URL
WorktreeSupport.domain: string | null — what a new worktree's hostname would be built under
WorktreeSupport.currentBranch: string | null — null for a detached head
WorktreeSupport.branches: Array<{ name: string, checkedOut: bool, current: bool }> — newest commit first
WorktreeSupport.instances: DbInstance[] — stopped ones included and marked
WorktreeSupport.reason: string | null — why worktrees are unavailable here

XdebugStatus.note: Three layers, deliberately not collapsed into one boolean. `enabled` is what the manifest asks for; `needsRebuild` is true while the image predates that ask, because extensions are compiled in and a toggle that looked done but changed nothing would be worse than no toggle; `active` is what the running container actually carries, and is null when there is no container to read. `hostPath` and `containerPath` are the two halves of the IDE's path mapping — the mapping is the step people get wrong, and both sides are already known here.

DeclaredComponent.id: string — lower-case letters, digits and dashes; it becomes part of a container name
DeclaredComponent.runtime: string — node, or one of the six LANG_RUNTIMES. php is refused BY NAME with the reason
DeclaredComponent.path: string — the directory in this repository it is built from, always inside the project
DeclaredComponent.domain: string|null — the hostname it answers on; null for a part not meant to be reached from outside
DeclaredComponent.start: string — the command its container runs
DeclaredComponent.port: number — the port it listens on INSIDE its own container; there is no host port
DeclaredComponent.container: string — stackvo-<project>-<id>, what the project’s other containers connect to
DeclaredComponent.note: The third of three declarations that put a container beside a project, and the distinctions are the design: `services` names a NEED satisfied from the catalogue and shared machine-wide; `sidecars` is SOMEBODY ELSE'S IMAGE, project-scoped, not built and not routed; a component is THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN CODE in a subdirectory, built here and routed at its own hostname. Folding any two together would make “how many of these exist” a question with two answers.
